title: 10 Instant Observations From Chiefs' Heartbreaking Week 8 Loss to Broncos
full_text:
Coming off their first loss of the season, the Kansas City Chiefs appeared to make a concerted effort to put forth a more inspiring performance. They managed to do so for most of Sunday against the Denver Broncos, although it wasn't in a winning effort.
Head coach Andy Reid's crew seemed to be in control for a good chunk of Week 8, only to fall short down the stretch and suffer a crushing defeat to a bitter rival.
With the 28-24 loss, the Chiefs fall to 5-2 on the year. Let's jump into 10 instant observations and takeaways from Week 8.
Blocking isn't the most head-turning element of the game, particularly for a skill-position player, but it should be discussed more. Especially for a team that operates in 12-personnel (one running back, two tight ends) with frequency, it's an important part of an offense. Travis Kelce, at age 37, being far and away the superior blocker between him and Noah Gray is an issue.
Gray's poor blocking chops showed up giaringly in the first half on two occasions — once in the run game and once in pass protection. Some of his shortcomings could be chalked up to a smaller and lighter frame , but his angles and leverage are oftentimes poor as well. This is a nitpick for someone who otherwise made an impact on Sunday, but it's long overdue to be mentioned.
Kansas City simultaneously flashed a much-improved offense over Week 7's production while also having a variety of rough moments that reminded everyone of why there's a long way to go. On one hand, quarterback Patrick Mahomes had a staggering 195 passing yards and two touchdowns. On the flip side, the Chiefs averaged only 3.5 yards per rush attempt and only kept the ball on the ground eight times.
Add in a 1-for-5 conversion clip on third down and there being three-and-outs on three separate occasions, and you get a more complete picture. This is a group that still needs to establish more consistency in play-calling decisions, execution, timing and more, but the first half of Week 8 was a step in the right direction. Not even a few dead drives in half No. 1 can take away from that.
Ending up with double-digit penalties for triple-digit yardage is inexcusable. Sure, one ticky-tacky holding call on right guard Trey Smith made up part of that total, but that doesn't explain the rest of the bunch from Sunday.
Some infractions were more procedural in nature, such as a false start on Kelce, an illegal formation charged to left tackle Kahlil Benson and an ineligible man downfield flag on right tackle Jaylon Moore. Others, though, were worse and simply cannot be repeated. Linebacker Jack Cochrane and safety Alohi Gilman each had unnecessary roughness penalties in Week 8, making life harder than necessary for the defense.
Some special teams issues and a rough outing for cornerback Kristian Fulton didn't help matters one bit. Moore's false start on a fourth-and-goal at the end of the game was the not-so-sweet icing on the cake.
Last week, I wrote a bit about defensive end Ashton Gillotte as someone whose stock is on the rise . Truthfully, it's easy to forget that he sustained a plantar fascia injury during training camp and started the 2026-27 campaign at a slow pace. He's ramped that up in a big way in recent weeks, however, and this game was no different.
Gillotte had a good run stop on Denver's opening drive, made a quality read on its second possession and also chipped in on a double-effort run stop in the second quarter that wasn't credited in the box score. The sophomore man continues to prove that he's a starting-caliber player, which is great for the Kansas City defensive line.
One thing that All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones made a name for himself for early in his career was tipping passes at the line of scrimmage. When defensive end George Karlaftis entered the league in 2022, his water polo background was brought up on broadcasts seemingly every week. That history continues to pay off years later, evidenced by two pass breakups in the second frame on Sunday.
Rookie pass rusher R Mason Thomas also had a batted pass on the Broncos' third drive. Defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga notched one in the third quarter to help cap off his solid day at the office. This is clearly something defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo and defensive line coach Joe Cullen emphasize, which pays off.
For weeks, plenty of folks who follow the Chiefs (this writer included) have wondered when rookie running back Emmett Johnson 's breakout would occur. It was only a matter of time before he found a way to make an impact, and he had a multitude of signature moments over the course of Sunday afternoon and evening to make his presence known in a huge way.
Starting with the supporting elements of his game, the Nebraska product had an amazing 15-yard run that looked reminiscent of many from starter Kenneth Walker III. On special teams, he had a 44-yard kickoff return late in the fourth quarter that helped put the offense in a great starting position. It was Johnson's output in the receiving game, though, that made a huge difference.
The first-year man was excellent out of the backfield, taking a beautiful pass from Mahomes to the house for 73 yards and also adding a 38-yarder near halftime. In the fourth frame, he recorded a third-and-2 reception to move the chains as well. If there was ever a week for Johnson to establish himself as a viable option down the stretch, it was this one.
THE ROOKIE EMMETT JOHNSON WITH A 73-YARD TD KCvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/sGCPC0rJYU
Rookie wideout Cyrus Allen got some more run in this one and even had a nice eight-yard reception on an out route in the third quarter. A clutch third-and-12 snag also provided a glimpse of the possible chain-moving, reliable threat he can become if he realizes his potential.
With that said, the Cincinnati alum seemed to slow up early on a deep pass from Mahomes. Perhaps Allen just didn't think the ball was coming his way and was too late to realize it was, but it was a rough look either way. A play like that could've given him a totally different stat line and earned him some good graces with Mahomes and the coaching staff, so it's undoubtedly a missed opportunity.
When the Chiefs brought in kicker Justin Tucker on the practice squad this week, it sent a clear message that starter Harrison Butker was on thin ice with the organization. Reid shot down high-level concerns regarding the longtime franchise favorite following Week 7's loss, but it might be time to push the conversation forward even more.
Sure, some rain made Butker's 54-yard field goal in the fourth quarter more difficult, but he's paid handsomely to make these kicks under pressure. That miss swung momentum to Denver's favor and things quickly devolved from there, so part of this loss falls squarely on the veteran placekicker's shoulders. His seat has to be warming up even more.
There's plenty of blame to go around in this one. The aforementioned penalties were a killer at various points in the contest, and Reid did himself and his team very few favors with how he managed the fourth quarter.
disaster 4th quarter from the Chiefs they didn't go for this, but asked Harrison Butker to hit a 54 yard FG on the next series https://t.co/w27sbvGdBR
You can lump in the defense's poor — and rapidly poor — response to the Butker miss into the pile, too. For a team that's led by vets both on the paying surface and on the sideline, this one stings. It's easily one of the more prominent and obvious collapses of the Reid-Mahomes era.
Don't get it twisted: Kansas City isn't doomed in the division race by any stretch of the imagination. That said, failing to maintain the head-to-head tiebreaker over a hot Broncos team is suboptimal. Rising to 4-0 in the AFC West and creating more padding to kick off the month of November would've been massive for a team that's now floundering just a bit.

title: Complete Chiefs Inactives for Week 8 vs. Broncos: Mansoor Delane and Others Out on Sunday
full_text:
For the fourth time in seven games, the Kansas City Chiefs are clashing with an AFC West rival on the gridiron. Sunday features a Week 8 matchup with the Denver Broncos , marking the second and final instance of the two sides seeing one another in the regular season.
Just like they did in Week 1's 31-10 drubbing of Denver in Week 1, injuries play a role in how this one unfolds. Kansas City is down a top starter on the defensive side of the ball, with Denver also missing a key secondary piece in addition to placing a promising young player on injured reserve.
With that in mind, here's who's inactive for Kansas City and Denver in Sunday's matchup.
Our inactives for today's Week 8 matchup against the Denver Broncos ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/YGrIHpkCKr
Earlier in the week , Kansas City deemed cornerbacks L'Jarius Sneed and Mansoor Delane questionable while also tagging edge rusher R Mason Thomas with the same designation. On Saturday, however, the team announced that Sneed was going on the injured reserve list with a knee issue and Delane was downgraded to out.
Thomas, who traveled separately after attending to a personal matter, is in Denver and will be active for Sunday's game.
Although he doesn't appear on the inactives list, defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott was ruled out after being a limited participant in practice this week. The sophomore lineman was designated to return from the physically unable to perform list on Wednesday, marking a huge step in his ongoing recovery from a torn ACL.
The good news is receiver Rashee Rice is back in the lineup after not having played since Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders. The star wideout, who's nursed a hamstring injury , has 13 receptions for 190 yards and a touchdown in four games this year.
👀 our inactives for #KCvsDEN . 📰 » https://t.co/NPfgwIa5vk pic.twitter.com/4c24nidQc3
The Broncos' injury situation is less than ideal, to say the least. All three, on top of safety Brandon Jones, were limited participants in practice to end the week.

title: Los Angeles Chargers Have a Real Chance to Be First 0-17 Team in NFL History
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are seven games into the 2026 season, and the conversation has already shifted from playoff expectations to a much uglier possibility.
After opening the year 0-7, the Bolts are staring at a situation nobody expected when the season began. They are not just trying to find their first win anymore. They are trying to avoid becoming the first team in NFL history to finish a 17-game season without winning once.
That is an unbelievable place for a team led by Jim Harbaugh to be in. Harbaugh was brought in to change the direction of this franchise, and there was a reason people believed the Chargers could be a serious team.
The offense has been a major concern . It is difficult to win consistently when a team is producing very little, and it becomes almost impossible when the offense cannot give the defense much room for error. Justin Herbert is the face of this team, but they need far more around him if they are going to change the direction of this season. Better play from the franchise quarterback would be nice as well.
The history makes this situation more interesting. The NFL has seen teams finish 0-16, with the Detroit Lions doing it in 2008 and the Cleveland Browns following in 2017. But neither team had to play 17 regular-season games. The league moved to a 17-game schedule in 2021, and no team has finished 0-17 since that change.
The last time the Bolts were this bad was over 25 years ago. LA Times columnist Mirjam Swanson noted that “They played like a team ready to accept another defeat and fell to 0-7 for the first time since 2000, when Harbaugh was their quarterback.”
The Chargers still have 10 games left, which means there is time to turn things around. Their remaining schedule includes matchups against the Texans, Ravens, Jets, Patriots, Buccaneers, Raiders, 49ers, Dolphins, Chiefs and Broncos. There are games in that group where the Bolts  should have a chance to compete, but that does not mean anything is guaranteed. At this point, even getting one win has become something this team has to prove it can do.
The problem is that the Chargers cannot keep treating every loss like an isolated bad afternoon. Seven games have produced the same result, and the offense has shown very little consistency. The team needs to find answers quickly, because the longer this continues, the more pressure builds on the coaching staff, the players and everyone involved in the organization. Could they become the first 0-17 team in NFL history? It is too early to say that is where this season is headed, but it is no longer an outrageous question. They are 0-7, they are scoring fewer points than anyone else, and there is not much evidence right now that things are about to change.
They do not need to start thinking about history just yet. They need to start thinking about winning a football game.
The #Chargers are set to be 0-7 for the third time in franchise history. A breakdown: 2026 Los Angeles Chargers Final record — ? 2000 San Diego Chargers Final record — 1-15 1975 San Diego Chargers Final record — 2-12 pic.twitter.com/SnOQ2Rc6Me

title: 3 Players Chargers Should Call About Before Trade Deadline to Keep Justin Herbert Alive
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are in the midst of a season collapse at 0-7 and with still little signs of life on offense. Chargers President of Foootball Operations and member of ownership John Spanos should greenlight general manager Joe Hortiz to begin looking to the future and trade assets that can bring back future draft capital.
The Chargers really have no business being buyers at the trade deadline. However, if they are building for the future and trying to protect franchise quarterback Justin Herbert and preserve his health and sanity, they could make a few minor moves with other teams who may be inclined to move a player or two before the deadline.
The Chargers offense has not been effective at all this season and it appears the run blocking from the entire team with the exception of the tackles has taken a nosedive off of a cliff and hit every rock on the way to bottom. The lack of run blocking and inefficiency in the run game has caused problems for the offense.
Los Angeles lost starting fullback Alec Ingold and replacement Scott Matlock struggled out of the bye week against the Rams. Cole Strange has been the worst guard on the entire team for most of the season, his blocking grades bare that out. The Chargers have rotated essentially every other offensive lineman on the roster at left guard and have yet to find the answer.
Let's dive in to a few names who could be low-cost options that the Chargers could target as a means to solve a short term problem but also with eyes to the future.
I have brought up Kieft before as a potential target and I just can't quit the idea of adding him to the offense. Kieft saw his snap counts drop to rookie tight end Bauer Sharp after suffering an elbow injury and Sharp has kept the job locked down. Kieft will be a free agent in 2027 and a move could be beneficial for his career and the Chargers could absolutely use him.
If the Chargers deploy a fullback in 2027 and beyond it might be worth to get one in the building before free agency to make a better judgement meanwhile protecting Justin Herbert. For some reason, the fullback position has been tasked with going one on one with edge rushers far too often in 2026, if this continues to be a trend, an upgrade could help keep Herbert upright.
Kieft has been able to handle defensive lineman one on one throughout his career and punishes defenders when used as a lead blocker. The Buccaneers have already found Kieft's replacement and the cost should be a simple flip of late round picks to bring a competent blocker into the building for the Chargers.
This trade target isn't about Justin Herbert and the offense. The Chargers are running out of corners and have been dialing up reclamation projects to fill out their depth. Kelee Ringo has not been a factor on defense this year for the Eagles, playing primarily special teams. The Chargers need special teams depth and cornerback depth this year and beyond.
Current Chargers special teams cornerback Deane Leonard has been dealing with a laundry list of injuries and is on an expiring contract. Ringo is a physical defensive back with plenty of traits to work with. His floor as a special teams player is worth looking into to help maintain the special teams rebound the Chargers are currently undertaking. Ringo's expiring contract and usage on the field should make for another late-round pick swap possible. If he works out, he could easily factor into the plans as cornerback and special teams depth going forward.
Capable depth offensive linemen do not usually get traded during the season. However, Rams backup interior offensive lineman Justin Dedich who can play all three spots has been languishing on injured reserve as the Rams roster has been completely full and they are choosing to use injured reserve activations on other players.
Dedich played an important role for the Rams last season but an injury suffered over the summer kept him out of training camp. The Chargers could use depth in the interior with experience. The true conundrum in this situation is the Chargers themselves are running out of IR activations. Players on injured reserve have been eligible to be traded since 2018 and the receiving team assumes the injury risk.
If the Chargers choose not to activate any of their own offensive lineman from injured reserve they could swing a late Day 3 pick swap with the Rams for a lineman who has been critical for them in the past but has been trapped on injured reserve this season.

title: Would Chargers Trade Tuli Tuipulotu to Desperate 49ers, Cowboys at NFL Deadline?
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers will sell at the NFL trade deadline.
That feels like an obvious fact. Yet the way the Chargers have worked the trade phones so far, reports say other NFL teams are confused about how general manager Joe Hortiz and the club in Los Angeles have moved so far.
At 0-7 and counting, that should change. Justin Herbert trade packages probably won’t surface, or matter if they do. But guys like Khalil Mack, Donte Jackson and others could probably be had for the right price (and they owe it to Mack to send him to a contender if he wants).
There’s also the matter of Tuli Tuipulotu. It shouldn’t be a thing for the Chargers. But it just might be.
…if they want to move him.
Yes, it sounds ridiculous. The Chargers roster Tuipulotu, who has 29 sacks in 57 games and is just 24 years old. Why would they trade him away?
Well, for one, as The Athletic's Daniel Popper noted while listing Tuipulotu as the No. 2 overall trade candidate, big spenders like the San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys would likely have interest.
“Tuipulotu took a big step as a player in 2025,” Popper wrote. “He has sustained that performance this season. Since the start of 2025, Tuipulotu ranks 12th in pressure rate among players with at least 250 pass-rush snaps.”
Tuipulotu is on the final year of his rookie contract and the team and player couldn't agree to an extension this past summer.
Two, there’s also the matter of this being the Chargers . Fans just watched the team trade for Odafe Oweh last year, get a breakout from him, then refuse to re-sign him despite approaching free agency with nearly $100 million in cap space. So they burned the trade asset for a half-season rental, then drafted Akheem Mesidor because he’s an “older” rookie while trying to replace Oweh’s production.
Which is to say, the Chargers don’t always make sense. And who knows? Maybe the Tuipulotu contract extension talks were worse than outsiders know. He’s going to come close to resetting the market. The Chargers still have roughly $26 million in free cap space right now but didn’t get something done.
One would think that Tuipulotu is a big building block and a nice one-two punch with Mesidor no matter what happens to the team and coaching staff next offseason. But the Chargers are in this hole in the first place because they don’t act like a normal, modern NFL franchise all the time.
So…don’t count out a good offer from a team like the 49ers or Cowboys suddenly causing some chaos over the next week before the deadline.

title: Chargers, Justin Herbert Trade Ideas Must Now Keep Jeffery Simmons, Bears Lessons in Mind
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers aren't going to trade Justin Herbert, but similar things were said before other NFL trade deadline blockbusters over the last week or so.
Sure, the Chargers are much more likely to trade Khalil Mack . No doubt the Chargers are getting calls from NFL teams around the league, even if those teams are leaving the phone calls more confused than anything else.
From an outsider’s view, the Chargers are much more likely to blow up the entire program before trading away Herbert. That means head coach Jim Harbaugh, offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel and even general manager Joe Hortiz, for starters.
But…these things were said before a different mega-trade happened last week, too.
Teams like the Minnesota Vikings could use a big swing for a star quarterback right now.
And teams like the Tennessee Titans and Chicago Bears have shown that, sometimes, all it takes is the right offer to actually be put on the table.
That’s a point raised by Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer this week, who fielded questions about a Herbert trade and pointed out that the Titans never actually moved star defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons until another team actually made the right offer.
“It can’t hurt to make that phone call if you’re the Vikings,” Breer said. “Do I think Joe Hortiz is going to say ‘no way, we can’t trade a franchise quarterback,’ yeah, I think he’s going to say no way.”
Point is, all of this is just smoke and talk until a team actually puts a major offer on the table. Teams aren’t likely doing that for Herbert, so it’s all moot.
Breer added this: “I will just say this about Justin Herbert. I don’t think a lot of what’s happened this year is on him. I think if you go back to last year and you talk to people around the league, a lot of people felt he was playing at an MVP level in a near-impossible situation…it reminds me of the way people talked about Matthew Stafford in Detroit.”
Chargers fans are probably tired of hearing about the Herbert-Matthew Stafford comparison. But with how they keep blowing things up around him and failing to build back up properly around him again and again, it’s not an unfair one to make right now.
As things stand, the Chargers remain focused on trying to make sure Herbert becomes and stays a top-10 player within their franchise, not somewhere else.
But the reality hurts: The Chargers failed at roster building this offseason while bringing on Mike McDaniel. The combo has produced the worst play of Herbert’s career. They’re beelining toward another rebuild and blowing things up around Herbert again.
Herbert’s no-trade clause in his contract notwithstanding, what really happens if a team like the Vikings slaps three or more first-round picks on the table, officially? Do the Chargers make like the Titans with Simmons and jump, or stand still some more?
That’s the problem for the Chargers: There’s no easy answer when it comes to trades, or even what to really do with Harbaugh and his entire staff. Staying the course is just as risky as blowing everything up again.
Either way, Herbert’s name isn’t going to leave trade speculation discussions, even after the upcoming trade deadline, considering the Chargers’ season is already effectively over.

title: Obvious Khalil Mack, Bears Trade is a Formality for Chargers at This Point
full_text:
By far the best thing the Los Angeles Chargers have accomplished this season is their efforts to convince everyone that they won’t be blowing things up or selling anything at the NFL trade deadline.
Little on the field by the Chargers has qualified for the “best” qualifier, so that’s all they really have left.
It’s time for the Chargers to trade Khalil Mack .
The Chargers have even confused other NFL teams with their unwillingness to talk shop so far. But they just hit 0-7 out of the bye, turning in their worst offensive performance of the season so far, which should get Mike McDaniel fired in organizations that make any sense.
A Mack trade is a close second at this point.
This isn't about the Chargers getting quality future assets. It’s about doing right by Khalil Mack.
After all, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport has made it pretty clear that the Chicago Bears would be interested in the idea of a reunion with Mack.
Mack himself, at least, is trying to keep things civil and professional before the likely move.
“You’ve got to be where your feet are man, ultimately,” Mack said, according to Eric Williams of Fox Sports. “That can be the most difficult thing when you’re dealing with a lot of outside noise and stuff. Just trying to be where your feet are at all time. That’s kind of been my thing in years past.”
Good on Mack, but where this is going is obvious. He had pondered retirement before agreeing to another one-year deal with the Chargers last offseason. If this is it, going out with this version of the Chargers would be unfortunate.
Mack is still playing great ball, too, hence the interest from contenders. Across 71 percent of the defense’s snaps, he’s ranked 23rd out of 110 EDGEs in total grade at PFF. He’s tallied 16 pressures, three sacks and five tackles for loss.
Mack’s expiring contract and the obvious lack of any leverage the Chargers hold in trade talks is going to be pretty appealing to contenders, too.
Sometimes the right move is the obvious one. The Chargers don’t seem to understand that fully yet. But once they do, letting Mack reunite with the Bears is a no-brainer, as is selling off almost anything else other teams might want before possibly blowing up the coaching staff next offseason.

title: Chargers Veteran Speaks Out About Growing Trade Speculation Following Sunday's Loss
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are finding themselves in a difficult position as the NFL season continues. Following Sunday’s loss to the Los Angeles Rams, veteran linebacker Khalil Mack addressed the growing speculation surrounding his future.
Per Eric Willaims of Fox Sports , Mack stated “That can be the most difficult thing when you’re dealing with a lot of outside noise and stuff. Just trying to be where your feet are at all times. That’s kind of been my thing in years past.”
Mack is certainly a name that could generate attention around the league. However, the Chargers seem to be at the point where they do not want anything to do with trading players whatsoever.
Despite the outside discussion, Mack’s comments following Sunday’s game showed where his attention currently remains.
With trade speculation continuing to circulate, the veteran defender addressed the situation without allowing the conversation about his future to become the main focus. That approach is understandable for a player who has spent years dealing with the expectations that come with being one of the league’s established defensive veterans. Situations like this are part of the business, particularly around this time of the season.
The timing makes the situation interesting. The organization has to evaluate where its season is heading and whether keeping its current roster together makes the most sense. Staring at a winless record is what makes this all very complicated. Those decisions become even more important when the deadline is approaching and other teams are looking for opportunities to improve.
Pro Football Talk and NBC Sports writer Josh Alper also noted that Khalil Mack is “playing on a one-year deal and has the kind of history of success as a pass rusher that could be appealing to a number of teams”
Mack’s experience also makes him an important part of the conversation. Players with his background do not come around often by any means. So losing a veteran presence can have an impact beyond what shows up on the stat sheet. At the same time, the Chargers have to consider what makes the most sense for the organization moving forward. There is still plenty that can happen before the deadline arrives, and his future remains something worth monitoring. Sunday’s loss only added fuel to the fire, but the veteran linebacker has made it clear that the outside noise is not going to take his attention away from the game.
Whether he finishes the season in a Chargers uniform or becomes part of a larger deadline decision remains to be seen.
Khalil Mack on trade rumors: “You’ve got to be where your feet are man, ultimately. That can be the most difficult thing when you’re dealing with a lot of outside noise and stuff. Just trying to be where your feet are at all time. That’s kind of been my thing in years past.”

title: NFL Trade Deadline Rumors Heating Up: Chargers Collapse Creates Firestorm of Demand
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are now staring down the barrel of a lost season and now face the tough decision of what to do with their tradeable assets. The Chargers were hoping to emerge from their week seven bye with reinforcements , improvements and solutions for their struggling offense. Unfortunately, their week eight loss and offensive showing against the Rams showed that the offense, along with quarterback Justin Herbert are simply still broken.
The Chargers bewildered the rest of the NFL by attempting to hold off on trading any of their potential trade assets heading into their week seven bye despite already being 0-6. Now, after dropping to 0-7 and showing minimal signs of life, the trade deadline looms even larger as calls for a sell off grow louder.
The Chargers have several players on the roster who are on the table to be potentially traded. As the deadline looms and the NFL schedule continues, injuries mount around the league and demand for current Chargers may increase. Let's dive into the Chargers who could be targets around the NFL.
The Chargers veteran edge rusher Khalil Mack has been and continues to be the most common name floated as a trade target. The Chicago Bears are the destination that has always made sense for Mack but their blockbuster trade for Jeffery Simmons complicates their available draft capital.
The Chargers appear finally ready to consider moving Mack based on his dwindling snap counts against the Rams. The future Hall of Fame edge rusher has earned the right to play for a contender in what could be his final season if not one of his final seasons. The Chargers front office should partner with him to find the ideal landing spot. Their unwillingness to discuss trade options may have narrowed the potential trade partners for Mack but he should find a new home soon.
The Chargers 2026 offense has not been successful and one of the key offseason additions, running back Keaton Mitchell, has not found success but neither has the Chargers rushing attack. Omarion Hampton and Kimani Vidal have led the snap counts for the rushing attack for the third week in a row.
As running backs go down around the NFL, teams in search of a change of pace back could find value  in bringing in Mitchell. Mitchell's contract also jumps in value in 2027 but his contract does have an out this offseason and based on 2026, the Chargers would be unlikely to give Mitchell a $3 million raise.
The Chargers have depth in the linebacker room and any one of their linebackers on expiring deals could be on the move. If the Chargers do not see Los Angeles native Daiyan Henley in their future plans, they could explore moving on from him. Attrition at the linebacker position is a regular occurrence in a NFL season and multiple linebackers have been injured across the NFL.
The Detroit Lions just saw their star linebacker Jack Campbell experience a terrifying injury in week eight. The Lions may need a starting-level rental and Henley could be a good fit in Detroit,
Defensive line is one of the key positions for contenders heading into the back half of the season for a playoff push. Dalvin Tomlinson came to the Chargers to fill a veteran role and has lived up to the billing. Tomlinson could fill a similar role for a contender as injuries mount around the NFL.
The Jacksonville Jaguars appear to heading for a playoff push and just suffered a devastating loss along their defensive line when DaVon Hamilton suffered a season-ending knee injury in week eight. The Jaguars were already rumored to be looking into adding defensive line depth before the injury, now it is all but certain.
The Chargers have very thin depth in the cornerback room but they have been getting surprise performances from their youngest players. Week eight was somewhat of a coming out party for second year player Isas Waxter, who was just signed to the active roster from the practice squad and he played well against the Rams.
Los Angeles has also added depth to the practice squad with former first round pick Kair Elam and on Monday following week eight, signed former Titans starter Jayln Armour-Davis to the practice squad. It is unclear if and when Jackson will be healthy but he is a capable veteran zone cover corner who could play reliable snaps for a contender in need down the stretch of the season. The Lions are also in need of defensive back help and could make sense for Jackson.

title: Mike McDaniel’s Firing Can’t Happen Soon Enough For Chargers
full_text:
With Justin Herbert looking lost and the season even more lost at 0-7, the Los Angeles Chargers need to fire offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel.
Things are so bad for the Chargers that reporters are starting to ask about benching Justin Herbert , for lack of a better term (“sitting” isn’t much nicer).
Foolishness to even consider it, of course. But that’s how rough things have become for the NFL’s obviously worst team.
There are arguments against letting McDaniel go right now. One of those is that it wouldn’t accomplish all that much. Ripping up the plan and giving Herbert yet another coordinator change isn’t the best idea. There aren’t great backup options, either, not with Adam Gase and Shane Day as so-so stand-ins.
And yet, something has to give. And it’s McDaniel.
There are levels to the firing-a-coordinator midseason thing.
Herbert is playing the worst ball of his career. He’s not just getting whispers of a benching, but there is a pretty common thought making the rounds that he might need a full reset.
Not just a coaching staff. A trade to an entirely new organization.
That falls on McDaniel. The Ringer’s Sheil Kapadia pointed out that the Chargers just had one of the five worst EPA/drive performances of the season. Not only that, it was the Chargers’ worst performance of the season outright.
After the bye, the Chargers got worse .
Now layer the other stuff on top. The rumblings about McDaniel holding an “all-hands” meeting after the bye was topped off with a report that the inspirational film he showed the unit was…from a joint practice session with the San Francisco 49ers over the summer.
Putting it all in context, things are ugly. We can bemoan the injury bug and how the loss of Tyler Biadasz was a domino effect. But if a supposedly elite offensive mind like McDaniel’s entire scheme falls apart to this extent because of one injury, there are bigger problems.
McDaniel appears to be attempting to run his offense while pretending he has speedier players than what the Chargers have on the roster. Promising younger players like first-round back Omarion Hampton (3.5 yards power carry) and tight end Oronde Gadsden (17 catches in seven games) have dramatically regressed. Free-agent adds on the line like Cole Strange have flopped.
Realistically, the Chargers need to reboot the entire coaching staff after the season. Another coaching change for Herbert stinks, but the alternatives aren’t pretty.
Showing McDaniel the door now, at least, would bump the chances of getting back to basics and helping Herbert through…whatever it is he’s going through at this point. That could set the foundation for a bigger rebuild in the offseason around him, at least.

title: The Morning-After Thunder: Chargers Drop to 0-7, Herbert Looks Broken, Offense Worse
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have dropped to 0-7 for the first time since the 2000 season and for the third time in franchise history. Los Angeles emerged from their week seven bye week with some limited reinforcements returning to the field and somehow the offense looked exactly the same if not worse.
It is no secret that the Chargers season has not gone according to plan in 2026. No one, even the most cynical, would have imagined the Chargers offense being worst in the NFL and the Chargers winless by week eight. That is the reality Los Angeles in living in right now.
The offense has struggled to find their footing but it was assumed with Ladd McConkey and Tre' Harris coming back from injury following a bye week, the offense would show some improvements. The offense did find some inconsistent success but could not find the endzone and finished the day with their worst EPA per drive on the season.
Three of the 5 worst offensive performances all season (EPA/Drive) happened today: Chargers, Colts, and Falcons. The Chargers offense somehow got worse during the bye. This was their worst game all year based on EPA. Their 2nd-worst game was against the Chiefs before the bye.
Franchise quarterback Justin Herbert did show flashes of his former self in the contest but he firmly threw multiple turnover worthy passes including two horrific interceptions right to defenders. It is clear Herbert is not seeing the field well and has lost confidence in what he is seeing.
Los Angeles' pass catchers had a much better day overall with their core starters back on the field but the run game was a complete shell of the lofty expectations they entered the season with. The root cause of the failures of the run game seems more rooted in the play calling than the players themselves.
The Rams seemed to have a beat on what the Chargers were planning in the run game and this was made easier by the obvious running back rotations. For Omarion Hampton, seven of his nine carries were to the inside and of Kimani Vidal's eight carries only three were to the inside. It was fairly predictable where the ball was going when certain personnel was on the field.
PFF grades for offensive line play need to be taken with a grain of salt, however it is safe to use this week's grades a baseline for the run game. The Chargers have good run-blocking tackles. Joe Alt and Travis Burke continued to show that this week and both are positively graded as run blockers. However, the interior of the offensive line continues to be a problem.
The Chargers interior offensive line finished with preliminary run-blocking grades of 54.7 for Jake Slaughter, 51.3 for Logan Taylor and 49.1 for Cole Strange. The Chargers have played seven games and unfortunately their highest-graded interior run blocker on the season is Trevor Penning with a 64.8 overall, a score which does include some reps for him as an extra offensive lineman. Penning is currently the 46th-ranked interior offensive lineman as a run blocker in the NFL among linemen who have played at least 20 percent of the run-blocking snaps.
The Chargers offense is lost, head coach Jim Harbaugh continues to make ridiculous use of time outs and challenges, the interior offensive line can't run block and the Chargers defense continues to go to a war while being put in terrible field positions to defend by the offense. The Chargers have tried to hold out and push back on trade propositions but it is time for President of Football operations John Spanos to give general manager Joe Hortiz the greenlight to build for 2027 and 2028.

title: Rams May Have Answer to Return Game Struggles in Preseason Standout
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams released punt returner and wide receiver Alex Bachman on Tuesday, leaving a need at the position. Since making the move, there has been a lot of uncertainty about who will take over the role.
Releasing Bachman was certainly needed as it was time for the Rams to raise the bar from “just catch the punt.” Bachman averaged 5.2 yards per punt return and 22.9 yards per kick return. Bachman offered more reliability than Xavier Smith, but it still wasn’t good enough.
While Konata Mumpfield is listed as the backup punt returner, it’s unlikely that he’ll take that role. Some have brought up Tutu Atwell, but that’s not something that he’s done throughout his career. Atwell returned 10 punts as a rookie in 2021 before getting hurt and then returned just four punts in three years at Louisville.
It’s certainly possible that the Rams could look into trading for Josh Downs or even Chimere Dike if he’s available. At the same time, Downs may cost draft capital that the Rams don’t want to part with and Dike hasn’t offered a lot as a receiver in his career.
Before the Rams make a move, they will likely move forward with players already in the building. One who makes the most sense is wide receiver Brennan Presley.
Presley was signed as an undrafted free agent last year and has had impressive moments in the preseason . Presley had 14 receptions for 125 yards in the preseason with a touchdown this year. During the 2025 preseason, Presley’s 164 receiving yards ranked fourth.
What a catch from Brennan Presley in the endzone! 🤲 📺 @CBSLosAngeles | 📲 https://t.co/R5m5kJYWYi pic.twitter.com/8zZMy6r9Sa
However, where the Rams will likely utilize Presley is on special teams as a returner. At Oklahoma State, he earned second-team All-Big 12 honors as a kick returner in 2021 and was twice named the Big 12 Special Teams Player of the Week. In 2024, he became the only Power Conference player to record at least 760 receiving yards, 200 kickoff return yards, and 50 rushing yards in a season.
In five years at Oklahoma State , Presley returned 51 punts and 61 kickoffs. However, most of his impact was felt as a returner on kickoffs. His 100-yard kickoff return against Oklahoma in 2021 helped lead the Cowboys to a 37-33 win.
We got Brennan Presley just chillen on the practice squad btw pic.twitter.com/N25BAk2dcr
Presley has had limited return opportunities in the preseason with the Rams. During the 2025 preseason, he had a 38-yard return on a kickoff and then averaged 29.5 yards per kickoff return during the preseason this year. As a punt returner, Presley has just two punt returns the last two years, averaging 5.5 yards per return. It is worth noting that Presley had seven muffed punts at Oklahoma State.
While Presley hasn’t been on the active roster, he has spent the last two years on the practice squad. As the Rams continue to look to improve their special teams, Presley might be exactly what they need. The Rams are currently averaging just 23.5 yards per kickoff return, which ranks 29th in the NFL. While it’s been better over the last four weeks, there is still room for improvement.
The Rams have spent much of the season trying to find answers on special teams. After adding Joshua Karty to help the kickoff coverage last week, they are focusing on the return game this week. Releasing Bachman was another step in working to improve in that facet. Presley’s upside is certainly intriguing, and his experience and speed make him an option worth exploring. His performance in the preseason has at least earned him that opportunity.

title: Myles Garrett's Return to Practice Could Change Everything for Rams
full_text:
For much of the season, the Los Angeles Rams have been waiting to reap the rewards of the big trade they made this offseason when they acquired edge rusher Myles Garrett. After managing knee swelling in training camp and then not playing at 100 percent in Week 1, Garrett has been on injured reserve since. However, Garrett is finally set to return to practice this week .
To be clear, that doesn’t necessarily mean that Garrett will play on Sunday against the Washington Commanders, but it’s also the first good news that the Rams have gotten on him in two months. With that said, NFL Media’s Ian Rapoport reported that when Garrett gets on the field for practice, it should all happen quickly, leaving this week in play.
“I want to be careful to even set any sort of expectations. I think taking it a day at a time is going to be the best way that we can approach it,” said head coach Sean McVay on Monday. “That's the right thing for him and to see how he responds. I think it's a real positive that we're starting his clock.”
This is the moment that the Rams have been waiting for. During the offseason, Aaron Donald came out of retirement in large part because he wanted to play alongside Garrett. Those two have yet to play a snap together as Donald didn’t make the trip in Week 1 and Garrett was placed on injured reserve ahead of Week 2.
Through the first eight weeks of the season, the Rams have been managing injuries to key players, Garrett being the first among them. The Rams have simply been trying to get by as they begin to get healthy and that is finally starting to happen.
Overall, the Rams’ depth has done well, all things considered. Josaiah Stewart was only expected to be a rotational player and has played 67.3 percent of the defensive snaps this season. Wesley Bailey was signed to the roster as an undrafted free agent and has played 30 percent of the defensive snaps, becoming a key part of the pass rush rotation.
Both players have two sacks on the year and Bailey forced a fumble last week against the los Angeles Chargers. However, Stewart’s 11.6 percent pressure rate ranks 70th out of 116 edge rushers. Bailey’s 8.5 percent pressure rate ranks 99th. Stewart and Bailey rank 61st and 78th in pass rush win rate.
The Rams have lacked consistent pressure off of the edge, and Garrett will certainly provide a huge boost to the defense and pass rush in that aspect if he’s healthy. While Jared Verse doesn’t have a sack this season for the Cleveland Browns, it’s fair to wonder what impact a healthy Verse could have had on the Rams’ defense.
Without Garrett, the Rams currently rank 21st in pressure rate, compared to second last year and 14th in 2024. The Rams were ninth in sack rate last year and 19th in 2024 and have dropped down to 27th this season. That’s despite going from the least-blitzing team to 16th. Chris Shula’s blitz rate has increased by nearly 10 percent to help the defense generate pressure on the quarterback.
Shula’s increased blitz rate has been a positive while Garrett has been out, and it will be interesting to see if that continues or if the defense goes back to what it has been the last few years when they’ve been comfortable getting pressure with four.
The Rams traded for Garrett in the offseason with the hope that he could take their defense and pass rush to the next level. Without Garrett, the Rams’ defense ranks sixth in EPA per play and their -0.15 EPA per pass ranks fourth. Garrett will be entering an already good situation without the pressure of having to do everything himself.
Still, this is what the Rams have been waiting for. The Super Bowl team that the Rams built this offseason is finally starting to come together as it gets healthy. They’ll still await the return of Davante Adams, Kobie Turner, and Terrance Ferguson, but having Garrett back in the lineup is a huge first step.
Without Garrett, the Rams have shown that they can play at a high level defensively. However, the Rams traded for Garrett so that the defense could take over games in JanuaryIf he returns healthy and can provide the consistent pressure that the Rams have been missing, this defense could become one of the NFL's most dangerous as they fight for a playoff spot. The Rams can finally start to look like the team they envisioned during the offseason. With Garrett set to return to practice, the Rams are one step closer to seeing that all come together.

title: Sean McVay Hints at Bigger Role for Rams Rookie CJ Daniels
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams have not played many of their rookies this season. Their first-round pick has been the emergency quarterback every week and Keagen Trost is a key depth player on the offensive line, but was only just taken off of injured reserve in Week 6. Undrafted free agent Wesley Bailey has been the team’s most productive rookie.
It’s no surprise that the Rams have brought their rookies along slowly. That’s typically how the Rams have handled rookies under Sean McVay outside of a few exceptions. With that said, if last week showed anything, it’s that the rookies may be ready to contribute.
Against the Los Angeles Chargers, the Rams were without tight end Colby Parkinson. While the offense started with 11 personnel, they adjusted to more 13 personnel in the second half, which meant more snaps for Max Klare . Klare finished the game with 25 snaps, 20 of which came after halftime.
For the first 7.5 games, the Rams had deemed Klare not ready. However, Klare was the 12th-best run-blocking tight end in Week 8 and showed that he should have gotten snaps earlier.
With some of the Rams’ issues at wide receiver, it’s fair to wonder whether CJ Daniels is next to see an opportunity. Daniels was a standout in training camp and the preseason. However, he had been inactive for the first six weeks and has played just five snaps combined on offense over the last two games.
Still, on Monday, head coach Sean McVay hinted that Daniels could see more opportunities. “There's a guy in CJ Daniels  that's really done a hell of a job that you're going to see get more opportunities moving forward,” McVay said.
Daniels would fit exactly what the Rams need at wide receiver with Davante Adams out. It’s unrealistic to expect him to replace Adams or solve all of the Rams’ problems in the passing game. However, it could be worth giving him a run in the offense, especially if the Rams don't plan on trading for a wide receiver .
As the game progressed, you really saw Ty Simpson start to get comfortable. With be interested if Rams let him off the reigns a little bit next week. Tight coverage on CJ Daniels and Simpson throws an accurate ball. pic.twitter.com/ZPOUISGzac
He has more size than Konata Mumpfield and Tutu Atwell and can play that “X” wide receiver role. Unlike Atwell, Daniels can win over the middle, and unlike Mumpfield, he provides a bigger target outside the numbers.
Those are things that Daniels showed throughout the offseason and then carried that into the preseason. Daniels had 0.36 targets per route run in the preseason, ranking 15th among wide receivers. He also used his size as he was credited with contested catches on three opportunities.
CJ Daniels with a very nice win on the deep out despite the CB aligning in off cov with outside leverage. Stetson Bennett with some excellent anticipation also. pic.twitter.com/FMk5qnYmiK
The Rams have had problems with their wide receiver depth, and it’s time for them to try something else. Mumpfield is averaging -0.32 EPA per target and has a targeted success rate of 38.1 percent. It simply has not been good enough at that spot.
At some point, the Rams need to find out whether Daniels can translate what he showed throughout the offseason into regular-season success. While they may have waited too long to get Klare involved when the opportunity came up, they shouldn’t make the same mistake with Daniels. The Rams have struggled to find consistent production from their depth receivers, and Daniels brings a different skill set to the offense. If Daniels can prove to be a reliable contributor,it would go a long way toward improving the passing game.

title: Rams Release Alex Bachman as Special Teams Overhaul Continues
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams have made another change on special teams as they head into Week 9. On Tuesday, the Rams released wide receiver and kickoff/punt returner Alex Bachman. Over the past several weeks, the Rams have been working to make improvements to their special teams unit, and Bachman being released is the latest indication of that.
Earlier this season, the Rams turned to Bachman after they released wide receiver Xavier Smith from the same role. While Bachman fielded punts without issue, he didn’t offer much as a returner. Among players with at least five punt returns this season, Bachman averaged just 5.2 yards per return, which ranked 31st. At some point, the Rams needed to raise the bar from ‘just fielding punts’. Bachman averaged just 22.9 yards per kick return, ranking 62nd out of 75 qualifying returners.
Despite not giving up a long punt or kick return, the Rams lost 3.6 in special teams EPA on Sunday against the Chargers. Bachman gained zero yards on a punt return in which there looked to be space to head upfield.
Alex Bachman gained 0 yards on this play, and the ball is in his hands in this screenshot. How? pic.twitter.com/QYDnMGkvYq
It’s unclear where the Rams turn to next at returner. Jordan Whittington was the only other listed kick returner alongside Bachman, and the Rams just placed running back Dean Connors on injured reserve. At punt returner, Konata Mumpfield was technically the backup to Bachman. However, it wouldn’t be surprising to see the Rams make a move this week for a returner.
Given the struggles on special teams this season, the Rams have made a conscious effort to improve. Last week, they signed Joshua Karty to help on kickoffs and also brought in Jon Rhattigan, who is a special teams player. Despite those changes, the Rams still lost 3.6 in special teams EPA without giving up a long return or missing any field goals last week.
Special Teams EPA through Week 8 pic.twitter.com/jkmVWblN8Z
In a corresponding move to releasing Bachman, the Rams signed cornerback Cam Lampkin from the practice squad to the active roster. After releasing Nyzier Fourqurean last week , the Rams have signed him back to the practice squad as well. The Rams also released linebacker Garrett Nelson from the practice squad.
Head coach Sean McVay has made it clear that the Rams aren’t satisfied with their special teams unit. The Rams have spent much of the season trying to find answers on special teams, and releasing Bachman is the latest attempt to raise the standard.

title: The Case For and Against the Rams' Top NFL Trade Deadline Targets
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is just a week away and there are several names that have been connected to the Los Angeles Rams. It’s still unclear whether the Rams will opt to make a move , and there are positives and negatives to each player they could consider. Let’s break down some top potential targets and make a case for why each would be a fit and why the Rams shouldn’t trade for them.
The Case For: There is no doubt that the Rams need help at wide receiver and Josh Downs would be a great fit . While he may not be the “X” that the Rams need with Davante Adams out, he would fit in perfectly alongside Adams and Puka Nacua. The Rams need a reliable target with speed and someone who can create underneath and find the soft spot in zones.Downs is a great separator, ranking fourth in first downs per route run on third and fourth down last season. His skillset is similar to Jamison Crowder, who had success in Sean McVay’s offense.
The Case Against: While Downs had a strong first and second season, he only had 566 yards last year and has 30 receptions for 330 yards this year. His size makes him less valuable as a blocker, which McVay does ask of his wide receivers. Despite having an opportunity, Downs has never been more than a WR3 in the Colts’ offense.
The Case For: Thomas is a former first-round pick and had over 1,200 yards as a rookie with 10 touchdowns. With Adams out, Thomas would slot right into the “X” receiver role and then would provide a bigger vertical threat once Adams does return. The Rams would have multiple years of team control remaining, including the ability to exercise his fifth-year option. He’d be someone the Rams could build the wide receiver room around alongside Nacua over the next few seasons.
The Case Against: While Thomas had over 1,200 yards as a rookie, he has just 824 yards since. He’s completely fallen out of favor and has struggled to get comfortable in a Liam Coen offense that is very similar to McVay’s. Thomas has struggled with drops and has had a low targeted success rate over the last two years. It’s possible that Thomas just needs a change of scenery, but the Rams might not be the right fit.
The Case For: It wouldn’t be a bad idea for the Rams to make a move for a nose tackle. Poona Ford is out for the season and the impact of his loss will be felt in the run game. Stewart would give the Rams exactly what they are missing without Ford: a run-stopping nose tackle in the middle of the defensive line.
The Case Against: Stewart would certainly fit a need, but the cost may simply be too high. A team would need to take on $6.7 million in salary to trade for Stewart. As it stands, the Rams only have $8,000 in cap space. They have some flexibility to open up some money, but $6.7 million would be a lot.
The Case For: There is no doubt that the Rams need special teams help and Chimere Dike is one of the best returners in the NFL. Dike is averaging 12.5 yards per punt return, which ranks 17th in the NFL. For reference, Alex Bachman averaged 5.2 yards per punt return. Dike kills two birds with one stone, adding wide receiver depth and providing a threat as a returner.
The Case Against: While Dike got more involved in the Tennessee Titans’ offense last week, he hasn’t provided much as a wide receiver consistently in his career. He had 423 yards total as a rookie and has just 124 yards this season. This isn’t like the Seattle Seahawks trading for Rashid Shaheed last year. If Dike offered more as a receiver, a trade could make sense. However, the Rams can’t afford to give up draft capital for strictly a returner.
The case For: The Rams have struggled getting to the quarterback this season. Their pass rush currently ranks 21st in pressure rate and 27th in sack rate. Josaiah Stewart hasn’t stepped up in the way that some expected and Wesley Bailey is still growing. Mack is a more experienced player and still had a 12.7 percent pressure rate this season, which is higher than Stewart and Bailey.
The Case Against: Mack would be an improvement over Stewart and Bailey, but once Myles Garrett returns from injury, he would be a rotational player. The Rams need a more productive pass rush, but it’s unlikely that Mack is the missing piece.

title: Sean McVay's Latest Comments Raise Questions About Rams' Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
Throughout the Les Snead and Sean McVay era, the Los Angeles Rams have typically been aggressive at the trade deadline . When the Rams won the Super Bowl in 2021, they traded for Von Miller who played an important role in the playoffs. Back in 2018, the Rams traded for Dante Fowler Jr. Even when the Rams haven’t necessarily been competitive, they’ve remained aggressive, trading for players like Jalen Ramsey and Austin Corbett.
However, last year, with Matthew Stafford playing at an MVP level and a clear need at cornerback, the Rams’ only move was trading for Roger McCreary. At the end of the year, the Rams fell in the NFC Championship game because they allowed Sam Darnold to throw for 346 passing yards and three touchdowns without an interception.
While the Rams don’t have as strong of a record this year as they did at this time in 2025, they are still a team pushing for a Super Bowl. An argument can be made that the Rams’ big trade additions came in the offseason in the form of Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie. With that said, this is still a roster with a glaring need.
Much like last year when it was widely known that the Rams had a need at cornerback, the same can be said about wide receiver this year . The Rams are currently without Davante Adams, who is dealing with a hamstring injury. Even when Adams comes back, there is always the risk of re-injury for a player who has dealt with hamstring injuries the last two years.
Additionally, Nacua has dealt with injuries all year. He missed two games with a groin/hip injury and recently managed an issue with his calf. The Rams are one Puka Nacua injury away from their top wide receiver being Konata Mumpfield. That was very nearly the case against the Las Vegas Raiders when Nacua’s calf injury popped up.
This season, Mumpfield is averaging -0.32 EPA per target with a 38.1 percent success rate. Jordan Whittington is averaging -0.43 EPA per target with a 25 percent success rate. While Atwell has stepped up at times in the past, he remains limited in what he can do because of his size.
The last thing the Rams should want is their season coming down to Stafford needing to target Mumpfield with the game on the line as he did last year. That’s not a situation the Rams should want to relive.
1- 3rd & 4 Witherspoon stays attached to Mumpfield, who Stafford is forced to go to after Ernest Jones takes inside leverage on Puka Nacua. Witherspoon's agility + tenacity show up late as he knocks down the pass with 5:06 left. #Seahawks pic.twitter.com/PtwdNFAMpe
Much like last year with cornerback, the need for a wide receiver is evident. It’s been that way since the draft. That’s not to say that the Rams made the wrong decision drafting Ty Simpson instead of a WR3. If Simpson works out and becomes a franchise quarterback, that was the right call. Where a conversation does start is in the second round when the Rams took a TE5. There were opportunities to sign a veteran ahead of training camp. However, the Rams have done nothing to address the need. CJ Daniels could become a solid role player as a sixth-round pick. It still seems unrealistic to expect him to solve the issue at the position.
Despite the wide receiver trade market heating up and options seemingly available, the Rams appear content with who is on the roster.
“What you look at is hopefully some of those trades will be guys getting back from injury that haven't played for us. That's the way that we look at it,” said McVay. “Like I've told you in years past, you always think about it, but with the amount of guys that have not been available that are key and focal points for really both sides of the football, we look at those guys hopefully being able to return within a month. That's where that value lies for us.”
It is true that the Rams are set to get players back. Myles Garrett and Terrance Ferguson could return to practice this week. Kobie Turner and Davante Adams will likely return within the next 6-8 weeks as well. Those players returning from injury will certainly provide a boost to the roster. Many in the media have called the Rams a “super team,” but the core of that super team has yet to play a single snap together.
However, the mindset that simply getting players back from injury is the equivalent of making a move at the trade deadline is not it in what is supposed to be an “all-in” season.
“The way we look at it is Myles Garrett, Terrence Ferguson, Davante Adams, Kobie Turner, those guys that you're expecting to be able to get back. Colby’s been in and out of the lineup, which is a huge deal for us,” McVay said on Monday. “I would never rule anything out, but it would have to make sense. There are sometimes you have to really ask yourself what kind of resources are you willing to give up? Where do you really have needs? I think at a lot of the spots that we would probably identify where there are maybe some things we can improve upon, it's more of we're getting guys back that we think can make big impacts that are on our roster that aren't necessarily eliminated for the rest of the season.”
While the Rams may not have a first- or third-round pick in 2027, that doesn’t mean there still aren’t moves that could be made. ESPN’s Benjamin Solak recently proposed a trade for wide receiver Josh Downs. In that proposal, the Rams would get Downs and a 2027 fifth-round pick for a 2028 third-round pick. On the cusp of a Super Bowl, that’s a move the Rams should make 10 out of 10 times.
It’s very possible that McVay isn’t being completely transparent publicly about the team’s intentions at the trade deadline. At the same time, Drew Brees noted on the broadcast during Sunday’s game that the Rams saw guys returning from injury as midseason additions. Brees may have been told that during the weekly team production meetings.
This isn’t a Rams team that necessarily needs to make a blockbuster move to improve the roster. However, as teams around the NFC make moves, the Rams need to be able to keep up. There’s a big difference in simply getting players back who were already part of the plan and adding a player who can address a weakness that has existed since the summer.
There is a lot riding on this season as the Rams look to capitalize on the final years of Stafford’s career. With several core players set to hit free agency this offseason, there is too much at stake for the Rams to just stand pat and wait for players to get healthy. The Rams don’t need to mortgage the future further at the trade deadline, but if an opportunity exists to add a player who can help them compete for a Super Bowl, it’s not something they can overlook.

title: Matthew Stafford's Arm Soreness Raises Serious Concerns for Rams
full_text:
Injuries have become somewhat of a theme for the Los Angeles Rams in 2026. However, despite injuries to some of their best players, the Rams have found ways to overcome them. The Rams have been without Myles Garrett since Week 1 and have managed injuries to Trent McDuffie, Davante Adams, and many others. However, just as the Rams seemed to be getting healthy, quarterback Matthew Stafford was seen leaving the locker room with a bag of ice wrapped to his right arm.
Rams QB Matthew Stafford left the locker room yesterday with a bag of ice wrapped to his right arm. Sean McVay said he's dealt with some soreness in the arm, but deferred to Stafford on how he's feeling
Through eight weeks of an NFL season, players are bound to have the typical wear and tear. However, seeing Stafford with ice around his throwing arm is certainly cause for concern and makes this a situation worth monitoring.
Head coach Sean McVay was asked about Stafford having ice around his arm, but didn’t provide any information. McVay simply played dumb as if he wasn’t aware of the situation.
“He's had some soreness there,” said McVay. “I think he'd be better equipped once you guys talk to him to answer that. I can't attest to stuff that I'm not necessarily aware of.”
This wouldn’t be the first time that Stafford has had elbow soreness. In 2022, Stafford dealt with elbow soreness. The Rams played the situation off as something not to be concerned about, but McVay said after the season , “People forget how big of a deal that was.”
The elbow injury clearly limited Stafford in 2022 and it’s something that the Rams have tried to manage over the last couple of years. During OTAs and training camp, Stafford only practiced on certain days.
Coming off of an MVP season, Stafford hasn’t necessarily had the start to the year that some expected. While there was bound to be some regression, Stafford hasn’t been consistent or as sharp as many are accustomed to.
Stafford’s 0.08 EPA per pass and 92.6 quarterback rating both rank 15th. He’s thrown eight interceptions this season, already matching his total from last year.
At times, Stafford has missed throws that he hasn’t missed in the past . The Rams’ passing game has also become less explosive as Stafford hasn’t pushed the ball downfield as often. Stafford has an average depth of target of 7.89 yards, ranking 16th. While that number is close to what it was in 2023 and 2024, over the last four weeks, Stafford has an ADOT of 5.5, ranking 25th out of 27 quarterbacks.
It has now been announced that Matthew Stafford has been dealing with Right elbow discomfort, which could certainly explain the low aDOT. Compensation from his prior back injury? Possibly some rotator cuff weakness leading to elbow overuse? Big impact on the Rams season if he… https://t.co/eJBfEs9GFx
More concerning, however, has been Stafford’s intended air yards per pass attempt. Over the last four weeks, Stafford’s intended air yards per pass attempt has been under 6.0 and has averaged 5.23. In the previous four weeks, he averaged 9.5. Stafford has had four straight games averaging under six intended air yards per pass attempt. He had only done that four times total from Week 2 of the 2024 season to Week 4 of this year.
Two of Stafford’s 10 lowest single-game averages in intended air yards per attempt have come this season. Three others came in 2022 when Stafford also dealt with elbow soreness.
Adding to that, two of Stafford’s 10 lowest single-game averages in completed air yards per pass attempt have come in the last two weeks. Stafford averaged 2.2 completed air yards per pass attempt against the Chargers and 2.1 against the Raiders.  Again, Stafford has averaged under 3.0 completed air yards per pass attempt in each of the last three games. That happened three times total from Week 17 of 2024 to Week 5 of this year.
Matthew Stafford's average depth of throw is down to 5.4 yards this past month. A bit nervous about his health. The offense is turning Aaron Rodgers-y. Related: Puka's aDOT is 3.4 yards in the two games without Davante Adams. pic.twitter.com/AlPWk5Dazf
It’s going to take more than elbow soreness to keep Stafford out of a game. Stafford is widely regarded as one of the toughest quarterbacks in the NFL. Despite Stafford being seen icing his elbow, it’s unlikely that he shows up on the injury report or misses practice.
This isn’t to say that Stafford having elbow soreness is a good thing, but it may force the Rams and McVay to lean more into the run game and become more balanced on offense . Stafford threw 50 or more passes in three consecutive games this season, which could have led to his elbow flaring up. Those three games rank among the five highest single-game passing attempt totals of Stafford’s career.
It’s certainly possible that Stafford’s elbow soreness and recent decline are unrelated. Regression was going to happen. However, Stafford being seen icing his elbow in combination with his recent drop in pushing the ball downfield certainly raises some red flags. Comparing the situation to 2022, it’s fair to wonder if there’s more to the situation than the Rams are letting on. The similarities to 2022 are enough to warrant concern, even if the severity of the injury remains unknown.

title: One Sean McVay Adjustment Changed Everything for Rams in Win Over Chargers
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams beat the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 8, and it was the tale of two halves , to say the least.In the first half against the Chargers, the Rams reverted to how they operated against the Eagles, relying heavily on 11 personnel. It wasn’t until Stafford hit Tutu Atwell for 40 yards in the two-minute drill that the offense finally got a first down.
Up until the final drive of the first half, Matthew Stafford had just 20 yards passing on six completions and the offense had just seven yards on four rushing attempts. The McVay offense accomplished something that not even the Jeff Fisher offenses did. No Rams offense this century had gone three-and-out on their first five offensive possessions.
Heading into Sunday, the Rams were forced to change their offense. Without Colby Parkinson, they were left with just three healthy tight ends on the roster, one of which was rookie Max Klare who had played just one career snap on offense before Week 8.
When the Rams were in a similar situation in Week 4 against the Philadelphia Eagles, they got back to 11 personnel. In Weeks 1-3, the Rams had operated out of 11 personnel at just a 56 percent rate, ranking 19th in the NFL. Against the Eagles, that was up to 88 percent, which was the second-highest rate for the week.
The Rams spent the offseason building an offense for 13 personnel. It’s partially why they drafted Max Klare. This is how the Rams want to operate moving forward and what they want their identity to look like.
In the first half against the Chargers, the Rams went back to how they operated against the Eagles, going back to 11 personnel. They started the game operating out of 11 personnel at a 75 percent rate. However, instead of Davante Adams getting a majority of the snaps across from Nacua, it was a mix of Tutu Atwell and Konata Mumpfield.
The Rams simply don’t have the personnel to operate out of 11 personnel like they used to. A big reason why the Rams became an 11 personnel team was because they couldn’t justify keeping one of Brandin Cooks, Robert Woods, and Cooper Kupp off the field. Additionally, Woods and Kupp were effective as blockers, eliminating the need for multiple tight ends.
However, with Adams out, it’s hard to justify having Mumpfield and Atwell on the field for a majority of the snaps. Neither are effective blockers, and because of that, the run game also struggles. That brings up an overall larger issue of the Rams needing a third wide receiver. For the time being, the Rams have to work with what they have.
To start the game, the Rams were trying to fit a square peg in a round hole and force something that they weren’t built to be. They averaged -0.43 EPA per pass out of 11 personnel in the first half with just a 46.2 percent success rate. The run game also equally struggled. They averaged -0.52 EPA per rush with a zero percent success rate trying to run out of 11 personnel. Granted, it was a small sample size of two carries for three yards, but the Rams were unable to get any sort of rhythm on offense because of it.
While McVay and the coaching staff may not have deemed Klare ready , he was certainly thrown into the fire in the second half. Klare had just five offensive snaps in the first half, compared to 20 in the second half. Out of Klare’s 25 snaps, 20 of them were him being used as a run-blocker. Among qualifying tight ends, Klare finished the week as the 12th-best run-blocking tight end, according to Pro Football Focus.
The Rams got back to their 13 personnel identity in the second half, and it worked. It opened up the entire offense. After using 13 personnel at a 20 percent rate in the first half, that was up to 63.6 percent in the second half. The Rams had 17 carries for 79 yards out of 13 personnel after halftime. They averaged 0.02 EPA per rush and had a 47.1 percent rushing success rate. That doesn’t mention the 0.65 EPA per rush and 75 percent rushing success rate out of 12 personnel.
Being able to run out of 12 and 13 personnel opened up the passing game in 11 personnel. Stafford was 5-for-7 for 52 yards when throwing out of 11 personnel in the second half. He averaged 0.2 EPA per pass and had a 57.1 passing success rate.
Again, the Rams spent the entire offseason building their offense around multi-tight end sets. It shouldn’t be a surprise when leaning into that ended up being a success and the turning point in the game.
As shown in Week 7 against the Raiders, if the Rams can get the run game going, the entire offensive playbook opens up. The Rams had 24 carries for 122 yards out of 12 and 13 personnel. They had just three carries for seven yards out of 11 personnel.
Moving forward, the Rams will certainly hope to avoid situations where they're forced to become something they're not. Ideally, Parkinson is healthy and the Rams should get Terrance Ferguson back very shortly, if not this week.
At some point, the Rams may need to utilized 11 personnel again. The Rams are clearly more efficentive in 13 personnel than they are in 11 personnel. With that said, 13 personnel is great in neutral and positive game scripts. When the Rams are forced into a negative game script, they may need to lean into 11 personnel more than they would like.
However, in neutral game-scripts, the Rams are a much better offense when they stick to what they’re supposed to be. The Rams are averaging 0.07 EPA per play in 13 personnel compared to 0.01 EPA per play out of 11 personnel. The Rams have been significantly more efficient with three tight ends on the field compared to three wide receivers.
The Rams have now shown in consecutive weeks what their offense is capable of when the running game becomes the focal point. While the initial offensive gameplan against the Chargers may not have worked, McVay deserves credit for recognizing what wasn't working and making the necessary adjustments. The decision to move away from 11 personnel and use Klare in 13 personnel allowed the Rams to take control in the second half and come out with a win.
