title: Miami Dolphins Week 8 Instant Takeaways: Second-Half Collapse Costs Potential Signature Win
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins really had a shot at getting their first signature win of the Jeff Hafley era, they really did.
But if it hadn't already been established, the game served as a reminder this is a team that's operating with a very small margin for error, and there were a few too many of those in the second half, along with a controversial officiating reversal that changed the momentum.
Truth to be told, this was an encouraging performance by the Dolphins in the big picture, even if they did let one slip away after leading 13-3 at halftime after completely shutting down an injury-riddled New England offense.
The Dolphins are making progress, that's what's important here. And, yes, they did make progress and still look much improved from the team they were in the early weeks of the regular season.
Dolphins fans no doubt will lament the replay official overturning the Dolphins' fourth-down stop when they were leading 13-10 in the third quarter, instead giving New England a first down that kept alive what became the touchdown drive that gave them the lead for good.
But it wasn't the only play that swung the tide.
Ollie Gordon II got flagged for an unnecessary and, frankly, stupid unsportsmanlike conduct for yapping at an opponent to turn a third-and-5 into a third-and-20 in that forgettable third quarter. Then Zane Gonzalez, elevated from the practice squad for a second consecutive week, badly missed a 43-yard field goal attempt to basically put the Dolphins in a position where there only shot was to recover an onside kick, which basically never happens in the NFL anymore.
Beyond that, New England simply was the better team in the second half when they outscored the Dolphins 21-6, though the Dolphins again were plucky and fought to the end, as we figure they'll do all season even if the wins aren't that frequent.
-- It figured that Gordon would have a tougher time against the Patriots, particularly with Kadyn Proctor missing the game with his concussion, and that's how it played out. And we wouldn't fret over his ability to have other big games.
-- While we don't necessarily complain about play-calling, there was a pretty obvious lack of urgency in the fourth quarter when the Dolphins were down two scores and still running the ball, and often letting the play clock run down.
-- This isn't their identity, but this was a game where the Dolphins needed to air it out in the fourth quarter, not be calling running plays on second-and-12.
-- Malik Willis was fine, even though his performance wasn't as good as it was against the New York Jets. He certainly wasn't the reason the Dolphins lost.
-- Guard Jonah Savaiinaea has no doubt made significant improvement in his second season, but there's still some lapses that show up in his game.
-- Jarrett Kingston did a respectable job in place of rookie Kadyn Proctor, though he had to overcome a shaky start.
-- On the flip side, Austin Jackson had one of his best performances of the season.
-- The defense hardly could have played better in the first half and it seemed as though everybody chipped in.
-- What hurt more than anything in the second half were the two big plays, the two long touchdown passes that accounted for almost half of Drake Maye's passing yardage.
-- Props to Jacob Rodriguez for creating a turnover with a perfect Peanut punch, though he overall had a pretty quiet game.
-- The pass defense continues to get shredded, with Maye completing 80 percent of his passes. The coverage on DeMario Douglas' 43-yard touchdown was particularly depressing as he caught a pass wide open between defenders and had so much space that he could zigzag the rest of the way to the end zone.
-- Chris Johnson is normally a very good tackler, which is why it was so baffling to see whatever that was that he attempted against Maye when he came in free from behind for what should have been a sack. He should have had redemption later on that drive with a fourth-down stop, but of course there came the overrule from the replay assistant when television replays didn't suggest anything obvious enough to overturn the original ruling.
-- That play was just yet another example why instant replay stinks.
-- Yes, Willie Gay Jr. looked kind of bad on Maye's rushing touchdown off an option play, but the reality is he was one defender against two offensive players. There didn't appear to be anybody outside to handle the pitch had he zeroed in on Maye, so he was kind of in an impossible position there.
-- The special teams again had a rough outing, but missed field goals will happen and long punt returns allowed unfortunately have become commonplace. What's unforgivable is Jaylen Wright fielding a kickoff near the sideline instead of putting himself out of bounds before touching the ball, which would have created a penalty on the Patriots and given Miami the ball at its 40. Those are fundamentals the Dolphins simply have to recognize.
-- Guess we could blame it, like everything else, on Miami being a young team. But those are the kind of mistakes we want to see disappear sooner rather than later.
-- In the final analysis, though, this was a frustrating loss because the Dolphins put themselves in position for the big upset and weren't able to deliver. The first part alone, though, was a sign of progress.

title: Examining the Outside Factors That Could Impact the Dolphins' Week 8 Game Against New England
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' Week 8 matchup against the New England Patriots won't be lacking for storylines, including Miami's quest for a second consecutive victory, but there are some that go beyond X's and O's.
The Dolphins will go into the game following their breakthrough 28-25 victory against the New York Jets to face the defending AFC champion Patriots, who have a 4-3 record following a Thursday night loss against the Chicago Bears in Week 7.
The Patriots will go into the game missing star wide receiver A.J. Brown and backup running back TreVeyon Henderson, while the Dolphins will be without rookie first-round pick Kadyn Proctor with star running back De'Von Achane on injured reserve.
New England will enter the game as a 7.5-point favorite, according to the FanDuel Sportsbook, but if you believe in the idea that weather can be an equalizing factor, then the weather in Miami Gardens on Sunday should be considered.
It was raining in Miami Gardens on Sunday night, but the forecast called for the weather to actually get worse — if not much worse — throughout the afternoon and into the night.
The outlook as of 10 a.m., according to Weather.com, read as follows: "Storms likely for the next several hours. Potential for heavy rainfall."
There also is a flood watch in several areas of the northern parts of Dade County, where Miami Gardens is located.
With the expectations of thunderstorms, we also can't help but look back to the Dolphins' 2018 season opener against the Tennessee Titans when two lightning delays lasting more than an hour each made the game last more than seven hours.
And obviously the field conditions could become a factor at some point with the ball getting slippery and footing also potentially becoming an issue.
The other outside factor in the Dolphins-Patriots game that needs to be watched, even though it hopefully won't affect the outcome one way or the other, was the officiating crew switch late in the week.
The officiating around the NFL has come under a lot of scrutiny this season, but it may have reached a high point (or low point maybe?) in the Green Bay Packers game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field last week, leading to Packers safety Xavier McKinney lashing out publicly after the game.
McKinney drew a fine from the NFL for using the term for bovine excrement in talking about the officiating, but he wasn't the only one complaining.
Ton Brady openly criticized at least one call for roughing the passer during the game, but the most egregious call came for an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty when Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown got up after catching a pass, a Packers defender tackled him thinking the play wasn't over but knocked down an official in the process, with the official responding by throwing a flag while on his back.
Likely as the result of not wanting the spotlight on the officiating crew of Alex Moore, the NFL took them off their scheduled assignment for the Sunday night game between Philadelphia and Washington and moved them to the Dolphins-Patriots game, which will be shown to a ridiculously small portion of the country as the "other" 4:25 p.m. on CBS opposite Kansas City at Denver.
Moore's crew, for the record, officiated the Dolphins' home opener against the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 3, calling eight penalties on each team. Moore also worked the Dolphins-Patriots game at Hard Rock Stadium in Week 2 of 2025.

title: Breaking Down the Dolphins Saturday Updates, but More Importantly What Went On with New England
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins made their customary practice squad elevations Saturday, including that should precipitate an upcoming move, but it was what went on with the England Patriots that really was newsworthy.
For the second consecutive week, the Dolphins elevated both kicker Zane Gonzalez and edge defender Max Llewellyn.
Gonzalez was a given considering the Dolphins don't have a kicker on the 53-man roster and it was his second such promotion. After one more elevation, the Dolphins then will have to sign him to the active roster and find themselves a new kicker. And for those wondering, there's no financial or cap incentive to just elevate kickers from the practice squad because that move entails the elevated player getting the prorated active roster salary for that week, along with the accompanying cap hit.
Llewellyn, for his part, actually will be out of practice squad elevations after this week because along with the Week 7 game against the New York Jets, he also was elevated in Week 2 for the game against the San Francisco 49ers.
Llewellyn could put himself in line for a permanent promotion with a strong outing against the Patriots on Sunday. The Dolphins already had five healthy edge defenders for the New England game with Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Malik Herring, Rodney McGraw and newcomer Jamree Kromah, but the latter just joined the team late in the week and it's almost a given to be inactive.
The big news with the Patriots came earlier Saturday afternoon when the team announced that both wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back TreVeyon Henderson had been downgraded to out after both being listed as questionable Friday.
To replace them, the Patriots signed running back Lan Larison from their practice squad to their 53-man roster and elevated wide receiver Ryan Miller from their practice squad. Yes, that's the same Ryan Miller who played four games for the Dolphins this season and has the team's longest offensive play of 2026 with his 77-yard touchdown reception from Malik Willis toward the end of the Week 2 loss against the San Francisco 49ers.
Brown and Henderson being out is big news for the New England offense, which already has wide receivers Romeo Doubs and former Dolphins player Mack Hollins on injured reserve. With those two out, the biggest threats for the Miami defense, besides obviously QB Drake Maye, will be running back Rhamondre Stevenson and tight end Hunter Henry.
New England's top three wide receivers for Sunday will be Kyle Williams, Efton Chism III and DeMario Douglas. Corey Kiner will become the second running back option after Stevenson.

title: The Chris Grier Firing One Year Later: Revisiting the Former Dolphins GM's Hits and Misses
full_text:
Halloween arrived Saturday, but for the Miami Dolphins it also marked the one-year anniversary of the firing of Chris Grier as general manager, a move that was met with almost universal approval from the team's frustrated fans.
His eventual replacement, Jon-Eric Sullivan, has on the flip side won over a lot of folks with his early moves in a massive rebuilding project that was almost necessary because of previous mistakes by his predecessors and the other decision-makers in the organization.
While Sullivan's draft class has the looks at this time of a slam-dunk winner with the early contributions of Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, Caleb Douglas and Michael Taaffe, though it probably will take some time to offer an accurate verdict, and the same goes for the most involving the veterans (though, again, the Jaylen Waddle trade looks a winner at this time).
Grier's firing came on the morning of October 31, 2025, hours after the Dolphins dropped a 28-6 Thursday night decision against the Baltimore Ravens at Hard Rock Stadium.
Sullivan was hired as GM in January after Champ Kelly finished out the 2025 season as interim GM, making one trade during his time.
That was the move to send Jaelan Phillips to the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for a third-round pick, a decision that was sound at the time and even more so now after the huge contract Phillips got in the offseason from the Carolina Panthers as an unrestricted free agent.
Grier had taken over that role in 2016 after more than a decade with the organization, though in many ways he assumed true GM duties in 2019 after the Dolphins moved on from Executive Vice President of Football Operations Mike Tannenbaum.
The Dolphins failed to win a playoff game during Grier's time as GM, extending a drought that began in Grier's first year with the team in 2000.
Along the way, Grier oversaw a series of personnel decisions that did lead the Dolphins to the playoffs three times, including his first year in 2016, but also came up way short considering all the financial commitments the Dolphins made.
In breaking down the Dolphins' personnel decisions, we should point out that the organization always went out of its way to talk about a collaborative approach but as GM the hits and misses should fall on Grier more than anybody else.
And, without question, it's in the draft where Grier had most of his misses.
-- The Dolphins whiffed on too many early draft picks over the past decade, a trend that started with first-round pick Charles Harris in 2017 and continued with Noah Igbinoghene in 2020, Liam Eichenberg in 2021, Channing Tindall in 2022 and Cam Smith in 2023.
-- The Dolphins also missed out on some big-time talent, which happens to every franchise but seemed to happen more often for Miami. Just last year, the Dolphins took Kenneth Grant at number 13, one spot before the Colts took Tyler Warren, and that decision still doesn't look very good 18 months after the fact. But while the final verdict isn't in on that dubious choice, here's a long list of more clear regrettable choices:
• DE Charles Harris over T.J. Watt in 2017 Round 1 • QB Tua Tagovailoa over Justin Herbert in 2020 Round 1 (yes, even though Herbert is struggling badly with former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel as his new offensive coordinator this year) • T Austin Jackson over WR Justin Jefferson in 2020 Round 1 • CB Noah Igbinoghene over RB Jonathan Taylor or S Antoine Winfield in 2020 Round 1 • OL Liam Eichenberg over C Creed Humphrey or LB Nick Bolton in 2021 Round 2 • CB Cam Smith over OLB Tuli Tuipulotu or G O'Cyrus Torrence or TE Tyler Kraft in 2023 Round 2 • OLB Chop Robinson over CB Quinyon Mitchell in 2024 Round 1
-- The Dolphins also made a lot of high-profile trades under Grier when they decided to go all in to try to make a deep run into the playoffs and came up short. In that department, the Dolphins got mostly decent value in most of those trades and it's difficult to complain about Grier's work if the mandate was to go for it.
In retrospect, giving up a first-round pick for Bradley Chubb was a questionable (or bad) move because the edge defender was an impact player for only one season, and that 2023 season ended prematurely because of his Week 17 knee injury.
The Tyreek Hill trade can be debated for a while, but it's impossible to call it an out-and-out miss for Miami.
Likewise, it's difficult to criticize the terms of the Jalen Ramsey trade after getting him for a third-round pick and a backup tight end, but the question is whether Grier should have known his personality could be an issue at some point.
The reality is that Grier usually got good value in the trades he orchestrated, with the caveat that it helps when the team is willing to make a financial commitment to a player whose team doesn't want to do that.
-- His best trade in terms of value probably was the huge Laremy Tunsil deal with the Houston Texans in the rebuild of 2019 that netted the Dolphins all sorts of high draft picks.
-- The Dolphins also got great value in a draft trade involving picks in 2021 draft when they got two future first-round picks to move down from 3 to 12, but from this vantage point that win was somewhat negated when they turned around and traded one of those future No. 1s to move back up to 6. And then it also says here the Dolphins made a mistake by taking Jaylen Waddle, even though he's a very good wide receiver, instead of Penei Sewell, who has become an elite tackle on his way to the Hall of Fame.
-- Grier did hit on some draft picks during his time, never more than his very first draft when the Dolphins landed Tunsil in the first round and Xavien Howard in the second. Christian Wilkins was a good first-round pick in 2019, and other hits have included Robert Hunt in Round 2 in 2020, De'Von Achane in Round 3 in 2023, Malik Washington in Round 6 in 2024 and Patrick Paul in Round 2 in 2024 as well.
In the end, though, the misses clearly stood out more than the hits and one year later it's difficult to argue against the decision the Dolphins made because it does appear the organization is on the right path, even though it might take a little bit of time to get there.
While he always took more blame that he probably deserved, it's also very difficult to give Grier a high grade as Dolphins GM.
Let's just say his tenure was uninspiring, though not nearly as bad as a lot of Dolphins fans want to portray it.
Sullivan, meanwhile, can do no wrong in the eyes of a lot of fans right now because of the massive contributions of the rookie class, though the caveat must be included is the fact the roster being stripped provided a lot of immediate opportunities for those young players.
That said, it's really difficult to find fault with many, if any, of the moves he has made so far.
One that stands out was the decision to bypass the popular choice of Rueben Bain Jr. with the Dolphins' first of their two first-round picks. While we're not even at the halfway point of their rookie season, Kadyn Proctor right now has the look of a future star on the offensive line — wherever he winds up lining up — while Bain has done nothing to dispell the concern some draft analysts and media members brought up about his shorter arms being a major detriment as an NFL pass rusher.
The Dolphins regulardly have had six or seven rookies in their starting lineup this season, a testament both to the rebuild and to Sullivan's work.
The real test will come in future years when we see how many of those players remain starters.
Again, though, Sullivan is off to a great start. And for some Dolphins fans, the best part is he's not Chris Grier.

title: What to Know About the New Dolphins Edge Defender
full_text:
For the second time this week and the 16th time in 2026, the Miami Dolphins have picked up a player on waivers and they reportedly tried to a third and 17th, respectively.
The Dolphins' latest roster addition is edge defender Jamree Kromah, who was awarded off waivers from the Chicago Bears, with the Dolphins released Robert Beal Jr. to make room on the 53-man roster.
This comes in the same week the Dolphins landed guard Christian Haynes off waivers from Seattle and also put in a claim for former Las Vegas Raiders defensive tackle Joshua Laulu, though Laulu was awarded to the Tennessee Titans with the second-highest waiver wire priority behind only the winless L.A. Chargers, who did not put in a claim for him.
Kromah is a first-year player out of James Madison, though it's actually his third year in the NFL.
He has appeared in two career games, both this season with the Bears, making his NFL debut against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 6 before recording his first two NFL tackles (one for a loss) in Chicago's 30-24 victory against New England in the Week 7 Thursday night game.
Kromah made a 53-man roster on his third try this summer after recording three sacks in the preseason, including two against the Cleveland Browns.
Kromah went undrafted in 2024 before signing with the Bears and eventually landing on their practice squad. New England signed him off Chicago's practice squad but waived him after three weeks without him appearing in a game and he rejoined the Bears practice squad, where he spent the rest of 2024 and all of 2025.
He had a strong final collegiate season at James Madison with 10 sacks, but was not invited to the scouting combine.
His draft projection was a priority free agent, with NFL.com draft analyst writing: "Kromah posted impressive impact production in 2023 after playing a bigger role than he had in the previous four seasons between Rutgers and James Madison. He’s muscular with very long arms and might have the frame for additional weight to bump inside. Kromah features jarring pop in his hands but might lack enough fluidity and athleticism to capitalize on it as a pro. He’s an effort rusher who is unlikely to create enough consistent pressure to warrant rush-down snaps, but he does have a shot at making the back end of a roster as a base end or future 3-technique."
As with the previous 15 waiver wire pick-ups this year, Kromah is an unproven commodity and the Dolphins just want to have him aboard to see if maybe he can turn into a hidden gem.

title: Vikings Suddenly Have a New Star RB Trade Target Who Isn't Jonathan Taylor in Week 9
full_text:
Fans are waiting for the Vikings to make a needle-moving deal before Tuesday's NFL trade deadline . The backfield is among general manager Nolan Teasley's biggest concerns, and many Vikings believers are dreaming of Colts star rusher Jonathan Taylor coming to the team. That said, Indianapolis won't deal Taylor unless the price is right , which could force teams like Minnesota to pivot.
That said, another running back might have recently become available.
A fourth-round pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, Braelon Allen has been impressive lately for the Jets . In three of his last four games, Allen has surpassed 100 rushing yards. He is averaging five yards per carry this season while also catching 17 of 22 targets for 81 yards.
The Jets' running back situation should interest the Vikings because Allen's breakout performance could make Breece Hall available through trade. He could be significantly less expensive to trade for than Taylor, while providing Minnesota with a legitimate starting threat.
The Jets are getting great production from a running back who is cheaper and younger than Hall. Allen is only 22 years old and is thriving in games where he plays more than 40 offensive snaps, which should force him to be on the field more often.
Allen has an excellent 82.4 Pro Football Focus grade this season that ranks him eighth out of 47 qualifying running backs. He has forced 26 missed tackles as a runner and averaged 3.6 yards after contact, making him one of the most effective running backs in the league.
Hall is still 25 years old and could be a great asset for a team like the Vikings. He played in the first three games of the season for the Jets before suffering a groin injury during practice that has kept him out of action since.
On Tuesday, Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich talked with the media, and The Athletic's Zack Rosenblatt reported that he's "assuming" Hall will return as the starter when he is healthy . While that sounds good for Hall, it lacks the authority of a response that confirms his status in the offense.
Hall has a 63.9 PFF grade this season and is averaging 3.2 yards per carry. On paper, it seems obvious that the Jets should move forward with Allen and test the trade market to see what kind of compensation they can get for Hall. Still, it was only a year ago that Hall hit the 1,000-yard mark for the first time, giving the Vikings good reason to see if a fresh start can get him back to that level.
He could also help with the Vikings' passing struggles, as Hall has caught all 10 of his targets for 102 receiving yards this season. For reference, Minnesota's RBs have combined for 21 catches and 132 receiving yards as of Week 9.
Additionally, Hall would be more than a rental. According to Spotrac , he's under contract with cap hits of $14.5 million and $15.5 million in 2027 and 2028 , respectively, with his deal including a potential out between those seasons that would result in just $3 million of dead money.
Vikings general manager Nolan Teasley needs to start a conversation with Jets GM Darren Mougey, who is good friends with head coach Kevin O'Connell. Hall would be an excellent addition for the Purple and Gold this season and should be explored as soon as possible, especially if landing Taylor becomes more of a pipe dream.

title: 2 Season-Saving Vikings Trades Nolan Teasley Needs (And 2 More He Doesn't)
full_text:
Despite the tough loss to the Lions, the Vikings still figure to be buyers at the Nov. 10 trade deadline . How aggressive they'll be is another question, but the issues on offense aren't going away , and it may take a trade or two to fix them.
Here are two deals Vikings general manager Nolan Teasley should pull off and two more he needs to pump the brakes on.
The Vikings were reportedly in on guard Quenton Nelson—until they weren't—so it's reasonable to think they're still in the market for a guard ahead of the deadline. Eagles guard Landon Dickerson checks many of the boxes Nelson did (Pro Bowl resume, flexibility for long-term options) and is two years younger than the former Colt.
Left guard Joe Huber has filled in admirably for the injured Donovan Jackson, but adding one of the top guards in the NFL from a team clearly falling into disarray would be a huge boost for the lackluster Vikings offense. Right guard Will Fries has also played well below his contract and could be moved on from relatively easily in 2027, paving the way for a Jackson-Dickerson interior.
Dickerson's price, both in draft capital and contract cost, would be very palatable for the Vikings thanks to his low base salary in 2026 and their extra third-rounder from the Jonathan Greenard deal.
Clearly, Jonathan Taylor is the big fish in the running back pond , but it's feeling more and more likely that the Vikings aren't willing to meet the Colts' steep asking price. It's been reported that Indy is looking for first-round value for their star running back, but Teasley may not be willing to part with that for a running back on the wrong side of 27.
If Minnesota wants to add some juice to their backfield without breaking the bank, New England's TreVeyon Henderson fits the bill. Last year's second-round pick had nearly 1,000 yards on the ground but has since been relegated to RB3 after some poor play and a rash of health issues. If the Patriots decide he's no longer part of their future, they could look to move him for help elsewhere.
Henderson could be the home-run threat that the Vikings desperately need. He ripped off four rushes of over 40 yards in 2025 and would be the explosive runner to pair with chain movers Jordan Mason and Aaron Jones. Minnesota already tried shopping Jauan Jennings to the 49ers , so shipping him off to New England—who currently has A.J. Brown, Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs all on ice—could be a win for both sides.
Hall has quickly become a popular consolation prize of the Taylor sweepstakes, but his fit and production don't really match what his asking price would be from New York. Assuming the Vikings find Taylor too pricey, they should feel similarly about Hall, who is younger but also doesn't boast the same impressive resume.
Despite their insistence that he isn't available, if teams start calling offering second-round value for Hall, it's going to be hard for the Jets to hang up the phone. But unlike Taylor, who is near the top of the leaderboards every season, Hall has just one 1,000-yard campaign to his name.
Most teams could probably connect the dots that sporting a jersey with J-E-T-S across the front probably has something to do with his lack of elite numbers. But at the same time, there have been few instances in which Hall has elevated a bad Jets team in the same way Taylor has carried the Colts for years.
If the Vikings are out on Taylor, Hall shouldn't be a conversation either.
The Vikings' quarterback play hasn't been good enough. Kyler Murray continues to miss receivers, take bad sacks and hasn't elevated the offense in any meaningful way. Despite his flaws, adding an outside hire at the deadline probably doesn't solve much either.
Cousins is familiar with the system and has been playing lights-out football in 2026. That's sort of a big problem, though, because it means the Raiders have little reason to deal him, especially for just a Day 3 pick. So would the Vikings really send, say, a third-round pick, for a 38-year old quarterback who still would likely need a few weeks to reacclimate to Kevin O'Connell's offense?
Trading for Cousins, or any quarterback, for that matter , just seems out of the question for an offense that can't afford to wait around a month while their new signal-caller learns the scheme. Cousins could certainly do it quicker, but the best option if Murray gets pulled is probably backup Carson Wentz.
He's not an elevator, but Wentz gets the ball out on time and accurately, and that's all fans are asking for at this point.

title: Ranking Vikings' Best QB Options If Kyler Murray Can't Face Bills in Week 9
full_text:
Playing quarterback for the Vikings is not for the faint of heart, and Kyler Murray’s short tenure with the team he grew up rooting for has been anything but easy so far.
Sure, he's playing quarterback for a 6-1 team, but on-field struggles and time lost to a concussion have only complicated matters. Now, Murray has a hamstring injury after a performance in Detroit that had many fans already asking for a QB swap.
If he can't play against the Bills on Monday, they may get their wish.
Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell spoke to the media on Monday and confirmed that Murray is still dealing with a sore hamstring , adding that they are going through a “full (evaluation),” and he will provide updates later in the week.
Kevin O'Connell provides updates on QB Kyler Murray, OT Christian Darrisaw, and S Theo Jackson. pic.twitter.com/hYX9lNT6fl
But what happens if Murray is unable to play?
Let’s break down the best paths the Vikings can take at the QB spot if they need to make a shift against the Bills.
I’ll start by saying that the likelihood of this happening is incredibly low, but since Brosmer's on the roster , we need to discuss it.
The former Gopher won over fans and the franchise alike with a surprising performance during training camp and preseason games in 2025, ultimately securing a roster spot. One thing definitely not in their forecast was Brosmer hitting the field in his rookie season. Unfortunately, injury luck had other plans, and Brosmer had to play before he was even close to ready.
ERNEST JONES 84-YARD PICK-SIX MINvsSEA on FOX/FOX One https://t.co/HkKw7uXVnt pic.twitter.com/VA6dvef6w6
Brosmer totaled 328 passing yards, four interceptions, a whopping 14 sacks taken, and zero touchdowns in seven appearances and two starts last season. His most noteworthy performance was a Christmas-night victory over the Lions, where Brosmer threw for three net passing yards.
O’Connell clearly wants to see what Brosmer has long-term, but there is no way the team can give him serious playing time this season.
I’d say this is the likeliest outcome we’ll see on Monday night if Murray is ruled out.
Wentz is a relatively steady hand who is familiar with the offense and, most importantly, feeds Justin Jefferson. The wideout’s lowest yardage total in seven games with Wentz was a 55-yard monsoon performance in Chicago in Week 2. Jefferson has already had fewer than 55 yards three times this season with Murray at QB; however, it's worth noting that Jefferson did leave the Week 3 win over the Bucs with an ankle injury in the first quarter.
JUSTIN JEFFERSON ON A FREE PLAY GBvsMIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ZKnmvwBDtR
If Wentz stays healthy, limits turnovers, and gets the ball to his playmakers, we may see a very different passing game on Monday night. Wentz may be an unlikely hero to rescue the Vikings’ sinking offense and carry it to the Lombardi, but they desperately need improvement at this point.
I don’t think the Raiders are in any rush to trade away Kirk Cousins with a 4-4 record, especially when he’s having quite the season, but having number-one pick Fernando Mendoza in the wings means it's worth a call. Cousins’ familiarity and success with O’Connell’s offense and Minnesota’s weapons make this an ideal fix for their 2026 QB woes.
Kirk Cousins has the Raiders back on top in a high-scoring game LVvsNYJ on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/jQI5vkJ8Xb
I’d put the likelihood of this happening at around 5%, as the Raiders would be embracing the unknown by shifting to Mendoza this early. Minnesota is running out of time and options to fix their QB situation, with the Nov. 10 trade deadline quickly approaching .
If Minnesota is going to make a move, Cousins is the best fit, and now is the best time.

title: Vikings Week 9 Stock Report: James Pierre Among Risers, Brett Thorson Falls
full_text:
Like the Vikings' offense, this season is about to become an absolute roller coaster, with the Bills on deck in Week 9 and the trade deadline to follow . While some Vikings have helped to steady the ship, others are making progress harder.
The Lions handed the Vikings their first loss of the year, and there was plenty of blame to go around. From missed tackles to a dud of a day on offense, it just wasn't in the cards.
So, after the defeat, who is seeing their stock rise, and who might be in for a long season?
Pierre notched his second interception of the season last Sunday and handed Jared Goff his first of the year. After ranking as their No. 2 cornerback in 2025, Pierre is once again a Pro Football Focus darling in 2026. He has an impressive 75.9 grade this season, ranking him 12th out of 102 qualifying cornerbacks.
James Pierre picks it off! MINvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XZ8sQnAqCx
With Isaiah Rodgers potentially dealing with an ankle injury that could force him to miss time, Pierre may see a spike in snaps this week against Buffalo. That's clearly not going to be an issue for the Vikings' defense, and Pierre has quietly become one of the best offseason additions for Minnesota.
Mason's second game back from injury was lacking, with just 20 yards on eight rushes, and he has yet to bring much juice to the backfield since recovering from a thumb injury. His 3.9 yards per carry and zero catches in the pass game this year are far from what the Vikings had wanted (and needed).
Mason is a solid RB2, but it's becoming clear the Vikings don't have a running back who moves the needle between him and Aaron Jones Sr. A sub-four yards per rush with essentially no impact in the passing game just isn't going to scare opposing defenses.
Van Ginkel will be 32 years old and a free agent next season. The Vikings could understandably be hesitant to offer him a new deal, but Gink just keeps making plays .
Van Ginkel notched another 2.5 sacks against Detroit, upping his season total to 6.5 and good enough for fifth in the NFL. He's got an interception and a forced fumble already as well, for good measure, and while it's reasonable to expect the drop-off to come, Van Ginkel just keeps defying the odds.
. @AndrewVanGinkel is having himself a day. 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/SJjsbNH9H9
Despite plenty of other mouths to feed in 2027, it's just hard to see how the Vikings won't want to bring their star edge rusher back for another year.
Thorson beat out veteran Johnny Hekker for the job this offseason, but hasn't really done much to show he'll be the guy in 2027 and beyond.
Against Detroit, he badly shanked one punt, and his 44.1 punt average ranks 28th in the NFL this season. Hekker wasn't much better when filling in, so it's doubtful the Vikings make another in-season move, especially with the all-important job of holding for Will Reichard on the line.
Punter is clearly the least of the Vikings' worries this year, but expect some competition again in the spring.

title: Under-the-Radar QB Trade Target Is Worth Vikings' Attention Amid Kyler Murray Injury Uncertainty
full_text:
The Vikings are coming off their first defeat of the season , a 15-19 road loss to the Lions. While the Purple and Gold are still on top of the NFC North with a 6-1 record, they face uncertainty heading into Week 9.
Monday Night Football will feature a game between the Vikings and the Bills in what should be a hard-fought contest. That said, the status of starting quarterback Kyler Murray is in question after he sustained an injury against Detroit.
On Monday, ESPN shared a report on Monday that Murray is dealing with hamstring soreness that could cause him to miss the game against the Bills.
With Murray's status in question, it might be smart to trade for a quarterback to help while he recovers— especially with less than a week to go before the 2026 deadline . Plenty of names have been thrown around in trade rumors, but one that isn't getting much attention could stand out to the Vikings.
The Vikings have been disappointing offensively this season and may not want to turn the offense over to backup quarterback Carson Wentz this week. Plus, if the Vikings are looking for an inexpensive option to hold down the position for a few weeks and provide more depth, Texans quarterback Davis Mills is an option.
Mills is in his fifth NFL season and has started 29 games for Houston since entering the league. The 28-year-old quarterback has completed 684 of his 1,107 career pass attempts for 7082 yards, 40 touchdowns, and 26 interceptions.
The Texans have Mills on a one-year, $7 million contract , according to Spotrac . He is scheduled to become an unrestricted free agent at the end of his season, which means the 2-5 Texans would likely be willing to trade him for a mid-round pick rather than let him walk after this year.
It all depends on how much faith the Vikings have in Wentz and his backup, Max Brosmer, to hold down the ship until Murray is ready to return. Although Wentz led Minnesota to wins against the Packers and Bears, he only averaged 138 passing yards on a 59.0% completion rate.
For now, the Vikings need to focus on preparing for the rest of the season and a possible playoff berth. Adding a quarterback with starting experience could help to add depth and options for head coach Kevin O'Connell, and if they can do so without giving up valuable draft capital, even better.
Minnesota can't afford to lose many more games this season with the strong competition in the NFC North. Every team in the NFC North has at least five wins and a winning record heading into Week 9, so defending U.S. Bank Stadium against the Bills on Monday Night Football needs to be a priority.
In the meantime, it's time for the Vikings to give the Texans a call before it's too late.

title: Vikings Are Missing the James Pierre Gold Mine Right in Front of Them
full_text:
The Vikings are getting a lot of love for their defense this season. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores's unit is giving up the fewest points per game this season (13.3) and is second in sacks (25), while guiding the team to a 6-1 record.
The frequency of blitzes by the Vikings this season has drawn national attention. Minnesota had the highest blitz rate in the league through seven weeks (71.4%), and that number likely rose due to the large number of blitzes the Purple and Gold sent at Lions quarterback Jared Goff in Sunday's 19-15 loss .
One player in Minnesota's defense who isn't getting as much attention as he should is James Pierre. The Vikings signed the former Steelers cornerback this offseason to bolster a depleted cornerback room, and he has thrived since his arrival, raising the idea that Flores & Co. must do a better job of maximizing Pierre's skill set.
As of Tuesday afternoon, Pierre has a Pro Football Focus grade of 75.9 this year , ranking him 12th out of 102 qualifying cornerbacks. He is also the 12th-ranked cornerback when it comes to pass coverage, with a grade of 75.3.
Pierre is no slouch in run defense either. His PFF grade in that area is 69.9, which is 35th at the position. When targeted by opposing quarterbacks, he allows a 23.6 passer rating, which is stellar for a defensive back.
While playing 173 defensive snaps for Minnesota this year, Pierre has accumulated 23 combined tackles (19 solo), four pass defenses, and two interceptions—including one against the Lions in Week 8. His production has been excellent while on a two-year, $8.5 million contract .
James Pierre picks it off! MINvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XZ8sQnAqCx
The crazy part of his amazing season is that Pierre is only playing 40% of Minnesota's defensive snaps. He's averaging 24.8 defensive snaps per game, finishing below that number twice in the last four outings. The Vikings need to figure out a way to get him on the field more , but that will be difficult with Byron Murphy Jr. and Isaiah Rogers above him on the depth chart.
Murphy has played nearly 91% of the Vikings' defensive snaps, while Rodgers is at about 88%. Murphy has a PFF grade of 62.3 this season and has three interceptions, so cutting into his reps doesn't make much sense.
It makes even less sense to take snaps from Rodgers and give them to Pierre. Rodgers has a PFF grade of 85.8 this season, ranking him as the third-best cornerback in the league. He is third in coverage at 86.2 and 18th in run defense at 76.7.
That said, Rodgers is reportedly dealing with an ankle sprain , which could result in more playing time for Pierre against the Bills on Monday.
While giving Pierre more time on the field sounds like a problem, it is an issue that is a gold mine for the Vikings this season. Having three cornerbacks playing so well this season not only raises the position's floor but could also allow Flores to play his defensive backs more situationally. Minnesota can also find out whether Pierre is a viable replacement option should Rodgers leave as an unrestricted free agent in March.
For a player with only a $2.985 million cap hit this season, Pierre is massively outplaying his contract. The only question is whether the team can figure out a way to get him more time on the field this season.

title: Vikings Verdict: Judging Kyler Murray, November Concerns & Other Overreactions Ahead of Week 9
full_text:
The Vikings stumbled for the first time this season, dropping one to the Lions in Detroit. Minnesota still sits atop the NFC North, but the walls could be closing in soon. It's not always the vibes for a 6-1 team are this off, but here we are in Week 9, and the Vikings are one of the most polarizing teams in the league.
So, will November be a death sentence for the Vikings' season? Is it time for a change at quarterback? Let's dig into those overreactions and more ahead of Week 9's matchup against the Bills.
They're already 20% of the way there after Sunday's loss to Detroit, and with Buffalo, Green Bay, San Francisco and Atlanta on the way, things aren't getting easier. Minnesota went 0-for-4 last year in November before going on a 5-0 run to end the season, and 2026 is shaping up for a similar result.
The Bills this week might be the biggest challenge, but after that, there's a chance the Vikings look significantly different. With a Nov. 10 trade deadline , Minnesota could still be buyers at 6-2, and if general manager Nolan Teasley can add a running back or maybe a guard, the outlook could completely change. Defense travels, and the Vikings still boast the league's best, so they'll be at least in on every game.
Still, the schedule is brutal, and while the Vikings likely notch a few wins this month, it also could go very wrong for Minnesota.
No defensive player earned All-Pro honors last year for Minnesota, but that looks like it's about to change in 2026 . There's still plenty of football left, but multiple Vikings defenders are already making a strong case.
Both edge players—Andrew Van Ginkel and Dallas Turner—are on pace for double-digit sacks, and Ginks' contributions in the passing game make his candidacy obvious. The linebacker duo of Blake Cashman and Eric Wilson have already combined for 7.5 sacks and six passes defended.
Blake Cashman steps up for the sack 😤 INDvsMIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/MSl2dfO6k7
Up front, Jalen Redmond has quietly put together another impressive year . The sack numbers haven't been there yet for Redmond, but his 89.9 Pro Football Focus grade against the run ranks first among all defensive tackles.
Going from zero to five All-Pros in one year would certainly be a leap, but these Vikings are making a case. Likely, though, a few of them see their production dip over the second half of the season.
Kyler Murray, by the numbers, has been fine enough. He's limited the big mistakes and has found ways to make plays with his legs. The problem, though, is that the Vikings offense hasn't scored more than 23 points with Murray at the helm, and his issues with accuracy and reading the field are becoming problematic.
So while Murray's mediocre play leaves a lot to be desired, the options to replace him aren't exactly overflowing. Carson Wentz remains the most realistic option, but the Vikings could theoretically explore a trade as well.
Does Wentz or a mid-season addition offer a better floor than Murray? Possibly, but it's hard to see head coach Kevin O'Connell pulling the plug on his prized free-agent acquisition after just five or six games. And yet, J.J. McCarthy was only given 10 starts before the Vikings moved on, so anything should be on the table depending on how Monday night against Buffalo goes.

title: Isaiah Rodgers Injury Could Thrust Forgotten Vikings Rookie Into Week 9 MNF Spotlight
full_text:
The NFC North looks a lot closer after the Vikings lost to the Lions on Sunday, marking their first loss of the season . It also wasn't a battle without casualties. Several injuries either forced a Viking off the field or may impact their ability to play in the next game, leaving Minnesota with some obstacles to overcome as the second half of the season begins.
One of the Vikings players who got banged up against the Lions was cornerback Isaiah Rodgers. According to The Athletic 's Alex Lewis, Minnesota head coach Kevin O'Connell described the injury after the game as an "ankle sprain," but didn't give more detail than that.
At this time, it is unknown how severe the sprain is. There is a possibility that it could take longer to heal than Monday night, which is when the Vikings face off against the Bills. If Rodgers is forced to sit out, Minnesota might need rookie CB Chuck Demmings to be ready to step up.
Rodgers is having an excellent season. He is currently Pro Football Focus 's No. 3 cornerback out of 102 qualifying players, with an 85.8 grade. The 28-year-old defensive back is a big part of Brian Flores' defense, playing 88% of the defensive snaps (376).
That said, it may be time to give fifth-round draft pick Demmings a bigger role if Rodgers can't go. The rookie has played only two defensive snaps this season, both of them coming against the Buccaneers in Week 2.
Demmings has a PFF grade of 62 but hasn't played enough snaps to rank among other players at his position. The former Stephen F. Austin standout has a solid pass coverage grade of 61.1 but hasn't played since the Buccaneers game.
The 6'1", 193-lb Demmings will need to prove this week that he deserves the snaps over the other cornerbacks on the roster. However, an impressive training camp and preseason , where he turned heads with his determination and athleticism, will likely help him get more opportunities this season.  He finished the exhibition slate with a 64.5 coverage grade on PFF , allowing only 2-of-6 passes for 38 yards with a break-up.
The upcoming Week 9 MNF clash with the Bills is the time to see what Demmings has to offer the Vikings. Minnesota's secondary will need all the help it can get against a Buffalo offense that averages an NFL-leading 12.7 yards per completion.
Of course, that is only if Rodgers's sprained ankle prevents him from playing in the prime-time contest. There is no need to put a player recovering from an injury on the field if there are players ready to step up and contribute
If winning the Super Bowl is the top goal, head coach Kevin O'Connell needs to ensure his players stay healthy for the long haul, not just take things one game at a time. That could mean putting Demmings in a sink-or-swim situation on Monday night.

title: 3 Vikings Flaws Must Be Addressed ASAP After Perfect Season Dies at Hands of Lions
full_text:
Sunday marked the Minnesota Vikings’ first loss since Nov. 30, 2025, but if fan and media reactions were your only measure, you might think the team was on a season-long winless streak. The wild part? The pessimism is more than warranted .
Minnesota’s stellar defense showed its first signs of humanity in the second half of Sunday’s matchup with the Lions, after the struggling Vikings’ offense failed to get anything going for most of the afternoon, resulting in a 19-15 loss. Turns out defensive coordinator Brian Flores’s unit won’t be able to drag the team to an undefeated Super Bowl run after all.
So, what comes next? Let’s break down three areas in desperate need of saving if the Vikings want to make a serious run.
The Kyler Murray era in Minnesota may be over after just five full games with the former Cardinals’ quarterback.
There was plenty of reason for optimism when Murray signed with the Vikings on a one-year league-minimum deal in March to compete with J.J. McCarthy. Murray’s patented athleticism, head coach Kevin O’Connell’s play design, and Minnesota’s stacked wide receiver core seemed like a dangerous combination. Training camp showed flashes of what could be, even as fair concerns lingered about the fit between QB and coach and the schemes they’ve thrived in previously.
So far, the on-field product has been a disaster, as Murray looks to be actively regressing. He appears to lack any confidence in his decisions and is leaving wide-open wideouts frustrated downfield. It's clear the complexity of O’Connell’s scheme is overloading Murray as he basically relearns how he’s always played football. It’s the only explanation for why he’s actively worse with the best offensive tools he’s ever had. This was always a possibility, but the time to shift plans is now.
While Carson Wentz isn't an exciting solution, he should serve as a solid placeholder while the Vikings explore the QB trade market . If they find no sellers, it may be panic time.
Minnesota spent most of the offseason touting their new and improved run scheme led by assistant head coach Frank Smith. The shift to an outside zone approach meant backs would have more opportunities to turn the corner and hit the gas for explosive runs.
So far, that has not been the case. Aaron Jones battled valiantly through injury while Jordan Mason was on injured reserve, but his inability to sustain runs longer than 5-10 yards downfield emphasized the need for a boost to the room. Current Colts RB Jonathan Taylor quickly became the top trade target for most Vikings fans.
Sunday further emphasized the failures of a run game that never truly seemed to improve in the way we were sold. Rookie Demond Claiborne’s inability to see the field certainly doesn’t help, as the Vikings had hoped his speed would provide some value this season.
The Vikings' offense has many issues, but the run game remains problematic. The team talked about prioritizing it for the 4th straight offseason. Tons of changes over time: RBs, iOL, TE, OL coach, etc. Right now, they rank 31st in rushing success rate and 27th in EPA/play.
Minnesota’s interior offensive line isn't doing the passing or running game any favors, and one lineman’s play in particular is especially concerning. Right guard Will Fries signed a massive five-year, $87.72 million contract in 2025, giving Vikings fans hope that the team had finally solved a long-term interior need.
Turns out, he’s been anything but reliable.
Genuinely hilarious rep from Will Fries here https://t.co/oSC7kOl84r pic.twitter.com/8g83cL1nH9
Fries has often looked like a revolving door , allowing pass rushers to blow past him with ease. Luckily, the Vikings can opt out of his contract after the season.
The Vikings may not find an immediate upgrade this season, but they still need more depth. Left guard Joe Huber has done well in relief of rising star Donovan Jackson, and starting center Blake Brandel still seems to be learning the position in his first year as a starter.
The team needs security on the interior line, especially with Fries’s already inconsistent play.

title: Vikings' Snap Count vs. Lions: Biggest Winners, Losers & Role Changes in Week 8
full_text:
The Vikings are undefeated no longer . The Purple and Gold were outscored 19-15 at Ford Field in Week 8, moving their record on the season to 6-1 while remaining on top of the NFC North.
Minnesota has relied on the defense and the leg of their kicker, Will Reichard, to keep them in games this season, but that formula didn't work against the Lions. The Vikings' kicker missed his only field goal attempt. Thankfully, the offense scored two touchdowns to keep the game competitive, but that isn't exactly a long-term recipe for success .
A big reason the Vikings were in this game until the final minutes is the play of key contributors. Deciding who to play and when is important for head coach Kevin O'Connell, but there were bound to be winners and losers from the snap count.
Josh Metellus was in for every defensive snap of the game—the only Minnesota defender to achieve that feat this weekend. The versatile safety led the team with 13 tackles against Detroit and added one broken-up pass.
Metellus has been a cornerstone of defensive coordinator Brian Flores's defense this season. He has played 426 of 427 defensive snaps for the Vikings so far and should continue to be used as much as possible going forward, especially if the safety room stays out of trouble .
Max Bredeson's declining usage hit a new low against the Lions in Week 8, playing only seven offensive snaps. Compared to the season opener, when he was in on 24 offensive snaps, that's a significant difference.
It's not surprising that Bredeson didn't record a single stat against Detroit. When a player only gets nine total snaps in a game, getting an opportunity to make a significant impact can be a challenge. It will be interesting to see if his snap count shrinks again next week.
It was a season-high 17 offensive snaps for DeeJay Dallas against the Lions, almost tripling his count from last week against the Colts. His usage is already surprising since he was elevated from the practice squad while rookie running back Demond Claiborne was inactive for the second week.
Dallas was a major benefactor of Jordan Mason's ineffective day. He actually ended with two more offensive snaps than Mason, despite having seven fewer rushing opportunities. Dallas finished with one rushing attempt for four yards.
Even with safety Theo Jackson suffering an injury in the game after playing only 25 defensive snaps and rookie Jakobe Thomas being inactive for the seventh time this season, Jay Ward couldn't get on the field beyond special teams.
Ward finished the game with one tackle, but could get a defensive opportunity in Week 9 against the Bills on Monday Night Football next week if Jackson is unable to suit up. Of course, that might mean taking snaps away from a veteran defensive back.
This season, Harrison Smith has been a rotational safety. Before Sunday's game against Detroit, he had played a maximum of 31 defensive snaps in games against the Colts and the Buccaneers.
Harrison Smith is playing in place of Theo Jackson (quad), who is questionable to return.
Smith picked up many of Jackson's potential snaps. Jackson's quad injury forced him out of the game, and Smith appears to be the player Flores and O'Connell were most comfortable with to pick up the slack.

title: Patriots' Robert Kraft Among 5 HOF Contributor Candidates for 2027
full_text:
FOXBORO — Could this be the year that Robert Kraft finally gets inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame?
On Wednesday, the Pro Football Hall of Fame announced that the New England Patriots owner is one of five finalists for the Class of 2027 contributor category. Kraft was named alongside Ralph Hay, Virginia McCaskey, Doug Williams and John Wooten. These names were narrowed down from a larger group of 42 nominees by the contributor subcommittee.
Kraft, who bought the Patriots in 1994 and has helped usher in a new era of dynastic football, advanced in this process last year. Kraft was first nominated in 2013 and has eligible ever since. He wouldn't get inducted into Canton, along with former Patriots head coach Bill Belichick — who was the coaching nominee in 2026.
"I would just say that's unfortunate," Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said last February after Kraft didn't earn induction . "In my experiences with Robert, he's more than deserving. He'll be in the Hall of Fame. I'm not in charge of deciding when that happens."
The Patriots have became a force in the NFL since Kr aft took over. During his time as owner, the Patriots have won 11 AFC titles and six Super Bowls. He also became the fastest NFL owner to reach 300 wins and has been a key member of several NFL ownership committees. In 2011, he was instrumental in helping to end the lockout ahead of that season.
It's a crowded group as it stands right now . Hay, who also reached this point a year ago, owned the Canton Bulldogs from 1918 to 1922 and was a key factor when it came to forming the NFL.
The late McCaskey was the principal owner of the Chicago Bears since 1983, and owned the team during their first Super Bowl over the Patriots in 1985. She was the daughter of Bears founder George Halas.
Williams played nine seasons in the NFL, winning Super Bowl MVP in 1987 and has spent the last 13 years in the Washington Commanders front office. He's also been a scout or front office executive in other years.
Wooten played offensive line for a decade before transitioning into scouting roles off the field. In 2003, he became chair of the Fritz Pollard Alliance, a group that hepps create opportunities for minorities in coaching and front office roles.
The Patriots have historically not been inducted into the Hall of Fame in recent years, despite having several people deserving of the honor. Last year, former kicker Adam Vinatieri was inducted as the first Patriots specialist to ever enter the halls of Canton.
The contributor category "recognizes individuals whose impact on professional football came through leadership, innovation and service to the game rather than on-field performance," according to the Hall of Fame. The voting committee will hold a meeting on Nov. 17 to narrow the group of five down to one.

title: Mack Hollins' Return Revitalizes a Broken Patriots WR Room
full_text:
On Wednesday, NFL Nework's Ian Rapaport reported that New England Patriots wide receiver Mack Hollins would be returning to practice , beginning his 21-day window to be activated off the injured reserve.
In his second year with the Patriots, Hollins landed on injured reserve after sustaining a calf injury in the second half of New England's win over Buffalo in Week 4.
A big one for the #Patriots : WR Mack Hollins is set to return to practice today, sources say. Hollins, a glue guy for NE, has been on Injured Reserve with a calf injury and would help immensely vs the #Packers . pic.twitter.com/8uhIzxvxZ8
Through the first four weeks of the season, Hollins was the Patriots' leading receiver in yards and receptions, making his injury a major loss for the offense. Despite Hollins' absence, New England's passing game has been able to deliver, putting up 282.3 receiving yards per game from Weeks 5 to 8.
At the time of his injury, Hollins was the second Patriots receiver to land on IR this season, following A.J. Brown — who was injured in Week 1. Two weeks after Hollins came up gimpy on his right leg, Romeo Doubs was sidelined and sent to the injured reserve with a shoulder injury.
Brown returned in Week 6 and played only two games, missing Week 8's contest against Miami with a knee problem that arrived during last week's practice. Doubs isn't eligible to return off the injured reserve until Week 12. Drake Maye was left with just three receivers signed to the 53-man roster last Sunday against the Dolphins.
While New England's been able to make-do with the weakened wide recievers by utilizing tight ends and running backs in the passing game, those positions aren't exactly healthy either. TreVeyon Henderson didn't play in Week 8 due to an illness and is also still recovering a high ankle sprain sustained a couple games prior.
In the second half against Miami, tight end Hunter Henry injured his foot, leaving his status for Week 9's game against the Green Bay Packers up in the air. These considerations provide more value to Hollins' activation, who is looking to make an immediate impact in his return to play.
Hollins has played a major role in big situations for New England's passing attack. Maye often finds the 6-foot-4 receiver on third and fourth down plays. Since his injury, Henry has assumed that role, but with the tight end potentially missing some time, having Hollins back in the fold brings a much needed security blanket to last year's runner-up for MVP.
Part of the struggle for New England's wide receivers this year has been finding consistency, and the player that's been hurt the most by this is Brown. The superstar wide receiver has hauled in just nine of 20 passes thrown to him and has struggled to find meaningful production on offense.
Adding another perimeter threat in Hollins creates opportunities for Brown that he hasn't had due to defensive gameplans taking him out of the game (as well as uncharacteristically unreliable pass catching abilities). In the three quarters they played together in Week 1, Hollins' separation caused Seattle's defense to not overcommit on Brown. Maye took advantage of this adjustment, placing a deep pass to Brown that slipped off his fingers.
The Hollins effect can be seen through the sample size of games he missed last year with an abdomen injury. The wide receiver landed on injured reserve late last season, missing the final two weeks of the regular season and two playoff games. In those games, Maye threw for an average of 35 yards less than his season average passing yards per game. Returning to action in the AFC Championship game and the Super Bowl, Hollins was the leading receiver for New England in both contests.
The 33-year-old Hollins is in his 10th NFL season and is the most veteran receiver residing in Foxboro. While he's never been known to be a top wideout option, his voice and demeanor had a huge impact on a receiver room that many defenses looked past last season.
Hollins has extended his interest in this Patriots team far beyond the field. In both weeks the Patriots traveled while he was injured, Hollins made the trip with the players to Chicago and Miami — something that isn't required of players on IR.
Last week, New England's receivers had an average of 2.75 years of experience in the NFL. Activating the veteran Hollins and hopefully seeing Brown return to play on Sunday will bring a transformational impact to New England's offense and its high-caliber quarterback.

title: Patriots Make Key Roster Decision on WR Mack Hollins
full_text:
The New England Patriots, after weeks of injuries upon injuries, are one step closer to getting back a big piece of their offensive puzzle this week.
According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport , the Patriots plan to have wide receiver Mack Hollins' 21-day window to return off of injury reserve begin Wednesday. Hollins has been on IR since Week 5 with a calf injury he suffered one week prior against the Buffalo Bills.
Hollins and the Patriots will have three weeks before a decision truly needs to be made on his return to the active roster, but because the team designated him to return, he's allowed to practice for those three weeks. This is the third of eight IR designations that the Patriots are allowed to use in the regular season, following wide receiver A.J. Brown and offensive tackle Marcus Bryant.
"Potentially, yeah," head coach Mike Vrabel said Monday about the possibility of both Hollins and fullback Reggie Gilliam returning this week. “Those guys are all working hard. We’ve got a long list of those guys, and I think (head athletic trainer) Jim (Whalen) and his staff, and obviously (director of sports performance) Frank (Piraino) and his staff are trying to do a great job with the return to play. We’ll see here where we come out from the game, where guys can help us and the spots that you have to make to get those guys back.
"So, there’s a lot of moving parts. We’ll try to make sure that the player is ready to return to practice. Then also, if they were to be available for the game, and then make the corresponding moves that would have to occur."
Hollins was a big part of New England's offense before he went down with the injury , recording a then-team high 15 receptions for 209 yards in the first four games of the season. He hasn't played in the last four games, but has been spotted on the team's road trips to both Chicago in Week 7 and Miami one week later.
The 6-foot-4 receiver has become a really trusted weapon for Drake Maye in this Patriots offense. Though his role in 2025 was limited in scope, after Brown's Week 1 injury this season, Hollins stepped up into a much bigger role — both as a pass catcher and as a leader for the younger wideouts.
The Patriots have gone through plenty banged-up receivers this season, with Brown dealing with both ankle and knee injuries and Romeo Doubs being placed on IR with a shoulder injury suffered in Week 6. Should Hollins return to the 53-man roster this week for the team's game against the Green Bay Packers, he'd join Brown, DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism III in the wide receiver room. They also have Kyle Dixon, Chandler Brayboy and Ryan Miller on the practice squad.
After a myriad of moves to start the week, including Bryant's IR activation and the releasing of two defensive backs , the Patriots do have one open spot on their 53-man roster for Hollins to potentially fill. We will see if he ends up claiming that opening.
There are also several other players who are eligible to return from their stints on IR, including safety Dell Pettus (ankle), offensive guard Greg Van Roten (thigh), edge rusher Quintayvious Hutchins (knee) and linebacker Khalil Jacobs (undisclosed).

title: 5 Edge Rushers Patriots Should Trade For After Gabe Jacas Injury
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is less than one week away, meaning movement is bound to happen across the league prior to November 10.
Teams have been identified as buyers or sellers ahead of the deadline with some organizations looking to upgrade their roster and others looking to trade valuable pieces for future draft capital.
The New England Patriots has been regarded as a buyer in this year's trade deadline conversation due to the pool of injuries that have plagued the Patriots roster. However, others argue that executive vice president of player personnel Eliot Wolf and head coach Mike Vrabel are looking to make their team younger and acquire picks at the deadline.
If the Patriots were to buy-in, one position they'll certainly be inquiring about is edge rusher. The conversation around the Patriots needing an edge rusher has been loud over the past several years. This season, New England may have solved their EDGE issues with the emergence of Elijah Ponder and second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas.
ELITE: #PATRIOTS ROOKIE EDGE GABE JACAS HAS BEEN A STEAL. Through 8 games: • 3 sacks • 24 tackles • 4 TFLs • 1 INT • 11th in PFF grade • 12th in pass-rush grade • 9th in pass-rush win rate Jacas ranks FIRST among all rookies in the last three categories. WHAT A PICK. pic.twitter.com/vcyM4zSiMx
Jacas, who leads other rookies at his position in multiple statistics, went down in the second half of New England's victory over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday. Right now, his injury designation is listed as a knee issue, which leaves the severity of Jacas' injury up in the air.
While more information will be replaced on Wednesday, when the first injury report is released, the Patriots will need to find a suitable replacement if the injury sidelines the rookie for an extended period of time.
New England also rosters Dre'Mont Jones at defensive end, and they have a number of practice squad players who can play on the perimeter of the line (Jose Ramirez, Xavier Holmes). If the Pats decide to look out-of-house for an Jacas replacement, here's who they should target:
Diaby is a 6-foot-4, 270-pound linebacker for Tampa Bay, who is generating a lot of interest from teams looking for an outside linebacker.
The fourth-year player has been an essential piece to the Buccaneers defense, which has kept its offense in a lot of games that haven't swung their way. Diaby is on the final year of his rookie contract. which means a rental situation could make the price of him much lower than other names on this list.
Unfortunately, Diaby sustained a grade two MCL sprain during Tampa Bay's 16-0 win over Atlanta on Sunday, and is expected to miss several weeks because of it. This makes the rental value of Diaby significantly less, but would also mean the Patriots wouldn't have to give up much for him.
It's unlikely that the front office adds to the hospital waiting room-like lineup they already have by adding another injured player, but if Diaby's return time is sooner than Jacas', there's a chance he's included in a deal.
The 13-year veteran might not be as nimble as he was years ago, but his defensive impact is certainly still seen in the locker room and on the field. The 0-7 Chargers are looking to find value in their veteran pieces.
Mack is proving that his career isn't on a sharp decline, as he's registered three sacks and 21 tackles this year, and still finds himself on the field for 70% of defensive snaps.
Adding a veteran force in the 35-year-old Mack could make all the difference for this punishing Patriots defensive line. Mack's physical ability fits the mold that Vrabel seeks in his trench players on defense. The $4.4 million cap hit on Mack's contract for the remainder of this season fits well with the cap space New England has after recently restructuring Hunter Henry's contract .
Johnson II is a former Pro Bowl defensive end who's on the last year of his rookie contract. Similar to Diaby, Johnson might be a useful rental piece for the Patriots.
Johnson was an offseason trade acquisition for the Titans, coming from the New York Jets. He's emerged as one of the top defensive free agent prospects of the 2027 offseason. Vrabel's history with bringing people from Tennessee to New England could translate here, depsite the two never overlapping in Nashville.
As a member of the 1-7 Titans, Tennessee will also be a team to watch as they move on from their valuable pieces, like Jeffery Simmons, who they sent to Chicago in exchange for two first-round picks among other draft capital.
Johnson has three sacks and 20 tackles on the year, and is a valuable rental option to finish the season with New England before purusing a contract somewhere else.
It's rare for a trade within the division to happen so close to the deadline, especially with a player as talented as McDonald IV.
Between 2024 and 2025, McDonald registered 18.5 sacks, but his role has been downplayed this season due to the arrival of first-round pick David Bailey in New York.
McDonald has one year left on his rookie contract and may try to build a name for himself as a top defensive end before he becomes a free agent in 2028.
Should New England call the Chargers about a trade for a defensive end, it might not be Mack they inquire about, but instead Tuipulotu. The fourth-year player meets the theme of almost of every other name on this list by having an expiring contract.
Tuipulotu has three sacks and 30 tackles on the season while also forcing two fumbles. In 2025, he had 13 sacks and 20 tackles for losses en route to his first Pro Bowl appearance.
Similar to Johnson, it's unlikely the Patriots resign Tuipulotu if they acquire him, unless they were to move around other players. Christian Gonzalez's record-breaking contract extension ahead of Week 1, and Drake Maye's eventual record-breaking extension next offseason make long-term trade acquisitions difficult to come by for the Patriots in November.
While there are certainly better options out there for the Pats to pursue at defensive end, these five names make the most sense due to less financial commitment and smaller prices than players like Maxx Crosby or Josh Sweat.

title: Patriots Roster Moves: OT Marcus Bryant Activated, Depth Pieces Reshuffled
full_text:
As they continue to prep for the Green Bay Packers in Week 9, the New England Patriots made a myriad of moves to both their 53-man roster and their practice squad.
One of those moves finally allowed a second-year player to be activated off of injured reserve, while others reworked how the depth looks heading into the middle of this season.
Here's a look at all the transactions the Patriots announced on Tuesday and what they might mean for the 5-3 squad moving forward.
The Patriots are activating offensive tackle Marcus Bryant off of injured reserve onto the 53-man roster ahead of his 21-day return to play window expiring on Wednesday. Bryant, a seventh round pick a season ago, was on his way to making the team during training camp before an ankle injury landed him on IR .
Ahead of roster cuts in August, the Patriots designated him as a player to return off of IR during the season. Three weeks ago, he rejoined the team in practice and was given 21 days to be elevated to the roster. Bryant , who'll now join Will Campbell, Morgan Moses, Caleb Lomu and Dametrious Crownover as the tackles on the team, will be likely used as a swing option on both sides of the line.
Last season as a rookie, the Missouri alum played in 12 games as a reserve — getting onto the field for 19 total offensive snaps and 56 total special teams snaps.
The Patriots had an open spot on the active roster before these moves took place, but also opened up another by releasing cornerback Kindle Vildor. A candidate to return on the practice squad, Vildor has bounced around between the 53-man roster and the practice squad in his first year with New England.
As a backup cornerback , the 29-year-old Vildor has played in five games this season and recorded six tackles, one pass breakup, a forced fumble and a special teams tackle. In recent weeks after the returns of both Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis from injury, Vildor was relegated to more of a special teams role. Against the Dolphins in Week 8, he played 13 snaps on special teams.
There is still one open spot on the 53-man roster, which could potentially go to either fullback Reggie Gilliam or wide receiver Mack Hollins. Both are eligible to return off of IR this week.
After linebacker K.J. Britt signed with the Detroit Lions , the Patriots had a spot to play with when it came to their practice squad. As first reported by ESPN's Mike Reiss, the team added linebacker Elias Neal, who spent the first few seasons of his NFL career with the Los Angeles Rams to fill that open 17th spot.
Neal has played in 10 total games and began this year on the Rams' practice squad. He was a game day elevation twice before being released on Oct. 27.
A few hours later, the team announced that they released wide receiver Cameron Dorner and offensive guard Jake Kubas from the practice squad, opening up two more spots on the practice-only unit. Dorner, who was one of the first UDFAs the team signed back in the spring, had a strong summer with the third-string offense . He was released from the roster after the preseason and returned on the practice squad.
Kubas, who played for the New York Giants this summer, signed to the team's initial practice squad and was one of the depth options on that unit alongside Andrew Rupcich, Xavier Newman-Johnson and Lorenz Metz. He wasn't called up once this year.
Reiss also reported that safety Elliott Davison , who was released Monday from the 53-man roster, will stick around and re-sign with the practice squad.
The Patriots currently have one open roster spot on the practice squad as they prepare for their first practice of the week tomorrow afternoon.

full_text:

They were without their top three receivers, their starting guards and their second-best running back. They'd also lose their top tight end in the process. Still, they left Hard Rock Stadium happy.y
"I thought we started OK," Mike Vrabel said after the 24-19 win. "We got going, we had a field goal, and then didn't finish off drives, missed a field goal, defensively gave up some longer drives, some conversions. I give them a lot of credit, they competed. ... But also, I think we hurt ourselves. Again, we just have to try to stay out of our own way."
