title: Patriots Trade Deadline Tracker: Every Rumor for New England with 1 Week to Go
full_text:
The NFL's trade deadline was pushed back a week this year, so the New England Patriots and 31 other teams will have until Nov. 10 to try and get deals done this season.
The Patriots , currently sitting at 4-3 and in second place in the AFC East, could end up being active on the market. Injuries across the board and potential depth issues at other places could led Eliot Wolf and Mike Vrabel to try and improve the team somehow, someway.
Aleady in this calendar year, the Patriots have made a few trades. Back in March, they shipped away Garrett Bradbury and Marte Mapu before acquiring A.J. Brown in a block buster deal with the Philadelphia Eagles three months later. During the summer, Kayshon Boutte was dealth to the Houston Texans and during roster cuts, the Patriots also sent draft picks for Corey Kiner and Walter Rouse.
So could they end up making a deal mid-season? Here's all the rumors, quotes and storylines that are surrounding the Patriots as the trade deadline looms.
The Patriots signed Carlton Davis last year to a three-year deal, but his name has now been thrown around in deals two years in. The veteran cornerback, who's missed several games with a neck injury, could be on the move — according to SI's Albert Breer.
"This is about the age of the team and if you look at the roster big picture," Breer said . "They’ve gotten older at a lot of key spots and they aren’t exactly flush with draft capital over the next couple of years. ... They’re going to have to find a way over the next, three, four, five years to make the roster younger particularly after they pay Drake Maye. They’re trying to creatively look at this."
Davis has been the Patriots' most physical cornerback when he's healthy, but the 29-year-old is one of the older players on the roster. The Patriots could try and offload both his playing abilities and his expensive contract for a chance to get younger in the secondary.
The Patriots have a lot of money tied up to the interior of their defense line, with Milton Williams ($28.5 million) and Christian Barmore ($17.1 million) being paid very well for this season. But Barmore, who's played just 41.9% of the snaps this season, hasn't been someone that's been a consistent player so far.
According to Breer , the defensive tackle "could be had" on the trade market after falling behind Cory Durden on the depth chart. Barmore has two more years after this season on his four-year, $84 million extension he signed in 2024 before hitting the open market.
This season, the 27-year-old has six total tackles, three sacks and a forced fumble.
Could the Patriots — the team with Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs on injured reserve — end up adding a wideout? ESPN reported that Indianapolis Colts wideout Josh Downs requested a trade after a pair of his teammates were shipped away on Tuesday.
Downs spent two seasons with Drake Maye at North Carolina, scoring a career-high 11 touchdowns during the 2022 season. The Patriots only have four healthy wide receivers on the active roster right now, but adding Downs for what could be a cheap deal might help elevate the passing attack.
Seven games in, Downs has 26 receptions for 307 yards.
A few days after the Patriots' 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears , Vrabel spoke with reporters about how the team is stacking up prior to their Week 8 game with the Miami Dolphins. One of the questions posed was about if the Patriots will be active on the phones.
His answer left the door open for a deal being made, but the head coach also didn't officially dig a potential move into the sand. Like most coach-speak, Vrabel discussed how the Patriots would make moves to try and improve the overall roster in totality, and not try to single out a certain spot that needs upgrading.
"We're going to try to do everything we can to help the team," Vrabel said. "I don't know if we will or we won't. I would imagine that we'll try to do everything that we can to help us, within reason, and makes sense for us. I don't know how you want to interpret that, but I'm sure we'll listen and talk, just like everybody else does."
Some positions that the Patriots could end up attacking are running back, offensive guard (with a myriad of injuries hitting that group), interior defensive line and some backup cornerbacks.

title: Drake Maye's Near-Perfect Second Half Leads Patriots to Win Over Miami
full_text:
The New England Patriots entered the second half trailing 13-3 to their division opponent Miami Dolphins, while Drake Maye threw for just 53 yards during the Patriots' first half struggles. When Maye came out of the break, he wore the helmet of an MVP-caliber quarterback, leading his team to comeback victory on the road against a divisional opponent.
In the second half, Maye threw for 146 yards and completed all but one passing attempt. He held a perfect passer rating of 158.3 and notched three total touchdowns.
His first score was a familiar sight for Patriots fans, as he found Kyle Williams 43 yards down the field for a touchdown. His second passing touchdown came in the fourth quarter on a scrambling throw to DeMario Douglas on the sideline, who finished the 48-yard score with his legs to give the Patriots a two-score lead.
With those two passing touchdowns, Maye holds the lead for most passing touchdowns of 30-plus yards (14) over the course of the past two seasons. This was also Maye's fifth-straight game with two or more passing touchdowns.
One of Maye's best plays wasn't attributed to his talented arm. The 24-year-old ran to his right on an option play, faked a toss to Rhamondre Stevenson, and cut past the defender who followed Maye's phantom pitch. The two-yard score gave New England the lead and shifted the energy of the game.
Maye compared his rushing touchdown to a two-on-one fast break in basketball.
"Hopefully you make the guy guess wrong and we did," he said postgame.
Eyes on the ball! Fake option pitch from Drake Maye sets up the touchdown. pic.twitter.com/UAXPK3KBjC
In addition to his impressive second half statistics, Maye had an 80% completion rate, completing 16-of-20 passing attempts — his best completion percentage of the season.
Maye contributed the offense's first half conservativeness to the rain impacting their game plan. He said, "This ball, you see different times with the weather, it can be an issue."
The third-year superstar quarterback was also able to lead the Patriots to their fifth win of the season without three of his top wideout receivers in A.J. Brown, Mack Hollins, and Romeo Doubs. Their victory over Miami was the second time this season New England was able to leave with a win after trailing at halftime ( their win against Buffalo in Week 4 was the other occurence).
"He'll be a great quarterback in the National Football League," head coach Mike Vrabel said.
"He just throws to the open guy and controls our offense and gets guys in the right spot," Vrabel said when asked about playing with a dwindled receiver group. "That's being one of the best quarterbacks in the league, that's what the job description requires."

title: 3 Patriots Who Could Be On The Move as Trade Deadline Approaches
full_text:
Are the New England Patriots buyers or sellers? We won't know for certain until the NFL's Nov. 10 trade deadline passes. Until then, speculation will continue to surround which players could be on the move if another team picks up the phone. Let's take a look at a few Patriots players whose names could come up in trade discussions.
According to Sports Illustrated's Albert Breer , the Patriots are willing to move Barmore, with a potential asking price of a fourth-round pick. "My understanding is the price would be about a fourth-round pick, and he may be tradable because if you look at his contract, he's making $13.3 million this year," Breer said. "His numbers balloon after this year, those numbers aren't guaranteed. So, a team could wind up walking away from that if they did trade for him. But this is a player that very clearly, you know, is available. And if somebody's willing to swing the Patriots a fourth-round pick, I think something could happen." Barmore's contract is set to become significantly more expensive following this season. According to Spotrac , he carries a projected cap hit of $23.6 million in 2027 and $24.6 million in 2028.
On top of that, Barmore has seen his role shift toward a more pass-rush-heavy assignment, resulting in a lower snap share compared to fellow defensive linemen Milton Williams and Cory Durden. "Just trying to find ways to have him affect the quarterback, try to make that his primary role," Mike Vrabel told the media. "We try to play everybody, try to play as many guys we can and find roles for everybody." With the Patriots getting solid contributions from depth players like Durden and Leonard Taylor III, and Barmore's future cap hits increasing, New England could view this as an opportunity to bolster their draft capital moving forward. If New England were to move off Barmore, however, they don't have an immediate answer to fill his production. No Patriot defensive lineman has more sacks (3.5) than Barmore through Week 8.
While no official reports indicate the Patriots are considering a trade involving Henderson, a series of interesting roster moves has fueled speculation about the second-year back. Henderson has struggled to replicate his rookie success, with his playing time fluctuating throughout the season. He's averaging just 18 offensive snaps per game. In his most recent outing, a Week 7 loss to the Chicago Bears, Henderson rushed just three times for nine yards.
Heading into Week 8, Henderson notably missed Wednesday's practice. Reporters spotted him in the Patriots' locker room, out of uniform, before he left the facility wearing a backpack. It was later announced that Henderson was dealing with an illness , which ultimately ruled him out against Miami. With Henderson sidelined, New England was expected to elevate running back Lan Larison from the practice squad for Sunday's game. However, the Patriots instead signed Larison to the active roster , bringing their total number of running backs to four. "Well, we just had a spot open and felt like that would give us some flexibility down the road," Mike Vrabel told the media Monday. The Patriots coaching staff has continued to express confidence in Henderson moving forward, but his varying role and the addition of Larison have raised questions about his place in the backfield. He would make an enticing option for any team looking to get younger at the position and add an explosive element to their rushing rotation.
Appearing on NBC Sports Boston, Breer also suggested veteran cornerback Carlton Davis could be on the move. Davis originally signed with New England to a three-year, $54 million contract that could reach $60 million ahead of the 2025 season. He's been a serviceable addition as a Patriot, particularly in the postseason, where he recorded two interceptions during New England's run to the Super Bowl. However, injuries have hampered his tenure in New England. In 2026, Davis has appeared in just four games while dealing with a neck injury. If the Patriots want to move on from Davis, they could wait until the offseason. His contract includes a potential out following the 2026 season that would leave New England with a $5.5 million dead cap hit. Still, if a cornerback-needy team expresses interest before the deadline, the Patriots could be willing to explore their options.

title: Patriots Lose Competitive Veteran LB to Lions
full_text:
The same day where the New England Patriots signed running back Terrell Jennings to the practice squad, they also lost someone.
According to ESPN's Adam Schefter, linebacker K.J. Britt has signed a contract with the Detroit Lions active roster. The 27-year-old, who was the only linebacker on New England's roster, will be a replacement for both Jimmy Rolder and Jack Campbell — who both got hurt on Sunday.
Britt signed with the Patriots in free agency this offseason after stints with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Miami Dolphins. His contract was a one-year deal worth $1.4 million and at the time, he would be entering a competition for a depth role behind starters Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss.
"Bunch of blue-collar guys. I like it. This is where I wanted to be," Britt said in May. "I wanted to come up here and work with guys that are like-minded, because you have some prima-donnas in this league. You have some guys who like to play the game because of the fame that comes with it. You’ve got some guys who love to play the game because it’s a game — it’s the game that you’ve been playing since you were young.
"A lot of these guys, man, they love ball. They love football. When you love football and you’re around a lot of guys who love football, it’s contagious. It makes you want to step up your game. It makes you want to compete at a different level. It changes how you approach everything. I can see it in this building."
He would have some bright spots during training camp and appear to be on the cusp of making the 53-man roster during points in time. During the second preseason game, he had three tackles, recording a TFL and forcing a fumble against the Indianapolis Colts . But the Patriots got production out of rookies Namdi Obiazor and Khalil Jacobs, who both made the initial roster over Britt. They'd sign Britt to the practice squad before the regular season began .
Britt got one elevation to the active roster through the first eight weeks of the season, making his Patriots debut in a 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Oct. 11. He had no defensive snaps and 14 special teams snaps, recording one total tackle during his playing time.
Most recenty, Britt — a former college teammate of Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis at Auburn — spoke to Patriots On SI about how to prepare for a player like Willis in practice.
"Freak athlete," Britt said. "Great competitor, loves football. Just a good dude. He's just overall a good dude. Once he gets going, he's explosive. He's dynamic and he can really run."
The Patriots now have an open roster spot on both their 53-man roster (they released second-year safety Elliott Davison Monday) and on the practice squad.

title: Saints Make Coaching Staff Changes, but Mickey Loomis Shouldn't Escape Blame
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints have fired run game coordinator T.J. Paganetti following their Week 8 bye, according to Nick Underhill of NewOrleans.Football.
The decision comes as head coach Kellen Moore attempts to fix one of the NFL's least productive rushing attacks, with New Orleans sitting at 2-5 through seven games.
The Saints have parted ways with run game coordinator TJ Paganetti, according to sources. Paganetti came from Philadelphia, where he helped architect the run game and was part of developing one of the league’s best offensive lines
The Saints are averaging just 86 rushing yards per game and 3.5 yards per carry, with their struggles reaching a low point in a 16-10 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris on Oct. 25.
New Orleans had one of the most embarrassing rushing performances in franchise history, managing only 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts and averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Paganetti joined Moore's staff in 2025 after spending 10 seasons with the Philadelphia Eagles , where he helped develop one of the NFL's most dominant rushing attacks.
During Philadelphia's Super Bowl-winning 2024 season, the Eagles rushed for a franchise-record 3,048 yards and averaged 179.3 yards per game, ranking second in the NFL.
However, that success never consistently translated to New Orleans.
While Paganetti deserves some responsibility, the Saints' problems extend beyond coaching.
While Moore is getting heat for the Saints’ offensive struggles, ultimately the biggest issue with the New Orleans Saints is the person who hired him: general manager Mickey Loomis .
Loomis is responsible for building the roster, including the backfield and the offensive line, the two weakest links on the Saints.
The running back room, featuring Alvin Kamara , Travis Etienne , Kendre Miller and CJ Donaldson , hasn't delivered consistent production.
Etienne's placement on injured reserve has further complicated matters, especially when the Saints signed him on a four-year, $52 million deal.  Kamara, by contrast, hasn't shown the same explosiveness that made him one of the NFL's most dynamic playmakers.
The offensive line also remains a concern despite significant investments, including first-round selections Kelvin Banks Jr. , Taliese Fuaga and Cesar Ruiz along with the free agent signing of David Edwards for $76 million
New Orleans has struggled to consistently create running lanes, particularly along the interior, leaving its running backs with limited opportunities.
Paganetti arrived in 2025 after spending 10 seasons with Philadelphia, where he helped develop one of the NFL's most productive rushing attacks. However, the Eagles also had considerably better offensive line personnel.
Moore and Loomis must now share responsibility for determining whether the Saints' struggles stem from their offensive philosophy, player development or questionable roster construction.
Firing Paganetti sends a message that the current production is unacceptable, but changing coordinators won't automatically solve personnel deficiencies.

title: Saints Midseason Stock Report: 4 Bright Spots Amid a Disappointing Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints enter their bye week with a disappointing 2-5 record despite the hype around the Saints being contenders to possibly win the NFC South.
While the season has been anything but positive, the team still has bright spots on both offense and defense.
Here's a look at four players who have performed above and beyond as we reach the midseason point.
Tyler Shough hasn't been perfect, but the second-year quarterback continues to show encouraging signs of development under coach Kellen Moore .
Through seven games, Shough has completed 67% of his passes for 1,721 yards, 13 touchdowns and six interceptions. He's also contributed 111 rushing yards and two touchdowns.
His pass yardage and touchdown totals are both in the top 10 as he is tied for seventh in passing touchdowns and ninth in passing yards, but for a majority of the season he was either No. 1 or No. 2 in passing yards.
Those numbers are impressive considering New Orleans' struggles establishing a consistent rushing attack and protecting its quarterback.
Despite occasional mistakes, Shough has demonstrated improved accuracy, pocket presence and command of Moore's offense.
If he continues developing and limits turnovers, the Saints should feel increasingly confident about their quarterback situation.
Wide receiver Chris Olave has shown why the Saints gave him a 4-year, $132 million extension.
Through seven games, the former first-round pick has caught 49 passes (fourth in the NFL) for 636 yards (third in the NFL) and two touchdowns, averaging 90.9 receiving yards per game.
He opened the season with four 100-yard performances in his first four games, including a dominant 182-yard outing against Detroit .
Chase Young has arguably been New Orleans' most impressive player on defense through seven games.
The former No. 2 overall pick has recorded seven sacks, establishing himself as one of the NFL's most productive pass rushers.
Out of 50 edge rushers with at least 125 pass rushes, Young ranked second with a 90.0 Pro Football Focus pass-rush grade.
Young is on pace to record over 15 sacks, potentially putting him in the conversation for Pro Bowl recognition.
Though Young draws much of the spotlight, Carl Granderson is quietly putting together a standout year as well.
Across seven contests, the experienced defensive end has registered 25 tackles alongside 5.5 sacks, highlighted by a 1.5-sack effort versus Pittsburgh .
Granderson's current trajectory puts him on track for roughly 13 sacks, setting up a potential career mark.
Combined, Granderson and Young have racked up 12.5 sacks, forming one of the few reliable highlights for New Orleans' defense.
Even with the unit's broader difficulties, his growth paired with Young gives the Saints a high-caliber pass-rush duo for the future.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' 16-10 Loss to Steelers in Paris
full_text:
Hoping to build momentum ahead of their upcoming bye week after a major victory last week, the New Orleans Saints instead fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday in Paris, exposing several recurring issues under coach Kellen Moore .
New Orleans' offensive struggles continued as missed scoring opportunities proved costly as the Saints fell to 2-5.
From an emerging young playmaker to a disastrous rushing performance, here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Saints' disappointing loss to Pittsburgh .
One of the few bright spots in New Orleans' disappointing loss was rookie wide receiver Barion Brown's emergence.
The sixth-round pick got a chance to show his explosiveness, finishing with three receptions for 57 yards and adding another 97 yards on four kickoff returns.
His biggest offensive play came in the first half when he caught a 49-yard pass from Tyler Shough , setting up Daniel Carlson 's 38-yard field goal.
Brown also returned a kickoff 42 yards in the second quarter, setting up a possession that ended with Shough's 1-yard touchdown pass to Devaughn Vele .
Despite those contributions, Brown received just three targets.
That limited involvement raises questions about whether coach Kellen Moore is maximizing one of the offense's most explosive young playmakers.
With rookie Jordyn Tyson still sidelined by a hamstring injury, Brown has a chance to become a more consistent contributor alongside Chris Olave and Vele.
New Orleans gets a vital jolt on offense from Brown's explosive speed and big-play dynamism.
Following a sluggish 281-yard performance against Pittsburgh, integrating him must become a top priority for the Saints. To fully leverage the rookie's skill set, Moore ought to scheme designed touches, vertical routes and run-after-catch opportunities for him. Given how much he has delivered on minimal opportunities, Brown has earned a larger role.
In a narrow 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, kicker Daniel Carlson missed a crucial 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter — his fourth failure in 11 attempts this season. This ongoing volatility in special teams poses a critical problem for the 2-5 Saints.
The fourth-quarter miss was particularly damaging because New Orleans had already wasted a promising red-zone opportunity earlier in the second half. Rather than positioning themselves to tie or take the lead with a field goal late in the game, the Saints remained trapped in a six-point deficit.
Carlson's 63.6% conversion rate stands in sharp contrast to Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who accounted for nine points by flawlessly making all three of his field goals (from 28, 47 and 39 yards).
With three one-score defeats recorded this year, New Orleans simply lacks the margin for error to withstand repeated scoring blunders in tight contests. Carlson's continuous field goal woes add to head coach Kellen Moore's list of bye-week priorities, as unreliable special teams only exacerbate the team's offensive stalls, defensive breakdowns and turnovers.
While much of the focus has centered on Tyler Shough's growth, an inept rushing attack still severely limits the Saints' offensive ceiling.
Sunday's outing represented a new low point for the ground game.
New Orleans generated a paltry 18 rushing yards across 17 carries, resulting in an abysmal 1.1 yards per carry.
The stat line is even more damning because Shough — a quarterback whose primary role isn't to lead the run game — was the team's top rusher with just 7 yards on three carries.
It is downright appalling that primary backs Alvin Kamara (six carries, five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries, six yards) both logged more rush attempts than total yards gained.
This embarrassing output highlights a backfield without a true lead option, further compounded by an offensive line that failed to establish leverage up front.
Such complete non-production is intolerable at any level of football—especially when relying on a developing quarterback to sustain drive after drive.
By stifling the run, Pittsburgh's defense put the burden entirely on Shough's shoulders.
Even with Shough connecting on nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans repeatedly stalled because it lacked offensive balance.
Unfortunately, this isn't merely a single bad afternoon.
The Saints' season-long inability to establish the run has made the offense predictable and easy for physical front sevens to counter.

title: 3 Takeaways From Saints' Loss to Steelers: Same Problems, Different Country
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints traveled across the Atlantic Ocean hoping to build momentum heading into their bye week and salvage their season. Instead, they returned home with its fourth loss in five games and it just seems like another repeating nightmare for Who Dat Nation.
New Orleans fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in Paris, dropping to 2-5 through seven games under second-year coach Kellen Moore . It was the NFL's first regular-season game in France.
Despite another efficient passing performance from quarterback Tyler Shough , the Saints struggled to establish their rushing attack, failed to capitalize on scoring opportunities and couldn't get off the field defensively when it mattered most.
The loss marked New Orleans' third one-possession defeat this season, reinforcing concerns about the team's ability to execute in critical situations.
Here are three takeaways from another disappointing performance from the Saints performance.
For all the attention surrounding Shough's development, New Orleans' inability to run the football continues to undermine its offense.
Sunday's performance might have been its most concerning yet.
The Saints finished with just 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts, averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Even more alarming, Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards on three attempts. However, he is a quarterback and that is not his job.
But for Alvin Kamara (six carries for five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries for six yards) to have more carries than rushing yards is disgusting.
It shows the lack of life in a running back room without a primary option, compounded by an offensive line struggling to create leverage.
That level of production is unacceptable for any offense regardless of the level of play, especially one relying on a young quarterback to consistently move the ball.
Pittsburgh's defense shut down the run, forcing Shough to carry nearly the entire offensive load.
Although Shough completed nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans could not consistently finish drives because it lacked balance.
The problems extend beyond one disappointing performance.
New Orleans has struggled to generate consistent production on the ground throughout the season, making the offense increasingly predictable against physical defensive fronts.
Because of the rushing problems, the Saints had to rely on Shough again.
Shough did everything you could ask of him, completing 30 of 38 passes for 278 yards and a touchdown. However, one costly mistake ultimately changed the game's complexion.
Trailing 13-10 at the start of the second half, New Orleans put together a 13-play drive that moved the offense inside Pittsburgh's 10-yard line as the Saints appeared positioned to take their first lead of the afternoon.
Instead, Shough threw a pass intended for Chris Olave , which Steelers linebacker Payton Wilson intercepted at the Pittsburgh 11-yard line.
The turnover erased a scoring opportunity and let Pittsburgh respond with a field goal, extending its lead to 16-10.
The interception proved costly, but it also highlighted the impossible position Shough has found himself in because of New Orleans' offensive struggles.
Despite completing nearly 79% of his passes, the quarterback could not afford even one mistake because the Saints had virtually no rushing attack to complement him.
That is an unrealistic expectation for any quarterback, much less one still developing at the NFL level.
Shough showed he could move the football against a Pittsburgh defense, distributing the ball effectively and keeping New Orleans competitive despite a one-dimensional offensive approach.
However, his play reinforced a troubling reality: when Shough plays well, the Saints can win; when he makes one mistake, the operation unravels.
Until Moore builds a credible run game and finishes drives, Shough bears an unreasonable load and New Orleans must create an offense where its quarterback does not need to be perfect to win.
Unless the Saints give Shough a credible rushing attack and adequate protection, they risk repeating a familiar chapter in franchise history: asking a talented young quarterback to overcome problems far beyond his control, much like Archie Manning decades ago.
Daniel Carlson 's fourth missed field goal in 11 attempts this season — a 52-yarder in the fourth quarter — kept New Orleans trailing in a 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, highlighting a critical special teams weakness for the 2-5 Saints.
The missed 52-yard attempt came while the Saints trailed 16-10 in the fourth quarter, keeping Pittsburgh's lead at six points. Carlson's 63.6% success rate contrasts with Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who converted all three attempts (28, 47 and 39 yards) for nine points.
The fourth-quarter miss was especially costly as New Orleans had already squandered a promising red-zone drive earlier in the second half. Instead of entering the final minutes needing only a field goal to tie or lead, the Saints remained six points behind.
Carlson's kicking struggles add to head coach Kellen Moore's bye-week concerns. For a team hampered by offensive inefficiency, defensive lapses and turnovers, unreliable special teams further shrink a narrow margin for error.
With three one-score losses this season, New Orleans cannot afford missed points. Sunday's loss highlights that the Saints lack the margin for error to overcome recurring scoring mistakes in tight games.

Up next for New Orleans is a formidable Pittsburgh defense that ranks among the league's top groups: 9th in total yards allowed per game (307.5), 8th in passing defense (204.3 YPG), and 6th in third-down conversion rate allowed (32.5%).
With both teams competing to stay viable in the playoff hunt, this international game provides New Orleans an ideal opportunity to show meaningful progress.

title: Zaire Barnes Has Become a Quiet Difference-Maker for Giants’ Special Teams
full_text:
You won’t find New York Giants linebacker Zaire Barnes appearing in any TV commercials or ad campaigns.
Heck, you might not even recognize him if you passed him on the street.
But teammates and opponents know full well who he is: one of the faces of the Giants’ revamped special teams unit and a quiet difference-maker.
Barnes, who has played 79% of the Giants’ special teams snaps this season, currently leads the team with 11 special teams tackles (six solos) and also has a forced fumble, according to league stats.
His special teams tackle total with assists ranks second most in the league, behind Smael Mondon of the Eagles, who has 12 combined tackles.
Barnes, a converted college safety, seemed surprised when told where he ranked league-wide.
“I give a lot of credit to all the guys on the special teams unit, you know?” he told New York Giants On SI. “Especially on the punt team — (punter) Jordan (Stout) gives us great punts, which allows us to cover.
“And (assistant head coach/special teams coordinator) Coach Chris (Horton) allows us to get schemed down, while trusting his guys to get down there and make plays. So it’s definitely a collective group unit thing.”
As a key part of that group, Barnes, who also serves as depth at inside linebacker, has embraced what many view as the dirty work that comes with special teams. He first developed that mindset with the Jets, who drafted him in the sixth round out of Western Michigan in 2023.
“When I was first drafted over there, they saw me as a special teams guy,” Barnes recalled.
“Things obviously changed with the coaching staff situation, but at the same time, I learned a lot of great things, a lot of great techniques from Coach (Chris) Banjo, Coach Gobe (Michael Ghobrial), Coach (Brant) Boyer — all those guys. They taught me everything, and I wouldn’t be here without them.”
Then there were his teammates like Justin Hardy and Marcelino McCrary-Ball, two he credited in particular with mentoring him.
All of that, plus his own inner hunger and motivation from not being a high draft pick, has driven Barnes to put aside any ego about not playing on defense or not being one of the team’s A-listers.
And he wouldn’t have it any other way.
Having fun on the job is important, and Barnes said there is plenty of fun to be had playing special teams, something he discovered with the Jets.
Barnes, who likes to be challenged, said special teams offers that challenge — and it might not be for everyone.
“You kinda gotta be able to think on your feet pretty quickly just as you’re running down there,” he said.
“You don’t know where a block could be coming from. And just being able to slow down while running full speed and being able to make a tackle or a block — I think it’s definitely a different skill set you gotta embrace.”
It’s also a mindset that has helped many players who weren’t big contributors on their position units build long, productive NFL careers.
“It’s all about just taking pride in your role and just understanding that this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity even to wear the uniform on any given Sunday,” Barnes said.
“I definitely wanna make an impact, be a leader for this unit, and I appreciate those guys having confidence in me going in there week in and week out and allowing me to be me,” he said.

title: Ranking the Giants’ 5 Most Beatable Opponents in the Race for the NFC East
full_text:
The New York Giants enjoyed a much-needed bye week, but as they return from the break, it's full steam ahead as they fight to maintain their lead and capture their first NFC East title since 2011, when they went on a deep, historic run to Super Bowl XLVI.
Head coach John Harbaugh's Giants earned some extra space between them and the two rival teams beneath them in the division standings, the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles, who each lost their Week 8 matchups to the Cardinals and Commanders while Big Blue watched from the couch.
With the 2026 season one of the most unpredictable ever, the reality is that getting over the finish line means the Giants must charge forth and handle their business in a select few games during the second half of their schedule that should lean in their favor.
One thing that Harbaugh's first year in charge has proven is that the Giants can compete with almost anybody with the gritty style of football they've displayed almost every week so far.
With their 4-2-1 start and momentum building as the calendar turns to November, anything can happen the rest of the way. But in looking at the rest of the Giants' opponents, there are five teams — one of which the Giants will see twice in the coming weeks — that New York should be able to record a “W” against, ranked in order of most challenging to easiest.
While the NFC East has failed to impress many outsiders, the NFC North is arguably the league's best division this season.
The group's four teams are all in the race for the postseason entering Week 9, including the Detroit Lions, who will host the Giants at Ford Field in Week 16, for the second time in as many years.
Last season, the two franchises played an offensive thriller in which the Giants built an early 17-7 lead behind the leadership of Jameis Winston, who started in place of Jaxson Dart.
The Giants' run defense was ultimately their biggest weakness in slowing down Jahmyr Gibbs and Detroit's backfield in the second half and overtime, leading to a tough 34-27 loss in extra time.
The story hasn't changed much for the Lions' offense led by quarterback Jared Goff, which sits among the top three in total production after seven games.
Still, their defense is what leaves hope for teams like the Giants, whose offense is newly functional, to contend in another potential shootout.
Detroit has struggled to protect the end zone, ranking 28th in opponent red zone scoring percentage (74.1%) and allowing at least 21 points in five of seven contests.
They could also trouble the Giants' desire to lead off with the ground game by allowing an average of 96.6 rushing yards per game.
Still, in the passing realm, they have been picked apart at the highest rate in the NFL, including allowing the most passing touchdowns (18) as their red zone efforts have plummeted.
The Giants' aerial attack hasn't flashed much beyond the talents of Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely, who have combined for 1,000 of the team's 1,700 receiving yards and 7 of 11 receiving touchdowns through seven games.
The way the group carved up the Texans defense in Week 7 behind the heroics of J.J. McCarthy suggests he could be the difference-maker in helping New York get over the top of the Lions this time around.
The Cleveland Browns might have been one of the biggest surprises early in the season, but what has held them back is their inability to put together a complete effort on both sides of the ball every Sunday.
Despite sitting at 5-3 and one game out of first place in the AFC North, the Browns share a similar lack of belief with the Giants because of who they've beaten.
The Browns opened the 2026 campaign with a 4-1 start behind three consecutive scratch-and-claw wins over the Buccaneers, Panthers, and Steelers.
Since Week 5, they've lost to the Jets with under 200 yards of total offense and two turnovers before barely etching out wins against the Titans and Ravens, and most recently getting blown out by Pittsburgh in the second meeting last Sunday.
Many outsiders doubted Cleveland because their quarterback situation seemed largely undecided at the start of the season. Deshaun Watson returned and reclaimed the reins from Shedeur Sanders, but the veteran's presence hasn't consistently reignited their offense.
As a result, the Browns have the league's fourth-worst scoring offense, which struggles to sustain long drives and chokes inside opponents' 20-yard line (48.0% red zone scoring rate).
Their best target is a second-year tight end in Harold Fannin Jr., and their backfield hasn't seen one back command the No. 1 role while averaging under four yards per carry.
Their calling card is the defense, which has limited opposing offenses to the sixth-fewest total yards and the fifth-lowest yards per pass attempt.
Both factors spell what could be a rock fight for the Giants, but the catalyst could be New York's RPO-style offense, in which the threat of McCarthy taking off could open up chances to gash the Browns on the ground.
If the Giants can strike a few blows in positive territory early and then control the flow of the game with their running back room, this matchup could turn into another one of the outings like the one against Tennessee, where Harbaugh and company dominate the clock and leave Watson few chances to make a push down the stretch.
Depending on how the next few weeks unfold for both rival franchises, the winner of the NFC East could be decided in the Giants' second meeting with the Dallas Cowboys in Week 17.
Harbaugh's tenure as Giants head coach got off to an impressive start as his team finally upended the Cowboys, 28-20, on the primetime stage behind nearly 400 yards of total offense and a pass rush that finally got pressure on quarterback Dak Prescott.
A lot will be different for Big Blue when they travel to Arlington to face Prescott and company again. They won't have Jaxson Dart under center or Brian Burns leading the outside linebacker room, and questions remain as to how healthy the Giants' roster will be at that point in a long season.
Based on what J.J. McCarthy has shown in his two recent outings, there shouldn't be much of a decline in what the Giants can achieve, as they'll likely have to trade punches with the Cowboys' offense, which is building its fifth top-10 season in the last six years.
Piling up points has been an imperative for Dallas given that its defense has been marred by injuries and its porous secondary has been the main culprit in allowing the NFL's highest average of 385.4 total yards per contest through eight games.
If the Cowboys' defensive woes show no signs of improvement as the second half progresses (they have matchups with the 49ers, Seahawks, Rams, and Jaguars remaining), the penultimate game against the Giants could be meaningless for Dallas if they rack up a few more losses in those tougher contests.
With the Giants at 4-2-1 and also set to face some of those same opponents in the next month, there is no guarantee the Cowboys won't take advantage of chances to catch up to their rivals and force an intriguing revenge game as the playoff picture comes into focus.
What we do know is they have the pieces to gash the Cowboys a second time, and if the pass rush can get home to Prescott a few more times, New York's fourth-quarter grit could be the key to sweeping their division foe.
The Giants will get their first chance to spar with the Philadelphia Eagles on the road in Week 9, but for the first time in almost two decades, Big Blue has a real shot to sweep the Birds.
Philadelphia will welcome the Giants to The Linc with an ugly 2-6 record and riding the second-longest active losing streak behind the winless Chargers.
Injuries to key pieces on both sides have largely steered their downfall from being a perennial contender for the NFC East and the Super Bowl, including the loss of starting quarterback Jalen Hurts to blood clots and multiple offensive weapons dealing with nagging ailments.

title: Eagles Are Down, Giants Are Rising: Why Week 9 Could Break the Philly Curse
full_text:
As New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh’s father, legendary college coach Jack Harbaugh, likes to say, “Who’s got it better than us?”
No phrase could more precisely describe the feeling in East Rutherford as the Giants return from their bye week having won without playing a snap.
While the Giants were watching from their living rooms, results around the NFC East fell perfectly in their favor.
The Dallas Cowboys suffered a crushing overtime loss to the Arizona Cardinals after Jacoby Brissett was benched and kicker Chad Ryland missed an extra point that would have won it in regulation.
Several hours later, the Giants also got some help from the Washington Commanders, who trounced the struggling Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday Night Football , leaving the other three division members with at least four losses. Meanwhile, New York sits pretty at 4-2-1 coming off the bye.
Harbaugh’s Giants are returning with growing belief in their chances to win the division and potentially make some noise in the postseason, but that all starts in Week 9 as they visit the Philadelphia Eagles for an important rivalry game with some sour history for the franchise.
And as the team returns with fresh legs and the trade deadline looms, SI’s Conor Orr continues to ride high on the Giants, lifting them two more spots to No. 15 in his latest MMQB NFL power rankings poll .
It’s no bold statement to say Philadelphia hasn’t been a friendly place for the Giants in one of their biggest rivalries.
Not only have the Birds dominated the regular-season series for much of the past decade, winning 13 of 17 meetings dating back to the start of the 2016 season, but they’ve also held down the fort at Lincoln Financial Field, winning every contest against the Giants since 2013.
Granted, the Eagles have been in the midst of a successful run in that timeframe, including five first-place finishes in the NFC East, eight playoff berths, and three Super Bowl appearances, two of which ended in championships.
That Philadelphia team hasn’t been seen this season, though. The Eagles got off to a hot start at 2-0 but have since lost six straight games, falling into the division’s last-place hole as mounting injuries have taken away key players on both sides of the ball.
The most notable absence is quarterback Jalen Hurts, whose season ended after Week 5, when blood clots were discovered during an evaluation of a cleat injury suffered the week before against the Rams.
Without Hurts running the show, the Eagles have struggled to keep up with their opponents in recent weeks. Philadelphia’s offense has dropped to 30th in points scored and 32nd in total yardage, both their worst rankings since 2020, the last time they finished last in the NFC East.
It hasn’t just been the quarterback situation that has led to their downfall. Running back Saquon Barkley has also been dealing with a hamstring issue that is limiting him in games, and the Eagles’ offensive line lost some serious strength when right tackle Lane Johnson abruptly retired.
The Giants won’t feel any lost love for the Eagles when they head down I-95 to battle their heated rivals and seek their second division victory of the season. With a weakened Eagles offense compared to a rising offense led by J.J. McCarthy, it’s fair to call this New York’s best chance in years to break the curse in Philadelphia.
Just over a year ago, the Giants hung close with the Eagles behind the talents of then-rookies Jaxson Dart and Cam Skattebo, whose rushing kept Philadelphia’s defense honest as the Giants led 14-10 late in the second quarter.
Not long after, the contest went south as Skattebo suffered a horrific season-ending ankle injury, and the vibes were sucked out of the Giants in what finished as a 38-20 rout that hastened the end of Brian Daboll’s tenure as head coach.
The Giants will return without a few key pieces, including Dart, who is out with a season-ending knee injury, and a potentially thin backfield, as they look to shake their little-brother status in this division series.
What they do have now is the right coaching in Harbaugh and a more capable quarterback in McCarthy, who proved to be the right starter two weeks ago in the win over Houston.

title: NFL Insider: Missing Draft Picks Are Complicating Giants’ Trade Efforts
full_text:
The New York Giants have made no secret of their desire to be involved in the trade market, as head coach John Harbaugh publicly invited teams interested in doing business with Big Blue to call.
According to NFL insider Jordan Schultz, the Giants have been making calls of their own. Schultz reported that the Giants have been among the most active in reaching out to other teams about trades.
However, the Giants, who have been heavily linked to Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor as trade talks heat up, have hit an obstacle in pursuing any acquisition: draft assets.
"The difficult part, teams have told me, is that the Giants don’t have a 4th- or 5th-round pick in 2027," Schultz reported.
Because Big Blue lacks fourth- and fifth-round picks in 2027 after using them in other trades, their efforts to make a deal have reportedly been complicated, as those picks are believed to be essential to making any sort of deal for Taylor.
While Tankathon projects a fourth-round comp pick being awarded to the Giants in the 2027 draft, that pick cannot be traded until it’s officially awarded, which won’t happen until next March.
Harbaugh, who said he is open to adding players before the trade deadline, acknowledged that it would probably be an uphill battle.
“It’s got to be something that is a need, that fits your financial profile, that fits your price tag,” the Giants head coach said.
“It’s not like we have a bunch of draft picks either. We’re not loaded with 12 or 13 draft picks, so we don’t have draft capital to burn. So, we have to be smart shoppers that way.”
Harbaugh didn’t rule out the possibility of dipping into the team’s 2028 draft class, telling reporters on Monday, “Yeah, it’s easier to put it on the credit card.”
Schultz’s report seems to back that possibility as coming to fruition, saying that the Giants may be willing to spend premium picks from the 2027 and/or 2028 drafts for the right player.
“From the sound of things, they’re pushing for bigger names who would require higher picks — and seem open to doing that,” Schultz said.
That would make sense, especially if the Giants hope to trade one of their quarterbacks (Jaxson Dart or J.J. McCarthy) next winter for premium picks in return.
The NFL trade deadline is 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 10. In addition to a running back, the Giants are thought to be looking for a defensive tackle to add to their defensive line.

title: Giants Reward Greg Newsome II’s Breakout Season With a Big Extension
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ cornerbacks room just locked in a key piece for the next three years.
Cornerback Greg Newsome II, who signed a one-year deal worth $8 million, including incentives, has agreed to terms with Big Blue on a three-year, $46 million extension that includes $32 million guaranteed, according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz .
Newsome, a first-round pick by the Browns in 2021, was traded to the Jaguars midseason in 2025.
The Giants were looking to replace Cor’Dale Flott, who went to the Tennessee Titans in free agency. They brought Newsome in to compete with Deonte Banks, Paulson Adebo, and, eventually, rookie second-round pick Colton Hood for a starting role.
Newsome grabbed a starting job early and has been a steady performer, enjoying the best season of his career, aside from a concussion that kept him out of the team’s Week 7 game.
He is currently allowing a 57.7% completion rate when targeted, which is a career low. He has also allowed just 52 yards after the catch, another career low, has yet to surrender a touchdown, and has four pass breakups and an interception for a career-best 62.0 coverage rating.
He has played 90% of the defensive snaps this season.
Extending Newsome gives the Giants flexibility to release Adebo next offseason, a move that would save $14 million against a $6.317 million dead money hit.
That money could be used to extend Deonte Banks, who is also in a contract year and has played well this season.

title: Giants Trade Deadline: Is Christian Barmore the Answer at Defensive Tackle?
full_text:
Should the New York Giants consider looking north via I-95 to fill their need at defensive tackle?
With the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline fast approaching, the Giants might be wise to check into the availability of New England Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore.
The sixth-year defender has reportedly been made available for trade by the cap-strapped Patriots, who are looking to create room beyond their $5.04 million in available space. If the Giants are interested in his services, New England may offer a reasonable asking price.
“They (Patriots) have listened and talked to other teams about trading him. My understanding is the price would be about a fourth-round pick,” said Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer during a recent appearance on NBC Sports Boston .
“This is a player that very clearly is available, and if somebody’s willing to swing the Patriots a fourth-round pick, I think something could happen.”
For the Giants, acquiring Barmore would come with its ups and downs.
A standout defensive tackle at the University of Alabama, Barmore was selected by the Patriots in the second round of the 2021 NFL Draft.
In his six seasons in Foxborough, the 6-foot-5, 315-pound lineman has compiled 175 total tackles, 51 quarterback hits, 26 tackles-for-loss, 21 run-stuffs, 19 sacks, and two forced fumbles. When healthy, he has been one of the most potent players on New England’s defensive front.
Just two years ago, Barmore missed all of 2024 training camp, preseason, and 13 regular-season games because of blood clots in his lungs.
Last year, his first full season since 2023, Barmore appeared in 17 games, compiling 29 total tackles, 11 quarterback hits, four tackles-for-loss, and two sacks.
In seven games for the Pats this season, Barmore has seven total tackles, 3.5 sacks, and one forced fumble.
Barmore’s ability to attack upfield makes him a potentially intriguing fit in coordinator Dennard Wilson’s defense, where he could contribute to both the pass rush and run defense. His knack for pushing the pocket and taking a stand against the run has earned him accolades throughout his career.
The veteran lineman plays with good leverage and is strong enough to take on double teams. He locates the ball quickly, chases with good effort, and has excellent range for his size.
Barmore has also demonstrated quick hands, which have made him effective in both stuffing the run and challenging the passer.
Barmore's best seasons came in 2022 and 2023 when working in tandem with linebacker Matthew Judon, who played under Giants head coach John Harbaugh with the Baltimore Ravens from 2016-20.
New England’s defensive duo was most effective in obvious passing situations. With Barmore drawing the attention of opposing blockers along the offensive line, Judon was often left one-on-one on the edge.
This freed the linebacker to pursue the quarterback, allowing Judon to set a career-high in sacks with 15.5 in 2023.
Given Barmore’s blend of size and athleticism, Wilson could use the former Crimson Tide tackle in a similar role, helping free players such as Abdul Carter, Kayvon Thibodeaux, and Arvell Reese to make the Giants’ pass rush more formidable down the stretch.
Despite possessing top-tier talent at his position, Barmore has seemingly fallen out of favor with New England’s defensive staff this season.
The 28-year-old has started only two games for the Patriots and has aligned on just 41.9 percent of snaps on defense, having slipped to third in the team’s rotation, behind starter Milton Williams and journeyman defender Cory Durden.
Barmore has demonstrated notable regression as a run defender. After logging a respectable 5.5 run-stuffs last year, he has failed to register a single run-stuff in 2026. Unsurprisingly, PFF has saddled him with a 44.8 run-defense grade.
Though he hasn’t statistically dazzled against the run, Barmore did his best work in those situations when supported by a dedicated nose tackle. Alongside Giants tackle D.J. Reader, he may find it a bit easier to focus on controlling the gap.
Like all major transactions, the Giants’ pursuit of Barmore is likely to come down to money.
On that basis, New York, with just north of $6.5 million in available salary cap space, is unlikely to encounter any insurmountable problems.
Barmore’s current salary cap number, per OverTheCap, is $17.1 million. By trading Barmore, the Patriots would save $8 million this season and up to $41 million over the next two, so they may be highly motivated to make a deal soon.
Many wonder what the financials for such a deal might look like.
“If Barmore were to be traded this week, the Giants would be on the hook for 10/18ths of his $12 million salary ($6,666,667) and a weekly installment of $75,000 for the ten games he would be active,” Patriots salary cap expert Miguel Benzan exclusively told Giants On SI. “The total would be $7,416,667.
“If Barmore were to be traded next week, the Giants would be on the hook for 9/18ths of his $12 million salary ($6 million) and nine installments of $75,000 for each game he was active  ($675,000 total),” Benzan continued. “The total would then be $6,675,000.”
To entice potential suitors, New England may want to highlight the fact that Barmore’s 2027 and 2028 salaries contain no guaranteed money.
Whether the reduced financial risk, combined with meeting many of their on-field needs, is enough to convince the Giants to trade for Barmore remains to be seen.

title: Giants Face Competition for Colts RB Jonathan Taylor, Odds Show
full_text:
Is today the day the New York Giants acquire Colts running back Jonathan Taylor?
If a move is coming for the Giants, it makes sense for it to go down today, as the players are off and don’t start a whirlwind stretch that will see them play two division games, a road game against the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday and a home date against Washington on Thursday, just four days apart.
But according to Hard Rock Bet , the Giants, who are at +375, are not the favorites to land Taylor. The Seahawks are the favorites (+225), followed by the Broncos (+250).
The good news for the Giants, if they want Taylor, is that circumstances might soon change those odds.
The Seahawks, who lost on Monday Night Football to the Chicago Bears, are fully healthy at running back after bringing back rookie Jadarian Price from IR to join Zach Charbonnet, Emanuel Wilson, George Holani, and Velus Jones Jr.
With Seattle’s backfield healthy, Denver would be the Giants’ biggest competition, if the odds are any indication.
The Broncos have been leaning on J.K. Dobbins, but he’s averaged only 3.25 yards per carry in eight games.
Their second option, R.J. Harvey, is more of a pass-catching back who doesn’t get a high volume of rushing touches. Thus far, he has just 24 carries in six games for 87 yards, a similarly paltry 3.62 yards per carry.
Taylor would certainly help boost the Broncos’ lethargic running game.
Others who are believed to be in the mix for Taylor’s services, according to the odds listed, include the Vikings, Packers, Bengals, and Patriots.
The Packers may be the most intriguing of that group given the situation with Josh Jacobs, who now faces new abuse allegations .
Green Bay appears intent on letting the process play out . Still, Jacobs’ situation notwithstanding, the Packers have the league’s worst rushing offense (60.6 yards per game) and average just 2.85 yards per carry, also last in the league.
With a chance to earn a postseason berth in the very crowded NFC North, they surely have an eye on fixing their struggling running game, and they appear to have the cap space ( $6.38 million ) to make a move.
The NFL trade deadline is 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 10.

title: Giants Trade Deadline: Which Veterans Make Sense to Deal?
full_text:
With the NFL trade deadline fast approaching, all indications point to the New York Giants being buyers rather than sellers.
But if there’s anything we’ve learned about this John Harbaugh-led team, it’s to expect the unexpected. That means that, in addition to potentially making a splash to land a player like Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, the Giants might be open to trading a player or two at positions of relative depth.
“I’ll put it out there,” Harbaugh said Monday when asked about the looming trade deadline. “We’re open for any call. Anybody who wants to call us, call.”
So which Giants players could draw interest from other teams? Here are three that come to mind.
Schmitz, in the final year of his contract, lost his starting job to Bryan Hudson in Week 4 and is now the backup.
Remember, the Giants added a couple of interior offensive linemen to their practice squad with some center experience, including rookie Geno VanDeMark and veteran Kendrick Green.
Schmitz, as we proposed last week , might interest the Green Bay Packers, a team in the uber-competitive NFC North. The Packers, who have gone through centers like crazy due to injury, hold a 5-3 record but sit in last place.
That said, if the season ended today, the entire NFC North would qualify for the postseason, with the Packers looking at the seventh seed. So an investment in a starting-caliber center to fill in while their starter, Sean Rhyan, recovers from a high ankle sprain wouldn’t necessarily be a bad move.
This might sound contradictory given how we have pounded the table for the Giants to add defensive line depth. Still, we were talking about defensive line depth that can be productive against the run, which, unfortunately, Alexander, the Giants’ third-round pick in 2025, has struggled to provide.
After coming on strong at the tail end of his rookie season, Alexander was perfectly positioned to earn a starting role on the defense. Instead, he has slowly fallen out of favor, largely because of his struggles in run defense.
Currently, Alexander ranks 49th in run defense grades among defensive linemen with at least 50 run-defense snaps. He also has a 3.6% run stop rate, which ties him for 111th in the same 133-player sample.
Things were so shaky for him that he was even a healthy scratch in the Giants’ Week 2 game against the Los Angeles Rams.
What Alexander can give a team is something in the pass rush. He has six pressures on the year, which puts him tied for 79th out of 88 defensive linemen with at least 100 pass-rush snaps.
It’s not much, but the Jacksonville Jaguars, whom the Giants face in Week 11, recently lost defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton to a season-ending quad injury, so they may be interested in doing business with the Giants again.
A potential trade of Nubin will probably be tricky, given that he’s been dealing with a neck injury that limited him to just one defensive snap in Week 7.
But Nubin, who earned a starting job as a rookie after being selected in the second round of the 2024 draft, hasn’t quite developed into the playmaker the Giants hoped he’d become.
In two and a half seasons of action, Nubin has 27 missed tackles (12.5% rate) and only 46 stops, both attributable to poor angles and positioning. He has a 106.8 career coverage rating and, even more strikingly, zero interceptions despite being a ballhawk at the University of Minnesota.
If the Giants subtract Nubin from the lineup, Ar’Darius Washington and Jason Pinnock can step in, with Raheem Layne on the practice squad. Washington and Pinnock are better in run support and can hold their own in coverage.
As for who could use safety help, Giants general manager Joe Schoen’s old boss, Brandon Beane in Buffalo, comes to mind. The Bills don’t have much salary cap space, just $3.927 million , so inheriting a player still on his rookie deal who would cost $87,549 per week on the roster could be an attractive option if, again, Nubin’s neck issue has resolved itself.

title: Giants Are Finally Favored at Philadelphia, and It’s Been a Long Time Coming
full_text:
Okay, 17 years , to be exact, but for the first time in nearly two decades, the New York Giants are favored in a game scheduled in Philadelphia.
According to FanDuel , the Giants are a 3-point favorite to beat the Eagles on the road, which, if they pull off the win, would be the Giants’ first victory in Philadelphia since 2013, when Eli Manning was still in his prime as the team’s quarterback.
The 2026 season has been a disaster for the Eagles, who were seeking their third straight division title. No team in the division has won three consecutive division titles since the Eagles did it from 2001 to 2004.
However, the Eagles (2-6), whose roster has been heavily depleted by injuries, trades, and retirements, are barely staying above water these days.
They have lost quarterback Jalen Hurts, who is dealing with blood clots in his lungs, and running backs Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley, and Dameon Pierce. They also traded center Cam Jurgens to the Ravens, and longtime tackle Lane Johnson retired.
The Eagles, who dropped their Week 8 game to the Washington Commanders 27-10, have lost six straight, with opponents scoring at least 20 points in five of the six losses. Some have grumbled that offensive coordinator Sean Mannion’s scheme isn’t a fit for the personnel they have.
The Giants are on the opposite end of the spectrum. They are coming off their bye after an impressive win the week prior against the Houston Texans. New York, which has had its share of injuries, is without starting quarterback Jaxson Dart and linebackers Brian Burns and Tremaine Edmunds, to name a few.
And yet, unlike the Eagles, the Giants have stayed afloat with Jameis Winston initially at quarterback before handing the keys to J.J. McCarthy, a reclamation project acquired from the Minnesota Vikings for a fifth-round pick.
Head coach John Harbaugh has his eye squarely on the finish line and a division title, which would be the Giants’ first since 2011. They are well on their way, holding a 4-2-1 record in the division, their next closest rival in the standings being Dallas, who has a 3-5 record after suffering a crushing loss to the Arizona Cardinals in Week 8
According to Covers.com, the Giants are 5-2 against the spread this year and 1-1 when favored. If the Giants keep stacking wins, there’s no reason they won’t be favored more often the rest of the way, even with a grueling slate of opponents starting in Week 11.

title: Harbaugh Says Giants Are “Open for Any Call”
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh is on a nonstop mission to keep the roster competitive as the team chases the NFC East title.
To that end, he confirmed he’s not afraid to call people around the league who might be in a position to do business with the Giants, even if that person is a team owner, as he did with Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk.
“I left a message because you’re turning over every stone, going to try everything,” he said on Monday after the team went through a light practice. “I’ll put it out there: We’re open for any call. Anybody who wants to call us or call anybody, call.”
Harbaugh drew criticism from national talking heads for reaching out to Strunk, adding that he didn’t speak with her but left her a message.
He insisted there are no rules specifying who can talk to whom in the league, noting that he knows all the owners. Giants general manager Joe Schoen, meanwhile, knows the general managers.
Together, they aim to find talent that fits the team in both the short and long term.
“We’re not part of any secret society oath that says you can only talk to somebody,” he said.
“We’re not in that. We didn’t get memoed on that. We’re not in that agreement. So, as I said, anybody can call us. We won’t be adhering to that particular agreement.”
There’s no telling at this point if the Giants’ aggressiveness in searching for roster upgrades will pay off, but Harbaugh said the plan is to stay proactive.
But that comes with a caveat: The goal is not only to find good players but to find players who fit what the Giants have been building under Harbaugh.
“That’s always the goal. Easier said than done. And it’s hard to find players that can make you better, because we have good players,” he said.
“So, it’s got to be something that is a need, that fits your financial profile, that fits your price tag. I mean, it’s not like we have a bunch of draft picks either. We’re not loaded with 12 or 13 draft picks, so we don’t have draft capital to burn. We don’t. So, we have to be smart shoppers that way.”
With the Giants’ 2027 draft picks dwindling, Harbaugh did not rule out dipping into the team’s 2028 draft capital to make a deal that, again, would have to meet certain criteria.
“For me, it wouldn’t want to be a one-on-one kind of thing. You want to have a short-term and a long-term win if you’re going to do it with draft capital,” he said.

title: 3 Jets Face More Pressure After Garrett Wilson Concussion News Creates New Obstacle in Week 9
full_text:
The Jets will look to avoid a season-worst fourth consecutive loss when they visit the Chiefs for some Sunday afternoon action in Week 9 . Beating Patrick Mahomes & Co. was never going to be easy, especially with how inconsistent Gang Green's performances have been this season, but a potential upset in Kansas City will be even tougher to pull off if the Jets are without star wide receiver Garrett Wilson.
On Wednesday afternoon, New York head coach Aaron Glenn told reporters that Wilson has been placed in concussion protocol and will be "day-to-day."
WR Garrett Wilson is in the concussion protocol Full injury update from Coach Glenn ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/la6Lq13a1G
Given that Wilson must clear the NFL's five-step protocol to get back into the lineup, there's a good chance that the Jets won't have him when they take on the Chiefs this weekend. As such, New York needs this trio to step up if it hopes to keep Sunday's clash competitive.
Alongside rookie WR Omar Cooper Jr., Adonai Mitchell is another Jets playmaker who needs to take things to another level if Wilson misses time. Fortunately, he proved he could do exactly that last week.
Even though his team didn't win, last week's loss to the Raiders was a career day for Mitchell, who converted nine targets into seven catches, 142 receiving yards and a touchdown. Considering how he had a 9-123-0 stat line in three games before that (mostly due to a nagging finger injury), it's safe to say that the former Georgia/Texas product is more than capable of being the Jets' lead pass-catcher.
An incredible 48-yard catch by Adonai Mitchell! 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/a7pOlkJn27
The Chiefs have a fairly middle-of-the-road pass defense this season, ranking 18th in passing yards allowed per game (222.9) and T-16th when it comes to yards per completion (10.2). With a career-high average depth of target of 18.2 yards this season , per Pro Football Focus , Mitchell has what it takes to take advantage of any potential miscues in Kansas City's secondary.
The Jets' passing attack hasn't been consistent this season, but another huge performance from Mitchell (sans Wilson) would boost optimism about the unit's outlook.
It's safe to say that Kenyon Sadiq's big seven-catch, 105-yard performance in Week 3 is nothing but a distant memory at this point. The rookie tight end has been nearly invisible since then, catching just five balls on 13 targets (38.5%) for 43 receiving yards without a touchdown in the last five games. Even though it's only his rookie season, that's pretty disappointing for someone drafted 16th overall in April .
All slumps eventually end, though, especially when a player is as talented as Sadiq. Despite the Jets being underdogs this weekend ( by 10 points, per DraftKings Sportsbook ), a clash with the Chiefs might be exactly what the doctor ordered.
As previously mentioned, Kansas City's pass defense hasn't been great, and that's even truer when it comes to stopping tight ends. Heading into Week 9, when it comes to TEs, the Chiefs have allowed:
In other words, it's a great opportunity for Sadiq (and Mason Taylor) to step up if Wilson is stuck in concussion protocol.
With Wilson's immediate outlook uncertain, a potential Breece Hall return in Week 9 would be huge for the Jets. The stud running back hasn't played since Week 3 due to a quad injury, but head coach Aaron Glenn revealed on Wednesday that Hall's situation is "trending in the right direction," per ESPN 's Rich Cimini.
Breece Hall is "trending in the right direction," Glenn says. https://t.co/O4Rn1Q6iOy
Hall's job is to run the ball, but that doesn't take away from the fact that his presence is a key part of the Jets' passing game. The Iowa State product has amassed 198 catches for 1,744 receiving yards (8.8 yards per reception) and nine touchdowns in 59 career games, which includes catching all 10 of his targets for 102 yards this season.
For comparison, New York's other two running backs—Braelon Allen and Isaiah Davis—have combined for just 149 yards on 22 receptions this season. That's just 6.8 yards per reception compared to Hall's 10.2.
Besides, having Hall available in pass-catching situations would allow the Jets to keep Allen on the field, looking to keep taking advantage of his ongoing breakout .
Assuming he can finally play for the first time since September, Hall's looming return certainly looks a lot more important for the Jets.

title: How Soon Could the Jets Start Cade Klubnik Over Geno Smith This Season?
full_text:
The Jets are 2-6 so far this season. One question is looming as New York continues to lose. Quarterback play hasn't been the most glaring issue for the team, but Geno Smith is 36 years old. The veteran quarterback is on a one-year deal, and the Jets have a rookie sitting on the bench.
The Jets look likely to miss the playoffs for a 16th consecutive season. If the team is even considering the QB position in the 2027 draft , they must see what they have in rookie Cade Klubnik. The fourth-round pick should get some playing time this season, but how soon could that happen?
The Jets drafted Cade Klubnik with the 110th overall pick in the 2026 draft from Clemson. Klubnik joined the Jets after an underwhelming last season as a Tiger, but some viewed him as a top-five pick before his last season in South Carolina. He showed some of that talent in the preseason and should get some run at some point this season.
Klubnik finished his first NFL preseason with a total stat line of 21-of-34 passing for 190 yards and an interception. He did not record a passing touchdown, but looked good on some touchdown drives. The former Clemson Tiger also started two of the three preseason games, showing he has the talent to run with the first-team offense.
Klubnik also matches the mold of a successful quarterback in today's game. Klubnik is 6'2" and has mobility that the Jets' offense lacks right now. If the Jets keep losing, calls for the rookie to start will only get louder.
Smith has been far from the biggest problem on the Jets this season. Through eight games, Smith has 1,913 yards, 12 touchdowns and only three interceptions. The veteran quarterback also comes off a game where he helped lead the Jets to 33 points (the second-most they've scored in the Aaron Glenn era).
What a throw from Geno Smith and what a catch by AD Mitchell 😱 LVvsNYJ on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/cxPa0KclpY
Smith doesn't deserve to be benched in a season where the Jets' offense has been more than competent. However, the season seems to be slipping away . The Jets are unlikely to see Geno as their quarterback beyond this season, as he enters the twilight of his career.
So when will they bench the veteran for the rookie?
Barring injury, Smith will start as long as the Jets still have any playoff hope. He seems to be the best chance to win right now. He is having his best season since he made the Pro Bowl as a Seahawk, and the Jets have been in almost every game this season. Klubnik is waiting in the wings, but a QB switch doesn't seem close.
Klubnik could realistically start as early as Week 11 against the Chargers.
If New York drops the next two and Smith looks terrible, Klubnik may get a chance against the struggling Los Angeles team. However, that would put the Jets at 2-8, still possible to make the playoffs, though extremely unlikely. The team will most likely stick with Smith as long as the playoffs are still possible.
That said, Jets fans will most likely see Klubnik start in Week 15 against the Cardinals. New York will likely be out of the playoff race by then unless they make a run soon. This will let Klubnik start against a team that has struggled much like the Jets this season .
Klubnik would avoid playing the Denver defense by a week, but still get to finish his season against some playoff hopefuls. While the road to Klubnik starting looks far away, the rookie will have his chance to prove the Jets don't need to use any of their three first-round picks at QB.

title: Making Sense of Jets' D'Angelo Ponds Plans as Questions Brew in Week 9
full_text:
Among the chief positive points surrounding the 2026 Jets season has been their dominant rookie class . All three first-round picks have stood out in some way and have received rookie of the week honors from the NFL.
Even fourth-round defensive tackle Darrell Jackson Jr. has enjoyed a positive start to his NFL career .
There's one member of the class, though, that has yet to stand out.
Second-round cornerback D'Angelo Ponds missed all of training camp and the first quarter of the season with an injury. After battling back, he received his first NFL start in Week 7 against the Dolphins.
Despite the positive tape, Ponds was sent to the bench last week in New York's loss to Las Vegas . So what gives? What will it take for the Jets to turn to Ponds going forward?
Against the Dolphins in Week 7, Ponds was targeted three times and gave up one reception for five yards. He was, however, called for a pass interference penalty in the end zone that gave the Dolphins an inevitable score.
But by and large, the first start of Ponds's career was a good one. It showed he could be a quality player in the slot. With more reps, the belief was that the Indiana product would be even better.
Ponds was effectively benched by the Jets in their loss to the Raiders and played just a single defensive snap. In his stead, Jarvis Brownlee Jr. got the start in the slot and was penalized twice while also giving up three catches on four targets, a touchdown, and a near-perfect passer rating.
So what gives? Why would the Jets move back to Brownlee in a clear lost season at 2-6? The reality is that the team still wants to win for their coaching staff and head coach Aaron Glenn believes that Brownlee gives them the best chance to be successful on the field.
Never mind the fact that Brownlee acknowledged he was late to multiple meetings and was benched in Week 7; this is only about what he can do on the field.
But now, with the team at 2-6 and needing to see what they have in their young talent, change may be coming.
Don't be surprised if the Jets look to move off of Brownlee in some capacity as the trade deadline gets closer. Ponds will eventually see the field more and more, but Brownlee is seen as a stopgap to that chance.
Once the team is firmly out of any hope of a .500 season ( something that would keep Glenn's job at any rate ), the focus must shift back to getting their rookie class as many reps as possible. That includes putting Ponds both in the slot and in the boundary—where he made his living as one of the best corners in college despite his small frame.
Ponds will eventually be a starter for the Jets. The longer the team waits, though, the more worrisome it is that they might have wasted a top second-round selection. They are better off playing him and moving on from Brownlee altogether.
