title: 49ers Have a New NFC Threat to Worry About
full_text:
Entering the 2026 season, the San Francisco 49ers knew the Seattle Seahawks were their biggest threat in the NFC.
The 49ers were demolished in the last two matchups against the Seahawks before this year. They needed to get over that hurdle, and sure enough, they did it in Week 5.
However, a new significant NFC threat has emerged, and it might even be greater than the Seahawks. That threat is the Chicago Bears .
They were always on the radar as a team that would stand in the 49ers' way, but after punching Seattle in the mouth on Monday night, they've become a much bigger threat.
Chicago is no joke. To go into Lumen Field on primetime, with the entire football world watching, and beat the Seahawks convincingly is a statement win.
The Bears have been a pretty sweet team this season, and that win in Seattle just catapulted them up the standings. The 49ers need to take notice of them, if they haven't already.
Not even they could beat up the Seahawks this badly. The Bears have a ton of momentum on their side, which went to another level when they acquired defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons.
He popped off the screen in every Chicago defensive series. His impact is already second to none. What he does alone is enough to boost the Bears, but he helps everyone else as well.
Suddenly, Montez Sweat and Grady Jarrett are picking it up. The secondary looks better thanks to the pass rush being a lethal force.
The Seahawks struggled immensely on offense against the Bears. As for Seattle's vaunted defense, Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams never wavered.
They struggled for a good stretch of the game against the Seahawks' defense, as expected. No one will ever have consistently successful drives against the Seahawks.
However, the Bears were efficient for the majority of the game. Johnson called an excellent game and won the chess match against Mike MacDonald.
Williams is playing better than ever with an amazing array of weapons at wide receiver, with Luther Burden III, Rome Odunze, Colston Loveland, and even Khalif Raymond.
Despite having an awesome passing attack, Chicago's rushing game is their backbone with D'Andre Swift. Just wait until they get Kyle Monangai back.
The Bears proved that they are serious Super Bowl contenders this year, but so are the 49ers. If these two teams meet in the playoffs, it's bound to be an electric matchup.

title: The Most Favorable Matchups on the 49ers’ Schedule After the Bye

title: Emeka Egbuka Injury Update: Latest on Bucs WR After Missing Another Practice
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have a tough task ahead of them. They're set to face off against one of the best teams in the NFC, the Chicago Bears, on the road in prime time on Sunday Night Football in Week 9.
Tampa Bay hasn't thrown the ball all that much the last two weeks — just 14 times — but it'll probably need to if it wants to beat the Bears. Quarterback Baker Mayfield is recovering from a thumb injury, and while he'll need to throw the football well, his receiving corps will need to step up, too.
The big question heading into Wednesday was whether or not wideout Emeka Egbuka, who has missed the last two games, would be able to play on Sunday night. After Wednesday's practice, the answer to that question remains up in the air.
Egbuka has been dealing with both a concussion and a foot injury over the past two weeks. Head coach Todd Bowles revealed last Friday that Egbuka is out of concussion protocol — his foot issue, however, still remains.
Egbuka practiced on Thursday and Friday last week, but he did not participate in practice on Wednesday. Instead, he was working off to the side with a trainer, so he'll likely be a non-participant in Wednesday's practice when the injury report comes out later tonight.
When asked about Egbuka on Monday, Bowles said he was "50-50" last week, so his lack of participation is definitely something to watch as the week goes on.
"I don't know. He was kinda 50-50 last week," Bowles said Monday. "We'll see how he progresses."
So far this season, Egbuka has netted 28 receptions for 240 yards and two touchdowns. He also has a rushing touchdown on the ground.
In Egbuka's stead — and without Jalen McMillan — wideouts Tez Johnson and Ted Hurst have taken on some work. The Bucs also just got wideout David Sills back from injured reserve, so he's another receiver who could step up in Egbuka's absence, should he not be able to go.
There is still a chance that he could, however. And if he does, Tampa Bay will need to use him against a Bears defense that has only gotten more formidable in recent weeks with the addition of star defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons. Egbuka will have two days to try and play, so Thursday's practice could be crucial.
The Bucs will play the Bears at 8:20 p.m. on Sunday night.

title: Buccaneers Star Vita Vea on NFC East Team's 'Radar' Ahead of Trade Deadline
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is approaching very fast. There's one week of NFL play left before it hits on Nov. 10, and naturally, teams are calling all around the league to try to make their squads better before that time.
There was a time when the Tampa Bay Buccaneers could have become sellers at that trade deadline had things not gone according to plan. It was sure looking that way — the Bucs lost their first four games of the season and were 2-5 heading into Week 8 — but now, the Bucs are 3-5, half a game out of the NFC South lead and very much in the mix.
That would seem to indicate the Bucs aren't really going to be sellers anymore. But if they got the right offer, anything could be appealing — and according to an NFL insider, one NFC East team could be looking to trade for one of Tampa Bay's star players on defense.
ESPN insider Jeremy Fowler reported that the New York Giants are keeping tabs on Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea ahead of the deadline, but that the Bucs don't plan to trade him at the moment.
"Another player on the Giants' radar is Tampa Bay's Vita Vea. (The Bucs are not expected to move him.) It would be a mild surprise if New York doesn't walk away with some help up front," Fowler wrote .
Vea's case is an interesting one. Vea held out of training camp for a significant portion of the year and even requested a trade for a new deal, and the Bucs gave it to him by giving him a one-year contract extension worth $30 million. He hasn't lit up the stat sheet since signing that contract and has clearly declined, so the Bucs may be wise to move on from him this season.
That being said, his ability as a space eater is still very valuable, and he remains a stalwart of a defensive unit that is currently top-three in the NFL by most advanced metrics. If head coach Todd Bowles still wants Vea in that unit, the Bucs will keep him around.
Tampa Bay plays a very tough Chicago Bears team on Sunday night. If the Bucs win, trading Vea feels out of the question — they'd be 4-5 with a shot to lead the NFC South entirely.
If the Bucs lose, though? Perhaps general manager Jason Licht picks up the phone, and perhaps the New York Giants can get some help on the defensive interior.

title: Buccaneers Not Worried About Lack of Passing Game
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have won their last two games against NFC South opponents. They've done so in quite an unusual way.
The Bucs have thrown just 14 passes in their last two games for 64 yards — quarterback Baker Mayfield didn't complete a pass at all in a 16-0 win against the Atlanta Falcons. Mayfield is recovering from a thumb injury, but over the past two weeks, he hasn't had to test it at all.
Now, the Bucs are facing off against the 6-2 Chicago Bears on Sunday Night Football. The Bears just traded for one of the best defensive tackles in football in Jeffrey Simmons and knocked off the defending Super Bowl champions the Seattle Seahawks. It's probably safe to say that the Bucs won't be able to win on the run game alone for the third week in a row.
So, are the Bucs confident that their quarterback can throw the ball if needed? Head coach Todd Bowles certainly seems to be.
Bowles spoke to the media on Monday, and during his time, he stressed that the conditions are mainly what caused the Bucs to abandon the pass entirely.
"I've seen it in practice. Like you said, the conditions [didn’t require it]," Bowles said. "Carolina just got away in the second quarter, and we kind of got ahead. Yesterday, it was kind of impossible to throw, especially early on. In the last part of the ballgame, we had the lead and we really didn't have to throw the ball. You saw what happened when they threw the football."
Despite that, though, Bowles is confident that the Bucs can pass the ball if they need to. Mayfield may be recovering from a thumb injury, but Bowles believes his recent practices have shown he can accurately throw the ball when it's necessary.
"But we see it every day in practice, [I am] very confident. I thought Baker [Mayfield] had a great week of practice throwing the football, but we knew what the conditions were going to be," Bowles said. "Obviously, as they turned out, it was pretty much a monsoon most of the ballgame, so we didn't have to throw it. We kind of [grinded] it out, but [I'm] very confident our passing game will be fine."
The Bucs will likely have to throw against the Bears, who are looking more like a Super Bowl contender every week. It will be cold, but conditions will be much more favorable to throwing the football on Sunday night.
The Bucs play the Bears at 8:20 on Nov. 8. When they do, it might be time for Mayfield to put his thumb to the test.

title: Week 8 NFC South Standings: What Are the Buccaneers' Playoff Chances?
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers got a big win against the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday, winning 16-0 (without throwing a pass!).
That win makes the Buccaneers, currently 3-5, 2-0 in the NFC South. It went a long way to putting them closer to the division lead — and it increased their chances to make the playoffs in a big way.
Here's what the NFC South currently looks like, and where the Buccaneers' playoff chances lie after eight weeks of football:
The Buccaneers beat the Falcons to move to three wins on the year. Tampa Bay has won three of its last four games, and now it has the same number of wins as the Panthers and Falcons do. The Bucs have beaten both of those teams, but because the Panthers have played one less game, Carolina is just a half-game out of the division lead. The Bucs will play the Chicago Bears next on Sunday Night Football.
The Panthers lost their game to the Green Bay Packers on Thursday Night Football. They'll play the Denver Broncos next on Sunday, another game they could potentially drop at home to give the Bucs an edge.
The Falcons will play the Cincinnati Bengals, who beat the Buccaneers during the first week of the regular season. The Bengals are 5-2, so that will be another tough matchup for the Falcons as they try to match pace with the Buccaneers.
The New Orleans Saints are coming off their bye week, and they'll also play a winning team. The Saints will face off against the Cleveland Browns at home on Sunday.
The Athletic's playoff predictor currently has the Bucs with a 41% chance to make the playoffs at 3-5.
If the Bucs beat the Chicago Bears — a very tough task — that number will jump to 54%. If all of their NFC South opponents were to lose on Sunday, that number would jump to 62%. If all NFC South teams lose and the Bucs also lose, the number is 43%, and if the Bucs lose and either the Panthers or Falcons win, it falls to 35%. A Saints win with a Bucs loss and a Panthers and Falcons loss puts their odds at 39%.
The Bucs' greatest threat is each team within the division, and the Bucs will play four more games against those teams for the remainder of the season. They'll be focused on winning those games, but they'll have to pick up some wins in between, too — and they have their first chance to do so on Sunday night against the Bears.

title: Buccaneers' Biggest Strength Is Finally Becoming Their Biggest Weapon
full_text:
Entering the 2026 season, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' offensive line was forecasted to be one of the best in the league.
Much of that came from the fact that they would finally be a healthy unit again, getting that much-needed continuity back after injuries decimated the group over the past couple of seasons.
It was the best of starts to the season for the unit, as they struggled to find that cohesion, particularly in the middle of the line.
However, the Bucs' front has seen a drastic turnaround that is showing brightly after putting together back-to-back performances for the ages.
After leading the way for the rushing attack led by Bucky Irving for over 250 yards against the Carolina Panthers, the offensive line showed their strength once again, this time moving the Atlanta Falcons' defensive front seven around for over 300 yards on the ground.
The middle of the unit — Cody Mauch, Ben Bredeson and Graham Barton — have had their ups and downs, but have since been the anchors of helping the run game.
With the inside starting to match the level of play of Tristan Wirfs and Luke Goedeke, it's starting to look much like we thought it would heading into the year.
Remaining healthy has been a huge aspect of that, and with everyone playing on the same page and understanding what is being asked of them, they have helped the Bucs become the league's top rushing attack at 168.6 yards per game.
The explosive run game has been noticeable with Zac Robinson opening up his zone-blocking schemes for the line, creating leverage that has led to wide-open holes for the backs to run through. The use of counter schemes has also been noted as something that has been a tremendous spark to the offense.
The Bucs' tight end production of Cade Otton, Payne Durham and rookie Bauer Sharp in the run game has also been an amazing result.
While the offensive line has been fantastic in the run game, they could use some polishing in protecting the quarterback when it comes to passing downs.
They currently aren't the best against the pass rush, but if they are able to take their confidence from running the ball effectively and use it when working in pass protection, the unit will undoubtedly help lead the Bucs to victories.

title: Bucs' Baker Mayfield Reveals Why He Didn't Complete a Single Pass
full_text:
It was an interesting game, to say the least, as the Tampa Bay Buccaneers ' 16-0 Week 8 defeat of the Atlanta Falcons brought them just half a game out of the NFC South lead.
The field and weather conditions made for a sloppy game overall, and ultimately led to both quarterbacks not throwing the ball or not being effective in throwing it.
That led to a huge game on the ground for the Bucs, who set multiple records in the process. However, with Baker Mayfield not completing a single pass on the day, it became the first time a team went on to win a game in that fashion in 52 years (the 1974 Buffalo Bills).
Following the win, Mayfield spoke about not completing a single pass.
“It’s winning – that’s the way I think about it. We won. [It’s] getting our guys lined up, making sure we are running the right run plays," Mayfield said. "Obviously, ball security [is crucial] in these conditions – we had some early ones. We decided to go to the shotgun and pistol sets – it’s just easier to receive the snaps instead of it coming back through your hands under center."
"So, going from there and just trying to manage the game. [It’s] time management and just trying to bleed the clock as much as possible. Just get everybody on the same page and go from there. That’s my job in these conditions and, listen, I will do whatever it takes to win. That’s all that matters to me.”
Mayfield nailed it on the head in his postgame press conference.
It's clear that the game script was going to demand Tampa Bay run the ball, and after doing so effectively against the Carolina Panthers just a week before, the Falcons knew it was coming.
That didn't matter, as the Falcons gave up over 300 yards rushing, with career highs on the ground by both Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell.
It didn't matter to Mayfield whether or not the ball would be put in his hands. It was all about winning, and that is exactly what they did.
Whether the Bucs can continue this type of play and still continue to stack wins remains to be seen, and at some point, Mayfield will have to throw the ball to help.
But for the time being, they should continue to lean on their strengths, which will undoubtedly be tested this upcoming week against a Chicago Bears' defense that ranks fourth in the league against the run.

title: One Big Concern Remains After Buccaneers' Back-to-Back Wins
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are coming off of fantastic wins against the division rival Carolina Panthers and Atlanta Falcons and find themselves only half a game back from first place in the NFC South after a terrible start to the season.
The main boon for this team has been their ability to run the football and play lights-out defense as one of the best units in the league in recent weeks.
One major question is on many Bucs fans' minds, and a growing concern is where the pass game has been in recent weeks this season.
Over the past two weeks, Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield has thrown the ball 14 times for 64 yards and a touchdown, and that includes him throwing just three passes in a monsoon against the Falcons.
The weather is typically attributed as the biggest reason as to why the team ran the ball as much as they did against Atlanta, but there are many who worry that Mayfield isn't fully healthy and the team simply can't throw the football with his thumb injury.
It is important to remember, though, that Todd Bowles and offensive coordinator Zach Robinson want to be a running football team.
"Everything we talked about – controlling time of possession, running the football, getting turnovers on defense, making plays on special teams, the things we had to do to win the ball game – that's what we talked about right before kickoff in the locker room," Bowles said. "So, it came to fruition. I didn't think it would come to fruition that close, but it came pretty close."
Time will tell whether or not the Bucs want to open up the passing attack more going forward with the 2026 offense. However, it is also important to note that right now, the Bucs don't need to pass the football much, considering the great level of success they have running the ball under Zach Robinson.
While it might not be the game plan many wanted the Buccaneers to have on offense to reach success, the plan the team has in place is working well.

title: Todd Bowles Gives Injury Update on Buccaneers Defensive Starter
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are on a bit of a hot streak. They've won three of their last four games, and now, they're just a half game out of the NFC South lead.
They'll want to keep that going, and to do that, they'll need as many starting players as they can to contribute. But one key defensive starter could be out for some time after Sunday's 16-0 win over the Atlanta Falcons — but it might not be too long.
Todd Bowles spoke to media on Monday, and he gave an update on edge rusher Yaya Diaby and whether or not he could miss some time.
Todd Bowles told the media Monday that Diaby sprained his MCL in the win over the Falcons. It corroborates an earlier Monday report by NFL Insider Ian Rapoport. Rapoport reported that it was a Grade 2 sprain and that Diaby could miss a little time, but that he wouldn't miss significant time.
#Bucs outside linebacker YaYa Diaby, who exited Sunday’s win early, is believed to have suffered an MCL sprain, source says. He’ll have an MRI this morning, but the hope is the injury is not one to cause him to miss extended time. pic.twitter.com/r1nJQnwxix
Bowles confirmed on Monday that Diaby has a sprain and that the hope is that he won't be put on injured reserve.
"He has an MCL sprain. Not sure how much he'll miss," Bowles said. We'll see how the week progresses and we'll go from there."
Diaby is in a contract year in 2026, and while he was slow to get going this season, he's made up for lost time in recent weeks.
Diaby had a hat trick of sacks against the Carolina Panthers in Week 7, boosting his total to three. So far this year, he has 11 solo tackles, three sacks and an interception, the latter of which he got against the Dallas Cowboys in a win on Thursday Night Football.
If Diaby misses some time, the Bucs will likely turn to players like David Walker, Al-Quadin Muhammad and Anthony Nelson to fill in for him on his side. Walker has been a standout edge rusher this season for Tampa Bay and is earning more snaps there, while both Muhammad and Nelson have been strong rotational pieces so far this year.
If Diaby does have to miss some time, he has at least one thing going for him. The Bucs will have a bye week in Week 10, so he could use that as a buffer to recover and miss fewer games than he normally would.

title: Every Record the Buccaneers Set in Historic Win Over Falcons
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers beat the Atlanta Falcons in Week 8. With that win, they moved within half a game of the NFC South lead and picked up their second win in a row for the first time in 385 days.
It isn't the fact that Tampa Bay won that has people talking, though — it's how Tampa Bay won. A rainy day brought a big change to the offensive game plan, and it resulted in a historic, record-breaking performance in Tampa Bay's 16-0 win.
Here's every record the Bucs became a part of when they beat the Falcons without completing a single pass:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers — and, by extension, quarterback Baker Mayfield — did not complete a pass against the Atlanta Falcons. That's an astonishing feat in itself, and it created a windfall that led to breaking more records.
The Bucs became the first NFL team since 1974 to win an NFL game without completing a pass. That game was on Sept. 9, 1974, when the Buffalo Bills defeated the New York Jets 16-12 in similarly rainy conditions.
The Falcons also set a new record on Sunday, though it's probably not one they're very proud of. Atlanta got shut out by the Bucs on Sunday, and with that, the Falcons became the first team to be shut out by a team that didn't complete a pass since 1942. Mayfield didn't complete a pass, but his passer rating (39.6) was higher than Falcons quarterback Michael Penix's (12.0).
With the conditions as they were, the Bucs had to run the football a lot, and oh, did they. The Bucs toted the rock to the tune of 324 rushing yards, which broke the franchise record for most rushing yards in a game — that record was previously set in 2015 against the Philadelphia Eagles, when the Bucs had 283 rushing yards that day.
Tampa Bay may not have passed much at all on Sunday, but it didn't last Sunday, either. Over the last two games the Bucs have played, they've completed just seven passes on 14 attempts — despite that, they've won both of those games by a combined 59-13.
The Bucs are set to play the Chicago Bears on Sunday Night Football in Week 9 on Nov. 8. They probably won't be able to win that game by completing fewer than 10 passes, but at this point, we're open to believing.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Buccaneers' 16-0 Shutout Victory Over The Falcons
full_text:
That's how many days had passed since the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last won back-to-back football games.
Thankfully, that dreadful drought has officially reached its conclusion after the Buccaneers secured a much-needed victory on Sunday, defeating the Falcons 16-0 for their second victory in as many weeks. With the win, the Bucs have now improved their overall record on the year to 3-5 while going 2-0 against NFC South teams.
Not only does this victory represent the first time the Bucs have won back-to-back games in well over a year, but it also provides some optimism for a team that was getting dangerously close to eliminating itself from playoff contention before the halfway mark of the 2026 NFL season.
Now, let's break down the good, the bad and the ugly we saw in this crucial Week 8 NFC South showdown between the Buccaneers and Falcons.
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers' rushing attack entered a new tier of domination on Sunday.
Following last week's 258-yard explosion, I don't think anybody expected the Bucs to surpass that mark again this season, let alone the very next week. The Bucs didn't just surpass that mark, though; they absolutely obliterated it by rushing for an absurd 324 total yards on the ground against the Falcons, a top-five rushing defense in the entire league heading into this game.
As has been the case for the majority of this season, Bucky Irving was electric running the football in this contest. When it was all said and done, Irving had ducked and weaved his way to 170 yards on the ground and 1 TD while averaging 6.3 yards per rush on 27 carries. Had he not fumbled the ball through the end zone early in the game, he'd have had another TD added to his resume.
As the game went on, Irving got some rest while Kenneth Gainwell took the majority of snaps, and boy did he take advantage of that opportunity. Gainwell rushed 25 times for a career-high 140 yards, and his relentless and slippery style of running was reminiscent of his partner in crime, Irving.
After a surprisingly disappointing start to the year, the Buccaneers' offensive line has officially re-established itself as one of the league's best. As a group, they deserve a ton of credit for the team's dominant rushing performance over the past two weeks.
The 324 total rushing yards achieved by the Buccaneers today vs. the Falcons is the most in franchise history.
Oh, how things can change quickly in the NFL. Just a few short weeks ago, the fans in Tampa were calling for Todd Bowles' job. Now? They would be wise to praise him for the job he's done with his young defense, which all of a sudden looks like one of the best all-around units in the entire NFL.
The Bucs' defense has been operating on all cylinders over their past four games, and they've produced some pretty astounding numbers in the process. Dating back to their Week 5 win over the Cowboys, the Bucs' defense has come up with 10 sacks, nine interceptions, two forced fumbles and two fumble recoveries with their opponents averaging just 13.8 points per game over that stretch.
For the first time all season, Alex Anzalone made a big impact on this football game. Not only did the veteran linebacker have two interceptions (in the rain) in the first half, but he also did a much better job fitting the run. Anzalone finished the game with six total tackles and, more importantly, appeared to be much quicker at diagnosing plays and reacting accordingly.
The Bucs don't need Anzalone to lead the team in interceptions this season (which he currently is) for him to meet the expectations he had coming into this year — they just need him to play sound, disciplined football without making costly errors. If Anzalone can do that, the Bucs' defense will be much better off.
Jacob Parrish and Zyon McCollum continue to impress. Not only did each player record an interception today, but they've both been incredibly consistent in all phases of coverage while also providing exceptional run support this entire season.
If the Bucs' defense continues to perform as it has been, the play of their two starting corners will be a big reason why. If the Buccaneers continue to churn out victories, don't be surprised to see one, if not both, players named to an All-Pro team by season's end.
Although it didn't matter in the end, Irving fumbled a ball through the end zone in the first quarter. Mistakes happen, sure, but this one was completely avoidable. Irving was far too cavalier carrying the football with a defender in close proximity and pursuit, and he got burned for it.
The play happened right in the middle of a torrential downpour at Raymond James Stadium, which should have been added motivation for Irving to keep the ball high and tight.
The Buccaneers became the first team since the Bills in 1974 to win a game without completing a single pass. It's an impressive feat, really, and a testament to just how dominant the Buccaneers were at running the football. That being said, it's likely not an achievement that Baker Mayfield is very proud of.
The Bucs become the first NFL team since the 1974 Buffalo Bills to win a game without completing a pass 😳 pic.twitter.com/kQQJ3S9fqr
All that matters, though, is that the Buccaneers won this football game, and Mayfield finished the contest without any setbacks to his injured thumb.
It goes without saying that the weather played a big role in the lack of success for both the Falcons and Buccaneers on Sunday. Especially in the first half, the rain was as relentless through the air as Irving and Gainwell were on the ground, and credit to the fans who stuck around to cheer on the home team — if only the grass at Raymond James Stadium were so resilient.
Even though he passed for more yards than Mayfield, there's no question that Michael Penix struggled more than any other player in this football game. Penix was 8/24 and threw for 125 yards and 0 TDs to go along with his four interceptions.
He should have had another interception on the opening drive when a pass intended for Drake London hit Jacob Parrish square in the hands, but the Bucs' talented young corner was caught off guard and couldn't secure it.

He is a graduate of the Communication Studies program at McMaster University, where he was also a varsity basketball player, and later an advanced scout. He lives with his wife and two children in Hamilton, ON. You can follow Collin on YouTube and Twitter.

title: Making the Case for Titans Taking a First-Round RB in 2027: The Perfect Tony Pollard Succession Plan
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans have a slow-rising problem that must be addressed in the backfield. For the time being, it's looking less and less likely that veteran RB Tony Pollard will be traded. He seemed like a surefire candidate entering the year, but Pollard's dominant play as of late demands otherwise.
That, and his usual second-hand-man, in Tyjae Spears, has been a non-factor this season. In six games this year, Spears has just 18 carries for 66 yards. He's added 15 receptions for 75 yards, two fumbles, and no scores.
Spears has consistently missed practices, most recently with a knee issue, and has fallen almost entirely out of the rotation even when he's active. Between Spears and rookie back Nick Singleton, the backfield looked like the least of Tennessee's futuristic worries prior to this season.
Now, as far as 2027 is concerned, it may be one of their biggest. Even if Tennessee doesn't trade Pollard by the deadline this year, the 29-year old is in the final year of his contract. Odds are slim that  Tennessee would sign him to a multi-year deal entering his 30s.
So, what is the best plan of action here? I'd argue that it isn't to wait on Spears, but to take the punch in the gut and draft another back next year.
No, this wouldn't mean Tennessee admits defeat with the Singleton pick. After all, the Penn State alumnus was a fifth-round pick and should've been seen as a project to begin with.
But take one look at the free agent slate for next season and tell me Tennessee has a better option. You're looking at a series of veteran backs beyond their primes; Alvin Kamara (31), Aaron Jones (31), and, of course, Pollard highlight the market. From there, it's mostly multi-year backups more likely to stay put than anything else.
Unless Spears takes a sudden fourth-year leap in the middle of his worst season yet as a Titan, it's time to look forward and take another swing. If Tennessee manages to draft a Jeffery Simmons replacement for the defense with their higher first-round pick, I've got an idea for the later selection.
Enter: Florida RB Jadan Baugh.
I spent all offseason harping on Tennessee to take Jeremiyah Love out of Notre Dame. Everyone is thrilled with Carnell Tate at the WR spot, including me, but the sensibility of going high on a long-term back remains clear.
NFLDraftBuzz.com predicts Baugh to land as a late first-round pick, slotting in as the favored RB1 in a draft class loaded with playmaking talent. Through eight games with the Gators this season, the junior has gone for 801 yards on 152 carries, scoring 13 touchdowns in the process.
Baugh hasn't fumbled the ball once this season. In fact, in three years with Florida, Baugh has only fumbled one time. The big-body back moves extremely well and maintains balance through contact; he's drawing early comparisons to Le'Veon Bell for a reason.
If the argument for keeping Pollard around past the deadline this season is that he's essential to Cam Ward's development, that same ideal should extend to investing in a long-term back to grow alongside Ward. To that end, Baugh is a dream pickup.
Of course, this all depends on whether or not he'd be available when the Titans' late-first (via the Chicago Bears) came to pass. But it seems like this will be a possibility come draft night, at least. If that's the case, I'd love to see Tennessee fully commit to a young backfield and take this stud.
If you're scratching your head wondering what a move like this would mean for Singleton... don't!
I'm as interested in the potential of Singleton as anyone else, but again, a fifth-round pick isn't drafted to be a plug-n-play starter in case something goes wrong. This is firmly a "wait and see" scenario for Tennessee, evidenced by veteran back Michael Carter getting midseason looks over the rookie.
If anything, some young competition would be good for the former Nittany Lion. Draft Baugh, give Singleton the offseason to develop and sharpen iron, keep one of Spears and Carter around as the resident veteran, and roll into the 2027 campaign with a refreshed ground game.
It's a future-facing approach that I think best suits the Titans' rebuild around Ward under center. Given a little luck on draft night, it's something that could realistically come to pass.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans NFL Trade Deadline Big Board: 7 Realistic Pieces Tennessee Could Still Trade
full_text:
The NFL's trade deadline is only six days away now, and the Tennessee Titans have been tabbed as potential sellers time and time again. Moving on from DT Jeffery Simmons certainly filled that cup to some extent, but there are still pieces on the board that look like potential trades.
As of yesterday, Tennessee doesn't look eager to make any moves. But there are guys that arguably should be sent out anyway, and others the team could trade, but would be better off keeping.
To compile everything into one spot, we've put together a Titans trade big board as your one-stop-shop for the latest on deadline possibilities. So far as anyone can tell, here are the players we could see Tennessee shop by November 10.
Ridley appears like the most likely trade candidate on this roster, and there's a real discussion to be had about the necessity of moving on from the veteran WR.
With just six catches for 91 yards on the season, Ridley's role in Tennessee's offense has clearly expired. Although, to a contending team with a need at the position, the 31-year old's value is more apparent.
A team like the Pittsburgh Steelers or the Kansas City Chies come to mind. This is not a ranked list, but Ridley still had to be mentioned at the top of it. It seems fair to say that no player fits the bill of a possible trade more than Ridley. The Titans have six days to get something, anything, done.
Coming off his three-interception performance against the Cincinnati Bengals (Hooker leads the NFL with five total), the Titans' veteran S has spiked his value. He looked like the best player in Robert Saleh's defense in Week 8.
Hooker, 29, has ground himself as a consistently reliable presence in the secondary. He appeals to contending teams for the same reasons that Ridley does, only Hooker is inarguably better at his position.
Tennessee should likely think twice about trading Hooker, especially after moving off one of their defensive anchors already. Under contract through 2028, the possibility of moving Hooker could be kicked down the road until the Titans' rebuild is a little more fleshed out.
All the same, for the right offer, it would make sense if Tennessee decided to double down on their draft capital in the coming two seasons.
Pollard appears to be the least likely to be traded of the bunch at this point. Coming into the season, it appeared that Tyjae Spears was set to succeed Pollard due to the latter being in the final year of his contract.
But Pollard has removed any doubt from his role as RB1 in Nashville. He's taken what began as a backfield split and turned it into a one-man-show. Pollard has five rushing scores and nearly 250 yards combined over the past two games.
That means his value is at an all-time high, but the veteran RB now slots in as a critical cog in Cam Ward's offensive machine. Tennessee would certainly have buyers for Pollard, especially if and when someone lands star RB Jonathan Taylor.
However, if Pollard is tied to Ward finally breaking out - as he did last week - risking throwing the QB off his course doesn't seem worth it. This one looks less likely by the day.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported last week that teams " in the market for an edge rusher believe Johnson could be available at the right price." Johnson was brought to Nashville in a trade this past offseason, and is playing in the final year of his rookie deal that originated with the New York Jets.
Johnson has three sacks this season and has been a fair contributor on Tennessee's defensive line. When Simmons was traded, Saleh tabbed Johnson as a potential emerging leader in his wake.
With ties to Saleh due to their shared time together in New York and Tennessee having just shed their best d-lineman, Johnson looks like a less serious candidate now than he did before the Simmons ordeal.
But the right price is the right price, and on defense, the Titans could be more likely to hit the reset button while Ward figures things out on the other side of the ball. That point is evidenced by the rest of this list.
Taylor pretty well removed himself from most trade discussions this past week. The offseason pickup, who was benched as recently as Week 6, posted a comeback performance fueled by his move from the outside to nickel.
On top of that, CB Marcus Harris injured his ankle and left the game; if Harris misses time, Taylor will be Tennessee's go-to option at nickel. He went from an obvious trade possibility to someone who looks almost immovable for the time being.
Taylor deserved a mention here due to how up and down his season has been, but he's closer to Pollard than Ridley as far as likelihood goes.
Martin is a similar candidate to the aforementioned Hooker. Where Hooker had three picks, Martin had three sacks against Cincinnati. The latter is a 30-year old veteran with an impressive journeyman resume that landed in Tennessee on a two-year deal.
He's sitting at 6.5 sacks on the season right now, which is already a career-high. The Titans are just halfway through their 2026 campaign.
As our own Dharya Sharma noted, Martin has risen into full blue-chip status as a trade potential. But like Johnson, he's now a primary playmaker with Simmons in the rearview. One or the other could be traded, but with DL John Franklin-Myers playing through a back injury, holding on to both seems like the safe play.
Finally, we come to LB Cody Barton. A 29-year old veteran who has steadily seen his snaps taper off this year, Barton now appears at risk of losing his spot on the inside to Cedric Gray, who is 24.
Once rookie Anthony Hill Jr. came on the scene and made it clear that he was the best LB on this Titans team, less surefire snaps were being divvied heavily in Barton's favor after Cedric Gray missed Week 1 with a concussion.
Barton remained in control up until a few weeks ago, when Gray's looks began to chip away at Barton's. Gray was one of the NFL's leading tacklers last season, and it seemed like only a matter of time before he re-assumed a similar role in Saleh's defense.
If Tennessee trusts Gray to succeed Barton, moving the latter would seem like the natural next step.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Deadline Debate: Do Titans Trade Tony Pollard at Peak Value, or Keep Him for Cam Ward's Sake?
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans' offense had its best game of the 2026 NFL season on Sunday, scoring 36 points in a losing effort to the Cincinnati Bengals.
Despite suffering their seventh loss of the year, the Titans were firing on all cylinders offensively in Week 8, especially quarterback Cam Ward and running back Tony Pollard. Ward threw for 304 yards and two touchdowns on 65% completion , while Pollard rushed for 117 yards and two scores on 5.6 yards per carry.
With Tennessee sitting at 1-7 and having already traded All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears, many have assumed the Titans are willing to deal some of their veteran talent. Pollard has been a name often mentioned in potential trade discussions, but the Titans may be better off keeping him.
Pollard has been one of the most consistent running backs in the NFL over the last few years, and has been elite in recent weeks. The 29-year-old has tallied 246 rushing yards and five touchdowns in the past two games and is top-ten in rushing yards (595) and touchdowns (6) this year.
As a result, Pollard's trade value is higher than it has ever been . A contending team that is looking to elevate its rushing attack may have interest in a savvy veteran back in Pollard, who is in the final year of his deal with Nashville. From the outside looking in, the chips are falling for a sensible trade.
With the Titans still rebuilding, it would make sense to move Pollard and acquire picks for the future. However, Tennessee should also heavily consider retaining the former Pro Bowler. Pollard is critical to Ward's development, as supplying a young quarterback with a stable run game is always a fantastic plan. Pollard makes Ward's life easier and sets up play-action passes, which Ward has had success with.
Ward looked comfortable this past week because, in part, he was freed up by Pollard's ground game. Especially with complimentary options like Tyjae Spears and Nick Singleton fading into the background, Pollard has worked himself into an important and singular role this season.
Overall, trading Pollard before the November 10 deadline wouldn't be a surprising move from general manager Mike Borgonzi, but keeping him to support Ward and help the offense afloat for the rest of the season looks like the more viable avenue right now for Tennessee.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Titans Reportedly Unlikely to Make More Trades — But Calvin Ridley Should be Moved at Any Cost
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans cutting a deal with the Chicago Bears to move franchise-defining DT Jeffery Simmons made the trade deadline look far less dire. Nobody expected the Titans to end up with two first-round picks with any of their other assets, after all.
But sometimes, making trades isn't all about the capital you get in return. Guys can be moved because their value has peaked, because they don't fit the scheme any longer, or both. Veteran receiver Calvin Ridley falls into the third category.
Today, Terry McCormick reported that "the Titans are not likely to make more trades, unless an offer over fair market value comes their way." However, Ridley should be moved no matter the return, save for something truly outlandish.
Ridley was brought to Nashville back in 2024 on an unimaginable four-year, $92 million deal. He's struggled to stay on the field since his first season, and even when Ridley does participate, his production is buried beneath talent younger than him.
The former Alabama sensation has shown flashes since his move to Nashville; after all, he surpassed 1,000 yards receiving in his first campaign. But it's undeniable that Ridley is a remnant of the Brian Callahan era. That's a time this franchise is still scratching and clawing to move past.
Ridley came into this season competing directly with rookie sensation Carnell Tate, big-name signee Wan'Dale Robinson, and second-year risers Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike. For him to start in Week 1, even after restructuring his contract in the offseason, was surprising.
The 31-year old receiver has since made it clear that he's not at home in this rotation. Ridley dropped his fourth ball of the season in Week 8 against the Cincinnati Bengals. He'd finish the contest with one reception on just three targets, and that was without Tate playing at all.
Ridley has just six receptions on the year for 91 yards. In Week 8, the aforementioned Dike had five catches for 71 yards. His steady decline in snaps has him at 218 on the year, per FantasyPros. For reference, Wan'Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate sit at 334 and 329, respectively.
As long as Ridley is getting work, he's taking valuable looks away from the likes of Ayomanor and Dike. The Titans, in an effort to fully commit to building a future-forward team around Cam Ward under center, should have Ridley at the tip-top of their trade block.
If that means taking a late-draft pick to move off an asset whose contract will expire next season anyways? So be it. Ridley was once an exciting prospect in Nashville, and he deserves credit for reworking his contract to remain a Titan for a little while longer.
But we're halfway through the 2026 season. With the November 10 deadline looming ahead, this is a need that has made itself painfully clear. Trade Ridley to a willing contender in need of playmaking help (see the Kansas City Chiefs, for example) wipe your hands, and press on.

title: 3 Bold Predictions for Titans After Bye Week: Is a Late-Season Winning Streak Realistic?
full_text:
We've officially hit the midway point of the Tennessee Titans' 2026 season as bye week is next on the schedule. The team is 1-7, but last week's defeat on the road against the Cincinnati Bengals yielded more positivity than negativity for the Robert Saleh era.
Moving forward, this team still has a whole lot to prove, and they'll have to prove it without star DT Jeffery Simmons. The outlook is presently bleak in Nashville, but if last week is a real indicator, the future is bright.
Regarding the future, I'm making three bold predictions for the rest of this season to ruminate in your mind as bye week comes to pass. Here are a few notes on what I believe will be an improved part two to Tennessee's campaign.
The Tennessee Titans falling just short to the Cleveland Browns in Week 7 cut short the team's chances of winning their first back-to-back games since 2022. However, I believe that curse will finally be lifted in December.
On the 20th and 27th respectively, the Titans play the Indianapolis Colts (home) and Las Vegas Raiders (away). Tennessee already beat the Colts once, marking their only victory of the season. Indianapolis has since initiated an apparent fire sale on the trade market and fired their general manager. Indy is 2-6 overall right now.
The Raiders, on the other hand, are 4-4. The team is vastly improved under first-year head coach Klint Kubiak, but after starting 0-3, the wheels have begun to fall off for Las Vegas. With ongoing discussions about Kirk Cousins' starting role at QB, they're very much in flux as a franchise.
Tennessee would certainly have to get hot late, especially on the road against the Raiders. But a bold take is a bold take, and having already come so close to breaking this historically bad streak, I believe it's fair to predict that the Titans won't waste such a close shave again. This window looks like their best shot.
With leading WR Carnell Tate out in Week 8 due to a shoulder injury, it was second-year pass-catcher Chimere Dike who stepped into the positional spotlight. Dike looked fantastic vs. Cincy.
The Pro-Bowl returner logged five catches for 71 yards and a second-half touchdown. As a result of his immediate impact in the offense, I'm predicting that Dike ascends all the way up into the WR2 spot for Tennessee.
Behind Tate, it makes sense to prioritize a young playmaker in Tennessee's ongoing rebuild. Dike is a great separator, and a look at his film ( per Drew Beatty ) reveals an ability to maintain speed and pick up consistent YAC. Wan'Dale Robinson's struggles make this end all the more probable.
Especially if the Titans move on from Calvin Ridley, Dike should be the first to get extended looks. His massive uptick in snaps last week was made good by a knockout showing. This should only be the beginning of Dike's rise in Brian Daboll's offense.
Cam Ward had his first 300-yard game in Week 8. For the first time this year, Ward fully looked like the franchise QB Tennessee drafted him to be. In the spirit of optimism, I'm predicting that Ward goes on to surpass 3,000 yards again this year on his way to a redemptive campaign.
Ward still has a lot of work to do to overcome a mostly poor first seven games. What had previously been seen in only flashes came out in full force as Ward threw for two scores and went without an interception. He led the Titans to 36 points, the most the team had scored in nearly six years.
There's something to that. There's something to Ward. If Dike is to elevate and Tennessee is to post a late-season winning streak, Ward will have to make his Week 8 showing less irregular. I'm predicting that he does just that, and that his progress reflects in a second straight 3,000-yard year.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Robert Saleh vs. Brian Callahan: How Saleh's First Titans Season Compares, and How He Can Finish Better
full_text:
Robert Saleh is 1-7 through his first eight games as the Titans' head coach. Brian Callahan went 2-6 through his first eight games with Tennessee. Callahan was fired six games into his second season, when the team was 1-5. Callahan finished 4-19 overall before the Titans let him go.
Their records may be similar, but Saleh's first half-season on the sidelines in Nashville feels much different than Callahan's. Now that we've hit the midway point of the 2026 season, it's time for a side-by-side comparison.
Not only are we conducting a progress report of sorts for Saleh, but we'll also lay out reasons to show that the rest of his tenure has the potential to be much different - to be much better.
One-to-two wins being the groundwork for either coach in this comparison is, of course, a terrible start. Even if there's hope to be had with Saleh, it's completely fair to recognize that this Titans team is one loss away from the worst possible start under him.
Of the Titans' eight contests this season, six have been decided in one-score fashion, including the Titans' Week 6 win over the Indianapolis Colts. Tennessee has scored 20+ points four times, and 30+ once.
Looking back to 2024, the results were less predictable. Through eight contests, only four were decided by one score. Tennessee put up 20+ points twice, and 30+ only once. On the surface, Saleh's Titans are playing closer games, and yet losing slightly more.
Even the Titans' 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans this year pales in comparison to the 52-14 drubbing Callahan's team took on the road vs. the Detroit Lions in 2024. Saleh has openly noted that Tennessee has to capitalize late.
The thing with Callahan's opening run? He had the Titans at 3-8 after a Week 12 victory on the road in Houston. After that improbable win, he'd go on to drop six straight to finish the campaign, and 11 of his next 12.
In fact, the very next game after his last win of 2024 was a 42-19 blowout at the hands of the Washington Commanders. The wheels completely fell off for now-released QB Will Levis, who threw three interceptions in that stretch and, at one point in December, two games without a score.
Mason Rudolph playing fill-in under center did Callahan's problematic play-calling no favors. Titans fans will surely remember the former HC giving up his play-calling duties just weeks before he was relieved in Nashville. That through-line haunted him well into year two.
Of course, Saleh is calling plays on the defensive side of the ball, and that's unlikely to change. Amani Hooker's three interceptions this past week didn't cover up the 43 points Saleh's defense allowed. He has his own issues in the opposite respect.
Saleh's 2026 squad appears both a step behind (being short one win) and a step ahead of Callahan's 2024 bunch. The Titans' present-day games are demonstrably closer on a weekly basis, and Cam Ward's performance from last week revived expectations that he'll be a long-term guy under center.
But Saleh still must succeed where Callahan failed. The successive coach has to find a way to close contests that Tennessee has failed to win up to this point. Three wins is the floor, and it's arguable that topping that dreaded number is the bar.
From here on out, the Titans play the Jacksonville Jaguars twice (once at home, once on the road), the Texans and Colts each one more time, as well as the Cowboys, Commanders, the Lions, the Raiders, and the Steelers.
Unlike Callahan's inaugural team, Saleh's has proven they can hang with just about anyone. Last week's road shootout with the 5-2 Cincinnati Bengals proved that, even when missing primary playmakers, the best version of this roster has elite flashes on either side of the ball.
Much of the makeup of these final nine games will have to do with Ward's progress at QB (a huge help for Saleh if he keeps it up), who else the Titans move before the November 10 deadline (if anyone), and how impactful rookies like Carnell Tate and Anthony Hill Jr. can be down the stretch.
But if these first eight games have taught us anything, it's that Saleh and Tennessee will have plenty of opportunities to win games. At the end of the day, it's success that will put Saleh in a different camp than Callahan.
There are reasons between the lines to expect that Saleh's tenure will end differently than the guy's before him. Because the end of Callahan's first season said so much about where he was heading in Tennessee, these next nine games are absolutely critical for Saleh to get over the hump.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Grading Every Titans Position Group After Week 8: Cam Ward Leads Offense to Season-Best Uptick
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans surprised the football world when they took the Cincinnati Bengals to overtime before ultimately falling in a 43-36 battle. Despite the loss, there were a lot of things to be encouraged by, especially offensively. The Bengals’ high powered offense kept swinging away, but the Titans punched back every single time.
Obviously, there are no morale victories in the NFL, but for a team that’s lacked offensive firepower all year long, this was a sight for sore eyes.
As for the other side of the ball, well, let’s just say it wasn’t nearly as promising. Having said all of that, let’s not waste anymore time and jump right into this week’s positional grades breakdown.
QB Cam Ward played arguably the best game of his career on Sunday. He topped 300 yards for the first time in his career, while also having an adjusted completion percentage of 80 percent (26/40), per PFF . Ward also connected on eight explosive throws — his most all season.
But as encouraging as those numbers are, the tape really stood out.
Cam Ward looked like a completely different QB in Week 8 for the #Titans . He was extremely effective working the MOF, kept the footwork/ball placement as clean as I've ever seen from him, (generally) worked well from within the pocket, and still sprinkled in a few highlight… pic.twitter.com/j9nxUDlZGc
For the first time this season, Ward played a complete game where he looked comfortable, decisive, confident, and accurate throughout the contest.
The second-year QB certainly had some plays he wants back, but this was a massive step in the right direction for his overall development. Ward had his offense going toe-to-toe with one of the most stacked offensive units in the NFL. And he notably did it without his top target, WR Carnell Tate, while also losing his top two blockers by the end of the game.
The overall use of tempo really seemed to help Ward get settled in, because for the first time all year, there was zero hesitation in his game. Once he saw something open, he ripped it, and it resulted in him looking like a true franchise quarterback for the first time all season.
Another thing that jumped off the page was his willingness to change velocities on a ton of his throws. That in itself is a massive improvement from earlier this season when he routinely missed some easy throws due to the unnecessary velocity he used on seemingly every throw.
Ward appears to be growing right before our very eyes, and it finally culminated in an incredible performance on Sunday.
Now the question becomes, can he sustain this success and build off it, or was this just an occasional flash-in-the-pan type of performance?
RB Tony Pollard had another phenomenal game for the second straight week. The Memphis product totaled 137 yards and two touchdowns on 24 touches (117 rushing, 20 receiving).
This is the second consecutive week where Pollard has topped the 100-yard mark, subsequently increasing his trade value one week from the deadline.
It’ll be interesting to see if Pollard is still on the team come next Tuesday, but if he isn’t, that means the Titans probably got another offer they couldn’t turn down as the team tries to load up on as many draft picks as they can before next April.
With Tate out with a shoulder injury, this group entered the game with minimal expectations. Yet, to my surprise, they performed admirably as a unit. Second-year receivers Chim Dike and Elic Ayomanor combined for eight catches for 107 yards and one touchdown.
Meanwhile, the veteran tandem of Calvin Ridley and Wan’Dale Robinson combined for 67 yards, a few backbreaking drops, and one touchdown.
It’s clear that once Tate returns, Tennessee needs to commit to the youth movement in that room. Robinson has been a massive disappointment and should honestly be relegated to a backup role after the bye.
As for Ridley, a trade would be the best-case scenario, but at minimum, he should be seeing minimal snaps the rest of the way. A divorce is inevitable at the end of the year, so giving those reps to your younger and more productive receivers makes a ton of sense, especially following the performances we saw Sunday.
TE Gunnar Helm had his best game of the season, leading the team in receiving yards (76) while also holding his own as a blocker. Tennessee could use more performances like this out of its young TE, especially in the passing game.
Helm is a big body with reliable hands in the middle of the field, and Ward took advantage of it throughout the contest.
As for TE Daniel Bellinger, he continues to be a valuable part of the run game while also finding his spots as a pass catcher, reeling in three catches for 36 yards.
In total, the two of them combined for 112 receiving yards on Sunday, resulting in Bellinger ( 88.2 ) and Helm ( 79.1 ) earning the team’s top two grades offensively.
OL Coach Carmen Bricillo deserves a ton of credit for the job he’s done this season. His unit entered the game already down to his third RG, and by the end of it, he was down his top two offensive linemen as well.
Both RT JC Latham and LG Peter Skoronski left the game prematurely and their status going forward is uncertain. Yet, despite the adversity, he continues to field a competent unit.
No position group on the team embodies the saying “next man up” like Bricillo’s unit. Ward was only sacked twice, albeit one of those was critical at the end of regulation.
They’ve also played a massive role in Pollard’s recent breakout, using gap schemes to help create sizable lanes for him to hit. Nonetheless, only allowing two sacks when you’re down three starters, two of which are Pro Bowl caliber, is undoubtedly still noteworthy.
A ton of credit goes to RG Atonio Mafi, LG Garret Dellinger, and OT James Hudson for holding their own against a formidable Bengals front.
And while losing Skoronski and/or Latham for any period of time is less than ideal, this group at least looks equipped to be able to handle it, should that end up being the case. In total, this group allowed a combined 16 pressures, two QB hits, and two sacks.
This unit may no longer have the household names outside of DT John Franklin-Myers,  but that didn’t stop this group from
Playing inspiring football on Sunday. DE Jacob Martin was a constant nuisance for Bengals QB Joe Burrow, recording seven pressures and three sacks before the day was done.
It wasn’t the cleanest performance as a whole, but for a group that lost their leader just a few days earlier, they more than held their own. The Titans’ DL combined for 16 of the team’s 22 pressures to go with Martin’s three sacks.
The trio of Anthony Hill Jr. (14), Cedric Gray (three), and Cody Barton (three), combined for 20 total tackles on the day. Hill, in particular, bounced back after a rough game in coverage last week, allowing just 17 yards on five targets to go along with his team-leading 14 tackles.
It’s clear that Hill is rapidly developing into a vital piece for this defense, and frequent performances like this are a big reason why.
If it weren’t for an absolutely ridiculous three interception performance by S Amani Hooker, this group would easily get an F. So, the fact that Hooker’s performance could only elevate this group to a D tells you how bad it really was.
After having solid games in back-to-back outings, CBs Cor’Dale Flott and Joshua Williams got a brutal reality check on Sunday.
The two of them gave up a combined total of 240 yards on 21 targets, most of which came against the Bengals’ star WR tandem Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.
However, it was Williams who they picked on most. Burrow produced a perfect passer rating of 158.3 when targeting the fifth-year corner, totaling an absurd 146 yards when throwing his way.
CB Alontae Taylor also got his first playing time since being benched a few weeks ago. He helped fill the void at nickel left by CB Marcus Harris’ injury, and he made his presence felt in the run game and as a blitzer.
Unfortunately, Burrow picked on Taylor in coverage,…

title: Titans' Snap Count Winners and Losers: Tony Pollard Dominates, Backfield Reserves Unseen in Week 8
full_text:
On Sunday, the Tennessee Titans lost to the Bengals in a 43-36 overtime shootout in Cincinnati. Following the loss, the Titans fall to a 1-7 record. For the second straight week, Tennessee has fallen despite possessing a two-score lead in the first quarter.
While another close loss hurts, there have been positives for the Titans that were unforeseen in the beginning of the season. It marked the Titans' highest-scoring game in five years.
Let's take a look at the winners and losers for the Titans' hotly contested matchup with Cincinnati.
Over the past two weeks, RB Tony Pollard has seen an uptick in snaps and delivered with monster performances. Against Cincinnati, Pollard rushed for 117 yards on 21 carries for two touchdowns.
In the first quarter, Pollard ripped a 41-yard rush where he broke through numerous Bengals defenders to score his first touchdown of the game. Through the first six weeks of the season, Pollard was averaging 31 snaps per game, according to Fantasy Pros .
Against the Bengals, he recorded a season-high 63 snaps. After playing 47 snaps the week prior against Cleveland, where he scored three touchdowns, he recorded more than 150 yards from scrimmage.
Prior to playing the Browns, Pollard only had one touchdown all season. Now, his total is up to six with more playing time. With the NFL trade deadline nearing on November 10, Pollard's breakout performances may lead the Titans to deal him to a contender.
After another poor performance against the Houston Texans, head coach Robert Saleh decided to bench CB Alontae Taylor against the Browns. However, Taylor redeemed himself with his best performance of the season against Cincinnati.
Ahead of the game, Saleh announced Taylor would be moved from an outside back to nickel corner, specializing in the slot.
In his new role Taylor played 51 snaps against the Bengals, and he was everywhere on the field for Tennessee. He recorded five tackles, two quarterback pressures, a tackle for loss and a forced fumble.
Taylor stepped up for the Titans' secondary, with CB Marcus Harris exiting the contest with an ankle injury.
Tennessee had high hopes for the former second-round pick, inking him to one of their most expensive contracts of the offseason with a three-year deal worth up to $58 million. Taylor may have found a good fit in a new position for the Titans moving forward.
There was real concern for the Titans' passing game heading into Cincinnati after the team announced rookie WR Carnell Tate would be out with a shoulder injury, but WR Chimere Dike stepped up with a breakout performance.
After only playing 13 snaps the week prior, Dike made the most of his 63 snaps against the Bengals. The second-year pro caught five passes for 71 yards and a touchdown, including the Titans' longest reception of 28 yards.
This season Dike has primarily served as a kick returner with limited offensive reps. In the previous two games, Dike had zero catches on a lone target.
Against the Bengals, Dike surpassed his season total of 53 receiving yards with an elevated role in Tate's absence. It was his first 70-plus receiving performance since Week 8 against the Colts last season.
For the second straight week RB Tyjae Spears and rookie RB Nick Singleton were healthy scratches. The pairing entered the season as the Titans' second- and third-string running backs, but they have completely fallen out of the rotation.
Pollard consumed 63 of 78 snaps of the Titans' backfield. The other backfield snaps went to RB Michael Carter and RB Julius Chestnut with 13 and two snaps, respectively. Carter and Chestnut only served as blocking backs; neither back received any touches.
Spears has zero touchdowns, 23 touches and 141 yards from scrimmage this season. Singleton has four carries for 12 yards and zero touchdowns, and he hasn't seen any offensive snaps since Week 4 against the Ravens.
It may take Pollard getting traded before Spears and Singleton return to action.
Isaiah is an award-winning journalist and photojournalist. A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: How Alontae Taylor Bought Himself Time With Titans After Comeback Showing in Week 8
full_text:
Entering Week 8, I tabbed CB Alontae Taylor as the next guy that the Tennessee Titans would trade. His pending move to nickel appeared clouded by fellow defender Marcus Harris, and Taylor's inability to make an impact on the outside seemed to make him an outlier.
Taylor's performance against the Cincinnati Bengals yesterday completely quieted that notion, at least for now. Not only did Harris unfortunately exit the contest with an ankle injury, but in his wake at nickel, Taylor played his best game of the season for Tennessee.
On top of forcing a pivotal fumble in the second half, Taylor finished second on the team in QB pressures, with five. The only player ahead of him was DE Jacob Martin (6), who had three sacks by himself. That's elite company, especially for a corner.
Taylor would finish the contest with five total tackles. All 47 of his snaps came at nickel. Harris' status is unclear, but regardless of how that situation pans out, Taylor more than made the case for his process to be trusted in Robert Saleh's defense.
That’s exactly why you want Alontae Taylor in the nickel. He’s an awesome blitzer and run defender.
He's facing the perfect storm to work his way back into a primary role, and Tennessee should be thrilled to take him off of potential trade boards.
After all, spending $58 million on a free agent only to bench him in Week 6 isn't something you can push under the rug. It appears that one of Tennessee's premier offseason pickups is beginning to make good on the investment that was made for him.
Taken with CB Cor'Dale Flott's own stready improvement over the past few weeks, the new faces Tennessee paid to lay down as the basis of Saleh's defense are beginning to fully look the part. Trading away Jeffery Simmons guaranteed that the defense would need a rest of some kind, but the fewer long-term assets the Titans have to move, the better.
Taylor quieting some of the noise around his play in Week 8 opens the door for more obvious moves for the Titans at the deadline. Tony Pollard, in the last year of his contract, may have played his way into some solid draft capital in the last few games.
Elsewhere on defense, S Amani Hooker and DE Jacob Martin are alluring veteran candidates whose value peaked with their own team-leading performances vs. the Bengals. Nothing has to be forced. If Taylor keeps climbing, he'll be just what Tennessee expected him to be entering this year.
That is, a starting, playmaking contributor at the center of a rebuild that's looking better by the game.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans Mill: Cam Ward's Best NFL Game Takes Trade Deadline Pressure Off Tennessee
full_text:
Going into Week 8, the November 10 trade deadline was beginning to look make-or-break for the Tennessee Titans. Little to nothing has been clicking on a consistent basis in Robert Saleh's first season, and little to nothing appeared off the table as far as the market goes.
Against the Cincinnati Bengals, the final result wasn't out of the ordinary. The Titans are 1-7 after yet another loss. However, Cam Ward having his best game as a professional throws all other worries to the wayside for a moment. Ward looked like a franchise QB.
All the sudden, who the Titans must move and the sort of capital they need to acquire in return feels slightly less important. Don't get us wrong, there are still trades Tennessee could very well make within the next eight days.
However, they're simply not as critical if Ward is playing at this level. Previously rising conversations about drafting a QB in 2027 have taken a backseat to one encouraging sentiment. That sentiment is the basis of today's Titans Mill.
If Cam Ward keeps playing like this, the Titans can keep building around him. That would mean the world to Saleh's tenure, as well as the franchise's rebuild.
In yesterday's loss to the Cincinnati Bengals, Ward threw for a career-high 304 yards, and rushed for a career-high 41. He passed 26/40 on the day, threw two touchdowns, and broke a five-game INT streak. Ward's 81.0 QBR was the second highest of any signal caller on Sunday.
The Titans' 36 points was the most the team had scored in five years. Ward made a questionable decision or two down the line (taking a sack at the end of regulation), but he looked improved in every other facet. He looked every bit of the franchise guy Tennessee drafted him to be.
In the case that the Titans had to draft or sign another QB next season, the Jeffery Simmons trade appeared to only be scratching the surface of in-season moves. Executing the football equivalent of a heart transplant right before a coach's second season is no easy feat.
Every pick is a little more important, and you have to hope the next guy doesn't disappoint in the same way. Saleh and his staff scrambling to fast track this rebuild around a different signal caller isn't off the table, but Ward could not have responded at a better time.
Now, when it comes to making deadline moves, the Titans have a defining performance from Ward in their back pocket. The pressure is temporarily off to have all the pieces together and ready by next season for a new guy.
Again, this isn't to say that Tennessee won't move pieces, or that Ward is safe. But the QB's career game removed the pressure for a full-on fire sale by November 10. It bought general manager Mike Borgonzi and Coach Saleh a little more time to see what the group they've got right now has.
The Titans may be 1-7 heading into the bye, but their trajectory is brighter right now than it has been since Week 1. Another game like this from Ward, and offseason projections may shift entirely. His pull is that serious.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Commanders Daily: Washington’s Depleted Front Has More Than Kyren Williams to Handle Against the Rams
full_text:
After missing the 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday night, Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw were both placed on injured reserve Tuesday . Reportedly, it marks the end of the season for Payne, who is dealing with a Jones fracture in his foot; Kinlaw underwent season-ending MCL surgery Tuesday, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Wednesday. It should be noted that without the starting two defensive tackles, the Commanders held the Eagles' depleted team to 91 rushing yards on 29 attempts, including 30 yards on 13 carries from Saquon Barkley, who has been dealing with back and hamstring issues, although he held no game designation against Washington. In place of Payne and Kinlaw, Tim Settle Jr. played 42 snaps (61%), and Shy Tuttle played 32 (46%), along with Byron Cowart, who played 11 (16%) after being elevated from the practice squad to the active roster. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn acknowledged the front seven's work: "I knew the run game on the defensive side was gonna be an important one, so I liked what that looked like of guys setting edges," Quinn said.
The Rams have a couple of backs that need some attention. Sunday, Blake Corum rushed for 73 yards on 11 carries, and Kyren Williams added 56 and a touchdown on 16 carries against the Chargers. Corum added 93 rushing yards the week before against the Raiders and has now scored a touchdown from scrimmage in four consecutive games.
one thing I loved is how mcvay stuck with the hot hand this entire drive, didn’t rotate in kyren at all and just let blake corum take over, whether it’s kyren, or blake… you need to ride the hot hand… pic.twitter.com/vMF4b0Zzwe
Corum can dump yards in spurts. On Sunday, he gained 55 rushing yards on five carries in the opening possession of the second half against the Chargers, including the 23-yard touchdown that gave the Rams a 17-9 lead. The Commanders' rotation will have to stay focused, as the Rams have multiple backs who need the front seven's full attention and aim to wear them down over four quarters. Corum understands what his coach needs out of him: "Our big thing here, Coach McVay always says, is stamina. And so I knew one of them was going to crack," Corum said Sunday . With Payne and Kinlaw both done for the year and Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton still in his 21-day practice window, Washington is thin up front. Cowart reverted to the practice squad Monday; his Eagles elevation doesn’t automatically make him available against the Rams. The key in this coming game, and in the weeks ahead, is the Commanders establishing a rotation that can effectively stop the run, without getting gassed in the process.
Kyren Williams's last 5 games: 74 Carries 334 Rushing Yards 5 Rushing Touchdowns Season Pace: 238 Car  |  1,164 Rush Yds  |  13 Rush TD #RamsHouse pic.twitter.com/K607x2bNc4
